sections.title: Supplement L: W. Picacho MRA -- Market Data, Phasing Model, and Concept Refinement
sections.content:
Supplement K analyzed the MRA financial incentives and site decision framework. This supplement incorporates newly available market research data to strengthen the quantitative case for the MRA location and introduces a phased development model that substantially de-risks the capital commitment. Together, Supplements K and L constitute the complete MRA opportunity analysis.
What This Supplement Adds to Supplement K
Supplement K answered: what are the MRA incentives, what does the Hub give up by leaving downtown, and what four questions should drive the site decision. This supplement answers: what does the market data actually say about demand at this specific location, how does a phased outdoor-first model change the financial risk profile, and how should the concept be positioned differently for the W. Picacho community versus downtown. These are the data gaps that remained after Supplement K.
L.1 Quantified Market Data: Who Is Actually in This Trade Area
The W. Picacho corridor serves a distinct demographic profile from downtown Las Cruces. This is not a weakness -- it is a different customer opportunity that requires a different positioning strategy. The data below is drawn from current census and traffic sources and should be used directly in Section 2 (Market Analysis) if the MRA site is selected.
Population and Growth
Metric
Figure
Source/Notes
City population (2025 estimate)
~117,000
Neilsberg; annual growth rate ~0.92%
Las Cruces metro area (MSA)
~229,000
Includes Dona Ana County; broadens the regional catchment for a destination food hall
Population growth trajectory
Projected 120,000-125,000 by late 2020s
Driven by aerospace, film, renewable energy, and AI data center sectors now entering the market
Median household income (citywide)
~$55,012
City average; W. Picacho corridor neighborhoods trend lower, toward $30,000-$40,000 -- real price sensitivity that shapes menu design
Hispanic/Latino population
~59-60% of city
Directly aligns with a culinary program leading with New Mexican and Mexican food traditions
Median age
~33.6 years
Young city; favorable for a social dining destination format
Traffic Counts: The W. Picacho Corridor Is Not a Low-Traffic Area
One concern about the W. Picacho location is whether it has adequate drive-by visibility and vehicle access compared to downtown. Traffic count data resolves this concern directly.
Location
Daily Vehicle Count
Implication
W. Picacho Ave intersections (corridor average)
~18,000-19,000 vehicles/day
Comparable to or exceeding many successful food hall locations nationally; strong drive-by visibility for a destination food venue
Downtown Main Street (comparison)
Lower -- downtown Las Cruces is a destination corridor, not a through-traffic corridor
The Hub at a W. Picacho location benefits from BOTH destination visits AND drive-by capture; downtown relies primarily on intentional visits
Motel Boulevard (corridor)
High traffic; existing commercial anchors (Walgreens, Subway, AutoZone at Picacho/Motel intersection)
Established commercial activity proves the corridor supports daily shopping trips -- natural occasion to add a food stop
Traffic Count Implication for the Business Plan
18,000-19,000 vehicles per day along W. Picacho is a stronger drive-by traffic base than most downtown Las Cruces streets. Combined with the residential density of the surrounding neighborhoods, this corridor offers a high-frequency customer base that visits for everyday occasions -- not just destination dining. A food hall that captures even 0.5% of daily pass-through traffic (90-95 vehicles converting to visitors) at $20 average spend generates $657,000/year in traffic-capture revenue alone, before any destination visits are counted.
Behavioral Evidence: Locals Already Show Up for Multi-Vendor Food
One of the strongest arguments against a food hall in a new location is the question of whether the local population will change its dining behavior. In the W. Picacho MRA trade area, the behavioral evidence says they already have:
Farmers & Crafts Market of Las Cruces, described by Visit Las Cruces as one of the top-rated farmers markets in the country, regularly draws crowds who move between multiple vendors in a shared outdoor format -- exactly the multi-vendor food experience the Hub provides in a permanent setting.
Food truck clusters operate throughout the city along Solano and Lohman, demonstrating comfort with ordering from non-traditional food service formats.
The Borderland Car Show & Food Truck Festival drew 25 food trucks and an estimated 5,000-10,000 attendees, proving that a curated, multi-vendor food event is not a foreign concept to Las Cruces residents -- it is already a proven draw when promoted.
Informal food truck park experiments in parking lots have emerged organically, showing market pull without any formal infrastructure. The Hub formalizes and upgrades what the market is already trying to create on its own.
What the Behavioral Evidence Does Not Prove
Event attendance at a festival or farmers market does not directly validate a permanent, year-round food hall at a specific address. The Borderland Car Show drew 5,000-10,000 for a single event; a permanent food hall needs 2,500-3,500 unique visitors per week sustained across 52 weeks. The behavioral evidence validates the format and the appetite -- it does not substitute for a pre-opening market survey or signed vendor LOIs as the primary demand validation tools.
Tourism Layer: The Hub as an Authentic Visitor Stop
The W. Picacho corridor's position near I-10 and in the path of visitors traveling between El Paso, White Sands, and Old Mesilla creates a tourism capture opportunity that downtown Las Cruces already exploits and the MRA location can equally access:
Tourism Data Point
Figure
Relevance to Hub
New Mexico tourism revenue
Record or near-record levels; billions in annual visitor spending
Las Cruces as second-largest NM city captures a meaningful share; Hub positioned as 'authentic taste of Las Cruces' stop
Visitor spending on food & beverage
~25% of total visitor spend
At statewide tourism revenue of $7B+, food & beverage represents $1.75B+ annually; Las Cruces's share is the relevant figure to pursue from Visit Las Cruces's data
Organ Mountains-Desert Peaks National Monument cumulative economic impact
$200M+ cumulative
Visitors to OMDP who pass through Las Cruces represent a capturable dining occasion; Hub's authentic NM culinary identity is the right product for this visitor
White Sands National Park + I-10 corridor traffic
Major through-traffic corridor
W. Picacho is directly accessible from I-10; a food hub with clear highway visibility and signage captures transit travelers in a way downtown cannot
L.2 Concept Adaptation: How the Hub's Menu and Positioning Shift for This Location
Moving from a downtown location to the W. Picacho MRA corridor is not simply a change of address. It is a repositioning of the Hub's primary customer relationship -- from NMSU students and downtown visitors to the working families and households who live within 1-3 miles of the corridor. This requires deliberate adaptation of three elements: the vendor mix, the pricing model, and the cultural framing.
Vendor Mix Adaptation
Downtown Hub Model
W. Picacho MRA Hub Model
Rationale
Hub Signature Restaurant -- owner-operated, 100% revenue, anchor slot secured without vendor recruitment students
New Mexican and Mexican concepts as permanent anchors -- 2-3 stalls leading with red/green chile, tamales, tacos al pastor, burritos
The 59-60% Hispanic population and existing food truck culture means these concepts already have built-in demand; they are not a risk -- they are the floor
Equal emphasis on all 10-13 concepts as novel discoveries
Core NM/Mexican anchors (4-5 stalls) + complementary concepts (Thai, Mediterranean, Asian Fusion) as secondary draws
Complementary concepts still expand the menu; they are framed as additions to a Mexican-food-first foundation, not replacements
Cider bar as primary beverage destination
Cider bar remains; add aguas frescas, horchata, and Latin beverage options alongside cider program
Price-accessible beverages serve the lower-income trade area; cider serves tourism and destination visitors; both coexist
$15-20 average entree price point
$9-14 average entree target for primary menu; $15-20 for specialty and cider-pairing concepts
Median HH income of $30,000-$40,000 in the immediate corridor means everyday affordability is not optional -- it is the core value proposition
The Borderland Food Hub Positioning Statement
For the W. Picacho MRA location, the Hub's positioning statement shifts from the downtown version. The following language is ready for insertion into Section 3 (Concept Overview) if the MRA site is selected:
Recommended Positioning Statement -- W. Picacho MRA Version
A year-round borderland food hub anchoring the W. Picacho corridor revitalization -- bringing together beloved New Mexican and Mexican vendors and complementary concepts in a safe, shaded, family-friendly setting with accessible price points for local residents, and an authentic one-stop taste of Las Cruces for visitors arriving from White Sands, the Organ Mountains, and I-10. Where Las Cruces families eat, gather, and celebrate food the way they always have -- just with a permanent home that's finally worthy of it.
This positioning deliberately frames the Hub as an upgrade to existing behavior rather than an imported concept. It leads with community identity, not culinary novelty. It names the MRA corridor explicitly, turning a location that investors might view as a risk into the story's central argument. And it speaks directly to the grant review criteria for NMFA, EPE, and equity-focused funders who want to see investment reaching the communities that need it most.
L.3 Phased Development Model: Prove Demand Before Committing Full Capital
The most significant new insight from this additional research is the phased development approach. The existing business plan commits to a full 8,000 sq ft indoor food hall buildout from Day 1 -- a $1.4M+ capital commitment before a single customer has visited. At the W. Picacho MRA location, a three-phase model allows the Hub to prove demand at lower capital risk before committing to the permanent enclosed structure.
Why Phasing Changes the Risk Profile
The downtown model requires full buildout because downtown rent rates ($12-18/sq ft NNN) make a partial opening economically inefficient -- you are paying for all the space from Day 1. The W. Picacho corridor's lower lease rates ($6-10/sq ft) and the availability of larger parcels near the Shoto site make a phased outdoor-first approach financially viable. Phase 1 generates revenue and market validation data before Phase 2 capital is committed. This is the model that Smallman Galley (Pittsburgh), La Marqueta (New York), and other incubator food markets used successfully.

Supplement M.1 Investor FAQ
What happens if grants are not awarded? The project does not assume grants are guaranteed. If awards are delayed or declined, the Hub shifts to Plan B or Plan C: smaller phased launch, proof events, expanded sponsor outreach, investor LOIs, revised scope, and reapplication with stronger validation.
What happens if SBA financing is declined? The Hub will evaluate CDFI/community lender options, investor-led equity, a smaller first site, food truck park operations, cider/event pad activation, and commissary partnerships before committing to full indoor buildout.
Who owns or controls the real estate? The preferred structure is site control through purchase, ground lease, or long-term lease with protections adequate for buildout investment. Final structure will depend on site selection, grant eligibility, lender requirements, and investor terms.
What security or priority do investors receive? Investor security will be negotiated with counsel and may include preferred return, milestone-based funding release, reporting rights, defined use-of-funds controls, collateral where available, or project-level equity participation.
How does the project proceed with $0 founder cash? The plan proceeds only if grants, investors, sponsorships, lender financing, vendor commitments, pre-sales, or phased-launch savings create a credible capital base. Founder contribution is operational leadership, business planning, grant pursuit, sponsor outreach, vendor development, and project execution, not personal cash.
What milestones must be met before full buildout? Minimum milestones include site control, capital stack commitments, lender or investor approval, core permits pathway, vendor LOIs, sponsor package pipeline, proof-event results, and a working capital plan sufficient for the Year 1 ramp.

sections.content:
This supplement documents the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub's alignment with two adopted city planning documents: Elevate Las Cruces (City Comprehensive Plan through 2045, adopted February 18, 2020) and the East Lohman Development Plan (subarea implementation plan, adopted September 20, 2021). Together, these documents create an explicit policy basis for the Hub that strengthens every grant application, every city partnership request, and every investor narrative. The Hub is not asking the City of Las Cruces to invent a new policy pathway. It is asking the city to fund and support a project that directly implements plans already adopted by City Council.
The Strategic Framing for Every City Meeting
Present the Hub not as a business seeking city support, but as a private implementation partner for adopted city policy. Elevate Las Cruces and the East Lohman Development Plan have already established the policy justification. The Hub delivers on it.
N.1 Elevate Las Cruces — The Comprehensive Plan Foundation
Elevate Las Cruces is the City's adopted comprehensive plan through 2045, organized around Community Prosperity, Community Livability, and Community Environment. It was produced through an 18-month public participation process including community-builder meetings, subcommittees, open houses, and three online surveys. Its findings represent the documented preferences of Las Cruces residents — and they align directly with what the Hub delivers.

Grant Application Instruction
When applying to NMFA, HFFF, EPE/MVEDA, DLCP, USDA, or any city-administered program: cite the specific Elevate Las Cruces survey scores above. Grant reviewers at the City of Las Cruces and MVEDA will recognize these as their own adopted priorities. Framing the Hub as a project that advances Ready Workforce (3.51), Economic Equity (3.47), and Entrepreneurship (3.37) simultaneously is the strongest possible alignment statement.
Growth Scenario and Land Use Policy
Elevate Las Cruces adopted a Consensus Scenario for growth through 2045 that explicitly favors centers, corridors, infill, and mixed-use nodes over isolated, auto-dependent fringe development. The plan projects 1.607 million additional square feet of retail and 1.103 million additional square feet of office growth city-wide, with downtown treated as an existing, high-priority mixed-use center — not a speculative future growth area. This means public tools and incentives are already authorized and expected to flow toward downtown projects.
For the Hub, the key policy implication is that locating downtown is the city's preferred investment geography. A downtown Hub site activates the city's highest-policy-priority center, qualifies for the Downtown TIDD, sits within or adjacent to the Downtown-Amador Proximo Qualified Opportunity Zone, and aligns with the Arts and Cultural District Plan (2018) that links cultural programming to economic growth. Allows city to invest public money in private ventures that create jobs
Primary grant mechanism for the Hub; city can contribute direct financial support tied to job creation commitments. Hub's 85–95 job creation projection is the core qualifying metric
GRIP (Gross Receipts Investment Program) -- El Paseo MRA Plan confirms: up to 50% reimbursement of GRT for infrastructure development costs; both new retail and targeted commercial businesses eligible; underutilized tool not yet in Hub's capital stack; evaluate with City Economic Development in Phase 1
Rebates a portion of local GRT for large sales-generating projects that build public infrastructure
Potential supplemental mechanism if Hub's annual GRT generation qualifies; verify current GRIP threshold requirements with City Economic Development
Commercial Retail District + Urban Character Area (Realize Las Cruces 2025 Code)
Provides land-use predictability and design controls for the downtown commercial core
Hub's downtown location automatically qualifies; design standards for pedestrian frontage, outdoor seating, and event space align with Hub's program
Infill Development Overlay / Urban Infill (Realize Las Cruces 2025 -- parking minimums eliminated in Urban Character Areas)
Reduces regulatory barriers for development on underutilized infill sites
Applicable if site is a redevelopment/adaptive reuse of existing building — which is the Hub's current concept; overlay may accelerate permitting and reduce fee exposure
N.2 East Lohman Development Plan — Implementation Lessons
The East Lohman Development Plan (adopted September 20, 2021) is a subarea implementation framework for a developing corridor in east Las Cruces. Although the Hub is positioned for downtown rather than East Lohman, this plan is strategically valuable because it shows how Las Cruces operationalizes comprehensive plan concepts at the district level — and it contains the city's clearest formal statement of market demand for food-oriented development, the city's most detailed financing tool menu, and an explicit endorsement of Sawmill Market as a development precedent.
Market Analysis Findings — Direct Evidence for Hub Viability
Finding
Source
Hub Application
Neighborhood-scale retail and restaurants are the strongest commercial opportunity in Las Cruces' growth areas, supported by household growth and daytime activity
East Lohman market analysis (RCLCO)
The strongest city-endorsed market analysis confirms the Hub's food-service format is exactly what Las Cruces needs more of — validated by the city's own hired consultants, not just the founder
Large-format retail is increasingly disrupted by e-commerce; smaller-scale food and service uses are identified as more resilient
East Lohman market analysis
Hub's small-stall, multi-concept format is structurally more resilient than traditional restaurant or retail formats — a point now backed by the city's own market analysis
~80% of East Lohman vision survey respondents wanted more neighborhood-scale cafes, restaurants, and small retail
Community engagement data
Even in a growth corridor 5+ miles from downtown, 80% demand for food gathering spaces. Downtown demand — with higher foot traffic, cultural programming, and tourism — is demonstrably stronger
Neighborhood retail at 30,000–50,000 sq ft is supportable through 2030; the Hub at 8,000 sq ft is well within viable scale
East Lohman market analysis (RCLCO)
Hub's 8,000 sq ft is the most market-appropriate scale for Las Cruces — large enough for a destination, small enough to fill and operate efficiently
Sawmill Market — The City's Own Cited Precedent
The East Lohman plan explicitly reviews Sawmill Community Land Trust and Sawmill Market (Albuquerque) as a development precedent. It notes that the Sawmill Market food hall emerged from phased mixed-use investment and that subsidized housing and affordability-oriented development did not harm commercial viability, market-rate demand, or private investment in trendy retail and restaurant space. The plan specifically states: the food hall attracted private investment that followed, rather than preceded, mixed-income neighborhood building.
The Grant Application Implication
The Las Cruces City Council has already endorsed Sawmill Market as a positive precedent in an adopted planning document. When the Hub presents Sawmill Market as comparable market analysis and validation in Section 9 of the business plan — or in grant applications to the City of Las Cruces — it is citing the city's own adopted planning documents back to city staff. That is a far stronger position than citing an outside case study.
Financing Tools Identified in the East Lohman Plan
The East Lohman plan identifies a broader menu of financing tools than the Hub's capital stack currently references. These were endorsed by City Council as appropriate mechanisms for catalytic mixed-use projects:
Tool
Relevance to Hub
Recommended Action
TIDD (Tax Increment Development District)
Already in Hub capital stack; East Lohman plan confirms it as standard tool for catalytic projects
Confirm with City Economic Development that downtown TIDD increment is available for Hub's block; request TIDD-funded public improvements (sidewalk, lighting, streetscape) concurrent with Hub buildout
LEDA (Local Economic Development Act)
Primary grant mechanism; city invests in private ventures creating jobs
Core application: $100,000–$200,000 target based on 85–95 job creation; cite Elevate Las Cruces survey scores for Economic Equity (3.47) and Entrepreneurship (3.37) in application narrative
QOZ (Qualified Opportunity Zone)
Downtown-Amador Proximo QOZ may apply to Hub site
Verify site-specific QOZ eligibility with tax attorney before investor presentations; if eligible, present to investors as additional tax incentive on top of 8% preferred return and 17–20% IRR projections
GRIP (Gross Receipts Investment Program)
Rebates local GRT for large projects building public infrastructure
Evaluate once GRT projections for Year 1–2 are confirmed; if Hub generates $500K+ in GRT, may qualify for rebate that supports public realm improvements
IRB (Industrial Revenue Bonds)
Tax-exempt financing for qualifying economic development projects
Lower-probability tool for a food hall; explore with City Economic Development only if SBA 7(a) is declined — IRBs may partially substitute for debt financing at lower cost
Deferred Fee Payments and Impact Fee Reductions
East Lohman plan identifies these as practical tools to reduce upfront costs for mixed-use development
Request upfront in site lease negotiation: ask City of Las Cruces for deferred permit fees, reduced impact fees, or fee waivers as part of NMFA agreement; the plan establishes this as precedent for catalytic projects
Design Standards the Hub Should Adopt
Both planning documents describe what a successful mixed-use food destination should look like physically. The Hub should incorporate these design elements not only because they produce a better customer experience, but because they align the project with adopted city design policy — which makes permitting smoother and grant narratives stronger:
Shaded outdoor seating Elevate Las Cruces and the East Lohman plan both emphasize public gathering space with shade as a design priority in the desert climate. The Hub's outdoor seating area should include shade structures, landscape, and comfortable seating that functions as public space, not just overflow seating.
Active pedestrian frontage Both plans require commercial ground floors to present active, transparent frontages to the public right-of-way. The Hub's counter/serving window design and any storefront glazing should prioritize street presence over internal focus.
Event capacity and public programming The comprehensive plan's cultural district goals and the East Lohman neighborhood center concept both treat community events as integral to successful mixed-use places. The Hub's monthly cultural festivals and quarterly night markets directly advance this policy goal — document them as community programming commitments in permit applications and grant narratives.
Rear or screened parking Both plans prefer parking that does not dominate pedestrian frontages. Any Hub parking should be rear-located, screened, or shared with adjacent uses — not a surface lot fronting the street.
Bike access and wayfinding Downtown mobility plans include active transportation infrastructure. The Hub should provide secure bike parking and appear in downtown wayfinding signage as a cultural destination.
N.3 How to Use This Analysis in Grant Applications and City Meetings
The following table translates the two planning documents into specific talking points for each funding source the Hub is pursuing:
Funding Source / Meeting
Primary Policy Citation
Key Talking Point
City of Las Cruces Economic Development (NMFA)
Elevate Las Cruces: Economic Equity (3.47), Entrepreneurship (3.37), Ready Workforce (3.51)
'The Hub implements three of the five highest-rated community priorities in the Elevate Las Cruces survey — Economic Equity, Entrepreneurship, and Ready Workforce. Every dollar of NMFA funding supports a project your own community already told you to prioritize.'
MVEDA / EPE Economic Development Fund
Elevate Las Cruces: food/hospitality as #2 employment sector at 13.1%
'We are directly expanding Las Cruces' second-largest employment sector with 85–95 new jobs, 12+ new food businesses, and $200,000–$300,000 in annual local agriculture purchases.'
DLCP / Renovate Main Street
Elevate Las Cruces: Centers and Corridors (3.00); Downtown TIDD
'The Hub activates downtown Las Cruces as the mixed-use center the comprehensive plan already designates as the highest development priority. Our project is a direct implementation of the 2016 Downtown Master Plan goals.'
USDA LFPP / NM Dept. of Agriculture
Elevate Las Cruces: Food Security (3.05); East Lohman: neighborhood food access
'We are creating a permanent, accessible food destination in a downtown corridor while committing 20–30% of vendor sourcing to New Mexico farms and producers — directly advancing Elevate Las Cruces food security goals.'
HFFF (Healthy Food Financing Initiative)
Elevate Las Cruces: Community Health (3.32); Food Security (3.05)
'The Hub brings diverse, fresh-ingredient food options — global cuisine, Mediterranean, plant-forward — to a downtown corridor where residents currently choose between fast food and Mexican/NM restaurants. This directly addresses the food variety gap in a food-access-constrained environment.'
Investor presentations (QOZ angle)
Elevate Las Cruces: Downtown-Amador Proximo QOZ designation
'Subject to site-specific verification, this investment may qualify for Qualified Opportunity Zone treatment, allowing investors to defer and reduce capital gains taxes — an additional return mechanism on top of the 8% preferred return and 17–20% IRR projections.'
Any city permit or zoning meeting
East Lohman: Sawmill Market as city-endorsed precedent; form-based design standards
'The East Lohman Development Plan, adopted by City Council in September 2021, cites Sawmill Market as a successful precedent for food-oriented commercial investment following mixed-use neighborhood development. We are the Las Cruces implementation of that same model — exactly where city policy says to build it.'
N.4 The Policy Case in One Paragraph
For any meeting, pitch, or grant application — use this:
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub is a direct implementation of Elevate Las Cruces (adopted February 2020) and the East Lohman Development Plan (adopted September 2021). It advances the six highest-ranked community priorities in the Elevate Las Cruces implementation survey: Ready Workforce (3.51), Economic Equity (3.47), Entrepreneurship (3.37), Community Health (3.32), Diversification (3.21), and Accessible Social Spaces (3.14). It uses investment tools — NMFA, TIDD, QOZ, GRIP — already identified and endorsed by City Council in both planning documents. It locates in downtown Las Cruces, which the comprehensive plan designates as the city's highest-priority mixed-use center. And it replicates the Sawmill Market model that the East Lohman plan cites as proof that food-oriented commercial investment creates value in New Mexico communities. The City of Las Cruces does not need to take a leap of faith on this project. The policy framework for it already exists.
Sources: Elevate Las Cruces Comprehensive Plan (adopted February 18, 2020; City of Las Cruces); East Lohman Development Plan (adopted September 20, 2021; prepared by Sites Southwest, Civic Plan Studio, Gateway Planning, RCLCO, and Wilson and Company); Volume IV Community Participation (implementation survey data); Volume III Scenario Planning; Volume II Community Profile.

sections.title: Supplement O: Realize Las Cruces 2025 Zoning Code -- Site Selection Analysis
sections.content:
Realize Las Cruces is the City's new character-based zoning code, passed by City Council in February 2025 and upheld after a public petition challenge in May 2025. It is the first major overhaul of Las Cruces land use regulations since 2001 -- a 24-year gap. The new code fundamentally changes how commercial and mixed-use development is classified, where food service uses are permitted, and what parking is required. This supplement documents the direct implications for the Hub's site selection, permitting strategy, and cost structure.
How to Access the Official Zoning Data
The City of Las Cruces maintains a public ArcGIS group layer called '2025 Zoning Code (Full Context Group)' containing four layers: (1) Owner Parcel -- most current parcel data from the County Assessor; (2) Overlays -- mixed-use overlay, town centers, urban/rural character; (3) 2025 Zoning Code -- primary layer with zoning district, character, town center, and mixed-use data per parcel; (4) Zoning District Underlay -- detail for Multi-Zoned Parcels (MZP). Access at: las-cruces.maps.arcgis.com (Item ID: d8afcd53b511453e91e8b09aa8221910). Note: a public parcel vacancy map is not yet available -- contact the City's NAT (Neighborhood Action Team) directly for parcel availability information.
O.1 The New Zoning Structure -- What It Means for the Hub
The 2025 code organizes all Las Cruces parcels along two axes: Character Area (how urban or rural the location is) and Zoning District (what uses and densities are permitted). A food hall with a cider bar and commercial kitchen sits primarily in the commercial use category, but the new code creates multiple viable zoning contexts beyond the old Commercial Retail designation.
Character Area
Description
Relevance to Hub
Urban Character Area
Compact, walkable development. Includes downtown and center-city neighborhoods. Prioritizes people over cars. Parking minimums eliminated or sharply reduced.
BEST FIT for the Hub. Downtown Las Cruces is designated Urban Character. Parking minimum elimination is a material cost advantage ($5,000-$15,000 per space avoided). Food hall, restaurant, and cider bar uses supported by right in Commercial Retail and conditionally in NH-3, Mixed-Use, and Town Center overlays.
Suburban Character Area
Contemporary residential neighborhoods, commercial corridors, light industrial. Dispersed land uses but with incremental density now allowed. Parking still required but at reduced levels.
SECONDARY option. NH-3 and Commercial Retail zones within Suburban Character areas can support food hall use but with more complex parking requirements and likely farther from downtown foot traffic and tourism.
Rural Character Area
Far-periphery of city. Lower density. Not relevant to Hub.
NOT RELEVANT -- Hub requires pedestrian access, foot traffic, and event capacity that rural character areas cannot support.
O.2 Zoning Districts Where the Hub Can Operate
Under Realize Las Cruces, food hall and restaurant commercial uses are not limited to the old Commercial Retail (C) zone. The new code creates commercial opportunities in multiple zoning contexts -- expanding the viable site search significantly beyond what the previous code allowed.
Zone
What It Allows
Food Hall Viability
Hub Notes
Commercial Retail (CR)
Full commercial use by right; broadest commercial permissiveness
STRONG -- primary zone for food hall
Most straightforward permitting path; look for CR-zoned parcels in Urban Character Area downtown first
NH-3 (Neighborhood District 3)
Transitional retail, office, and housing; up to 60 units/acre in urban; blends commercial and residential
VIABLE -- food service and retail allowed; confirm specific use with City planner
Expands site search to mixed-use corridor locations; especially relevant for W. Picacho MRA sites if zoned NH-3
Mixed-Use Overlay
Overlay applied on top of base zoning; promotes horizontal and vertical mixed-use on specific corridors
VIABLE -- food hall fits the mixed-use model; overlay activates commercial permissions on otherwise residential parcels
Mixed-use overlay parcels visible in the Overlays layer of the 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS group; check specific corridors
Town Centers
Designated intersections and nodes intended to become walkable neighborhood anchors; commercial and residential mixed by design
STRONG -- Town Centers are explicitly designed for food, retail, and community gathering
Check Overlays layer in ArcGIS for Town Center designations near target sites; Town Center designation may also unlock additional NMFA and city incentive eligibility
NH-2 (Neighborhood District 2)
Horizontal and vertical mixed-use; housing + services co-located; up to 50 units/acre urban
LIMITED -- food service may be permitted as accessory or ground-floor use; verify with City planner
Not the primary target zone but may be relevant for ghost kitchen or commissary kitchen component if co-located with housing development
NH-1 (Neighborhood District 1)
Primarily residential; small daycares, workshops, and cafes legal in some contexts
UNLIKELY for full food hall; cafe or small-format use only
Not a viable zone for a full 8,000 sq ft food hall with cider bar; not a target for site search
O.3 Parking Minimum Elimination -- Cost Impact
One of the most financially significant provisions of the Realize Las Cruces code for the Hub is the elimination of auto parking minimums in Urban Character Areas. Under the old code, a food hall of 8,000 sq ft could have faced a parking requirement of 40-80 spaces (1 per 100-200 sq ft of dining area) -- at $5,000-$15,000 per surface space and $20,000-$50,000 per structured space. The 2025 code eliminates this requirement in Urban Character Areas.
Parking Cost Savings -- Urban Character Area Hub Site
If the Hub site is in a downtown Urban Character Area, parking minimums are eliminated under Realize Las Cruces. A 40-space surface lot requirement would have cost $200,000-$600,000. Elimination of this requirement directly reduces buildout cost and can free that budget for kitchen infrastructure, cider bar equipment, or working capital reserves. Confirm Urban Character designation for your specific parcel using the 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS layer before finalizing buildout cost projections.
Note: Even without a parking minimum, providing some customer parking remains a practical necessity in Las Cruces given the city's car-dependent transportation patterns. The goal is to negotiate shared parking agreements with adjacent properties or nearby public lots rather than building dedicated parking into the Hub buildout cost. The Realize Las Cruces code also allows up to 50% of any remaining parking requirements to be substituted with bicycle parking -- further reducing the surface parking footprint if any minimum remains applicable.
O.4 Multi-Zoned Parcels (MZP) -- What to Watch For
Some parcels in Las Cruces are classified as Multi-Zoned Parcels (MZP), meaning they contain multiple zoning districts. The 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS group includes a Zoning District Underlay layer specifically for these parcels, showing each zoning district within the parcel boundary. Character, mixed-use, and town center designations typically remain consistent across the parcel even if zoning districts differ.
For site due diligence: if a target parcel shows as MZP in the 2025 Zoning Code layer, review the Zoning District Underlay to confirm which zoning district covers the portion of the parcel where the Hub would be located. A parcel that is partly Commercial Retail and partly NH-2, for example, may have very different use permissions depending on where the Hub's footprint falls.
O.5 Site Search Protocol -- Using the ArcGIS Layers
The City's 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS group layer is the authoritative tool for site selection due diligence. The following protocol should be used for every candidate site before any lease negotiation or architectural planning begins:
Step
Action
ArcGIS Layer
What to Confirm
1
Check parcel character designation
Overlays layer -- Urban / Suburban / Rural character boundaries
Is it Urban Character? If yes, parking minimums are eliminated.
2
Check base zoning district

O.6 Implications for the MRA Site Option (Supplement K/L)
The West Picacho and Motel Boulevard MRA (analyzed in Supplements K and L) gains additional significance under the Realize Las Cruces code. MRAs are explicitly encouraged for redevelopment under the new code, with mixed-use corridors identified as priority locations. If the W. Picacho MRA site parcels are designated as NH-3, Mixed-Use, or Commercial Retail in the 2025 Zoning Code layer, the Hub would have clear permitting pathways without needing any rezoning. The MRA's TIDD and other incentive tools are also explicitly linked to the new code's redevelopment priorities.
Action Item -- MRA Zoning Verification
Before finalizing any site decision in the W. Picacho MRA: open the 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS layer and check the specific parcels identified in the Shoto hub area (referenced in Supplement K) for their current zoning district and character designation. The character area (Urban vs. Suburban) will determine whether parking minimums apply. The zoning district will determine the permitting pathway. Do this before any lease discussion with the MRA property owner.
Source: Realize Las Cruces character-based zoning code (passed February 2025; upheld May 2025); City of Las Cruces 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS public group layer (las-cruces.maps.arcgis.com, Item ID d8afcd53b511453e91e8b09aa8221910); Las Cruces Community Development Department (lascruces.gov/property/remodeling-and-construction/las-cruces-land-use-development-and-preservation/); KRWG reporting on Realize Las Cruces (April 2025); Reimagining Albuquerque analysis of Realize Las Cruces (May 2025).

sections.title: Supplement P: MRA Plan Analysis — West Picacho/Motel (Nov 2025) and El Paseo/S. Solano (Apr 2026)
sections.content:
Two Metropolitan Redevelopment Area plans have been adopted by the City of Las Cruces that directly affect the Hub's site strategy, grant positioning, and community mandate. The West Picacho and Motel MRA Plan (adopted November 2025; GRT increment financing approved March 2026) explicitly names a food hall, eatertainment district, and commercial kitchen as named community development priorities. The El Paseo and South Solano MRA Plan (adopted April 16, 2026) cites the Farmington, NM food hub/commercial kitchen as a successful MRA case study and calls for a business incubator along its corridors. Together, these two documents constitute the strongest available evidence that the City of Las Cruces has formally endorsed the Hub's model in two separate planning documents — before the Hub has even opened its doors.
P.1 West Picacho and Motel MRA Plan — Direct Site and Policy Alignment
The West Picacho and Motel MRA covers approximately the corridor from the BNSF Railroad tracks west along West Picacho Avenue to Valley Drive, including Motel Boulevard. It was created in March 2023 when City Council unanimously designated two MRA areas. The plan was produced by Stantec Consulting and adopted November 2025.
P.1.1 — The Food Hall and Eatertainment District Are Named in the Plan
Strategy 3.4 — Direct Quote from the Adopted MRA Plan
"Work with owner/developer to create an 'eatertainment' district in the northwest corner of the Tashiro catalyst site... Investigate potential for a commercial kitchen in the eatertainment district to complement small-scale start-ups/food trucks." Strategy 3.5 adds: "A shared commercial kitchen can help launch home businesses to food trucks to restaurants or catering." Community Big Ideas section: residents explicitly named 'a food hall' as a desired use for the Tashiro Drive vacant parcel. These are not general policy statements — they are named project recommendations in an adopted plan.
The Tashiro Mixed-Use Hub (Catalyst Site 1) is approximately 42 acres at the southeast corner of Tashiro and Valley Drives, privately owned. The plan envisions low-to-medium density housing adjacent to existing single-family blocks, with commercial/retail along Valley Drive, and an eatertainment node at the site's northwest corner — adjacent to the Field of Dreams sports facility. The plan notes the city expects to provide development incentives and active recruitment to attract desired uses.
P.1.2 — Community Survey Data Supporting Hub Demand
Survey Finding
Data
Hub Application
Restaurants as most-needed business
51.21% of 703 respondents identified restaurants as the #1 most-needed business type in the W. Picacho area
The Hub's Signature Restaurant, Mediterranean, Southern BBQ, and plant-forward concepts directly address the documented demand for food variety that the W. Picacho community currently lacks
Residents leave for services
~60% of residents regularly travel outside the area for shopping and amenities
This is the variety-seeking customer the Hub is designed for -- and the behavior the Hub stops by keeping dining dollars in the community
Support small businesses #1 funding priority
'Support small and local businesses' ranked #1 in the facilitated funding priority activity
Hub's 12+ businesses launched Year 1 and incubator pipeline directly serve this priority
Vibrancy as top community desire
Residents said they want 'local restaurants, small businesses, walkability' -- with vibrancy cited as a key theme
Hub's programming (food festivals, live music, Loteria nights, cider bar events) directly creates the vibrancy the community says it wants
Median household income $26,139
MRA median income is nearly half the citywide median ($53,987); unemployment 20.7% vs. 6.2% citywide
Hub's graduated rent ($2,000/month for incubator stalls), 70% minority entrepreneur commitment, and workforce training pipeline are ideally calibrated for this demographic -- and make the Hub a strong candidate for NMFA, HFFF, and EDA distressed-area grant categories
P.1.3 — MRA-Specific Funding Sources (W. Picacho Site)
A W. Picacho MRA site unlocks a different set of grant mechanisms than a downtown site. The following are directly applicable based on the MRA plan's own funding matrix:
Funding Source
Amount
Eligibility Basis
Action
EDA Public Works & Economic Adjustment Assistance
Up to $3,000,000 (50% of project costs)

Contact EDA Rep Ali DeMersseman (720-237-6079; ademersseman@eda.gov) in Phase 1; confirm CEDS alignment with MVEDA
Community Foundation of Southern NM -- Economic Development Retention & Revitalization Grant
Rolling; supports new business formation
New businesses and entrepreneurs; fund small businesses unable to open during pandemic period or expanding staff
Contact: (575) 521-4794 / info@cfsnm.org; rolling application; strong fit for first-time food entrepreneur incubator stall candidates
NM Destination Forward Grant
Up to $500,000; no match required
Tourism infrastructure; 'food trails or other related facilities' and 'agritourism farms, food trails' explicitly listed as eligible
Hub's cider bar + NM food entrepreneurship showcase positions as tourism infrastructure; apply through NM Tourism Department; FY2027 cycle opens spring 2026
NM Brownfield Grants (EPA)
$500K-$4M
Any brownfield site contamination assessment or cleanup; W. Picacho has industrial land history
If Tashiro or other W. Picacho target site has environmental history, pursue brownfield assessment grant before site acquisition; contact EPA Region 6: Althea Foster (214) 665-2268
MRA Facade/Storefront Improvement Program
Up to $25,000 matching (like Renovate Main Street)
MRA-designated corridor businesses; storefront improvements
Once Hub is operating in the MRA, apply for facade and signage improvement matching funds through the MRA's storefront program
P.2 El Paseo and South Solano MRA Plan — Policy Support and Funding Tools
The El Paseo and South Solano MRA Plan (adopted April 16, 2026) covers approximately 1,200 acres between downtown Las Cruces and NMSU, centered on El Paseo Road and South Solano Drive. While the Hub is not currently targeting this corridor as a primary site, the plan contains three elements of direct relevance: a food incubator case study, an explicit business incubator recommendation, and the most detailed explanation of MRA financing tools available for any Las Cruces site.
P.2.1 — Farmington Food Hub: NM MRA Precedent Now Cited by Las Cruces
The Farmington Harvest Food Hub Case Study — Cited in Las Cruces' Own MRA Plan
The El Paseo MRA plan (April 2026) includes Farmington, NM's Harvest Food Hub and Kitchen at San Juan College as a successful case study for MRA-supported food entrepreneurship infrastructure. Key details: the project provided a commercial kitchen for entrepreneurs and a local food distribution center; the City of Farmington's MRA Plan identified the need and provided support for land acquisition and funding; NMSU's Local Food, Local Places grant covered operating costs for the first five years of programming and facility needs. This is the second NM MRA planning document in Las Cruces to identify food hub/commercial kitchen infrastructure as a city-endorsed development model. The Hub's commissary kitchen component is directly aligned with this precedent.
Application to the Hub: the Farmington model used NMSU as a primary program and funding partner. The Hub's commissary kitchen, combined with NMSU's existing food entrepreneurship curriculum at the Arrowhead Center, creates the same partnership structure. The USDA Local Food, Local Places grant that funded Farmington's operations for five years is a directly applicable funding mechanism the Hub should pursue in Phase 1.
P.2.2 — Business Incubator Explicitly Called For in El Paseo MRA Plan
The El Paseo MRA plan states directly: 'There is potential for a business incubator to serve the surrounding commercial areas and support new entrepreneurs and employment support for residents looking for work in a newly revitalized area.' It also recommends 'supporting potential entrepreneurs and businesses looking to relocate or expand their operation.' While the El Paseo corridor is not the primary Hub target, this language establishes that the Hub's model is city-endorsed across multiple MRA planning documents simultaneously -- a strong multi-document policy alignment argument for NMFA and HFFF grant applications.
P.2.3 — GRIP, DreamSpring, and Additional Financing Tools
The El Paseo MRA plan provides the most detailed description of GRIP (Gross Receipts Investment Program) available in any Las Cruces planning document:
Tool
Description from El Paseo MRA Plan
Hub Application
GRIP (Gross Receipts Investment Program)
City ordinance allowing property owners who develop their property to be reimbursed up to 50% of the owner's gross receipt taxes for infrastructure development costs (water, sewer, roadway improvements). Both new retail and certain targeted commercial businesses are eligible.
Currently not in Hub's capital stack. Evaluate with City Economic Development in Phase 1 -- a Hub generating $1M+ GRT in Year 1 could see $500K+ in infrastructure cost reimbursement over time. Particularly valuable for MRA sites with infrastructure improvement needs.
DreamSpring New Mexico
Small business and micro-loans $1,000-$2,000,000; mission is 'to increase access to business credit, make loans, and provide training and support that enables entrepreneurs to realize their dreams'
Applicable for individual incubator vendors who need startup capital before signing a stall license; Hub can refer vendor pipeline candidates to DreamSpring as a pre-qualification resource
The Loan Fund
CDC/504 loans and equipment financing for non-profits and certified development companies; real estate, equipment, building renovations, operating capital
Could support Hub's commissary kitchen equipment financing as an alternative to full SBA 7(a) coverage; evaluate in Phase 1 as part of SBA fallback capital plan (Supplement C)
Downtown TIDD Case Study
TIDD established 2009; funded through GRT + property tax increment; generated more revenue than projected; Renovate Main Street program offers up to $25,000 matching grants for retail/restaurant/entertainment businesses
Confirms Renovate Main Street matching grant is an active, proven mechanism -- not just a listed tool. Apply for $25,000 facade/signage match once Hub has a downtown site under lease
P.3 Two-Site Strategy: Downtown vs. W. Picacho — Updated Comparison
The two MRA plans, read together with Supplement O (2025 Zoning Code), support a two-track site evaluation that should run simultaneously through Phase 1. The table below summarizes the updated comparison:
Factor
Downtown Site
W. Picacho MRA (Tashiro)
Advantage
Policy endorsement
Elevate Las Cruces; East Lohman Plan; Downtown TIDD case study
West Picacho MRA Plan, Strategy 3.4/3.5 -- food hall and eatertainment district named explicitly

Recommended Phase 1 Action

At the same time, continue downtown site search using the ArcGIS 2025 Zoning Code layer (Supplement O). Whichever site secures a viable term sheet first advances to Phase 2. Keeping both tracks open until Month 3 is lower risk than committing to one site before lease negotiations begin.
P.4 Grant Narrative Language — MRA Plan Citations
The following talking points, directly grounded in the two MRA plans, should be used in every grant application, city meeting, and investor presentation:
Audience
MRA-Based Talking Point
City of Las Cruces Economic Development / NMFA
'The West Picacho and Motel MRA Plan, adopted November 2025, explicitly directs the City in Strategy 3.4 to work with a developer to create an eatertainment district with food hall and commercial kitchen components at the Tashiro catalyst site. The Hub is the operator that plan is recruiting. A NMFA investment in the Hub directly implements your own adopted MRA plan.'
HFFF / Small Business Incubator grants
'The El Paseo and South Solano MRA Plan (April 2026) cites the Farmington, NM Harvest Food Hub as a successful MRA-supported food entrepreneur incubator -- and calls explicitly for a business incubator along the El Paseo/S. Solano corridor. The Hub is the Las Cruces implementation of the model your own planning documents have endorsed.'
EDA Public Works grants (W. Picacho site)
'The West Picacho MRA corridor has 20.7% unemployment -- more than three times the city average. EDA Public Works grants are designed for exactly this context. The Hub's 50-70 total jobs (direct Hub + vendor staff + indirect regional multiplier), 12+ businesses launched in Year 1, and $200-300K in annual local agriculture purchasing are the measurable economic outcomes EDA requires.'
USDA LFPP / Local Food grants
'The El Paseo MRA plan cites NMSU's Local Food, Local Places grant as the mechanism that funded the Farmington food hub's first five years of operation. The Hub's commissary kitchen, combined with NMSU's Arrowhead Center partnership, replicates this exact structure in Las Cruces.'
NM Destination Forward grant
'The W. Picacho MRA plan identifies restaurants and amenities as the most-needed businesses (51% of 703 survey respondents). The Hub's cider bar -- featuring 8-10 NM cideries -- plus the Hub Signature Restaurant, Mediterranean, and Southern BBQ concepts that have no local competition create a genuine tourism destination. The Destination Forward grant program explicitly lists food trails and food-based facilities as eligible uses.'
Sources: West Picacho and Motel Metropolitan Redevelopment Plan (City of Las Cruces Economic Development Department; Stantec Consulting; adopted November 2025; GRT increment financing approved March 2026); El Paseo and South Solano Metropolitan Redevelopment Area Plan (prepared June 30, 2025; adopted April 16, 2026); Community survey data from W. Picacho MRA engagement process (703 respondents); Farmington, NM Harvest Food Hub case study as cited in El Paseo MRA Plan.

sections.content:
West Picacho and Motel MRA (April 2026) + El Paseo and South Solano MRA (June 2025)
Las Cruces has three active Metropolitan Redevelopment Areas. Two of the three MRA plans have been finalized and contain direct, explicit references to food halls, commercial kitchens, food entrepreneurship incubators, and 'eatertainment districts' as priority redevelopment goals. This supplement documents what those plans say, how they affect site selection, and how the Hub can position itself as an implementation partner for the MRA program -- unlocking additional funding, political support, and City Economic Development partnership.
P.1 West Picacho and Motel MRA -- Plan Summary and Hub Relevance
Prepared by Stantec Consulting for the City of Las Cruces Economic Development Department. Adopted April 2026. Covers the West Picacho Avenue / Motel Boulevard corridor, west of downtown. Study area population: 4,136 residents (3.6% of city total).

Where the Plan Explicitly Names Food Halls and Commercial Kitchens
This is the most significant finding from the W. Picacho MRA plan. The community engagement process and the professional planning team's recommendations both explicitly name food halls and commercial kitchens as priority uses. These are not interpretations -- they are direct quotes from the adopted plan.
Plan Section
Direct Quote / Finding
Hub Application
Community Big Ideas (p.22) -- public engagement map exercise
'Converting existing motels into temporary or permanent housing. Activating the vacant parcel on Tashiro Drive as a recreation or multi-use space, potentially including: Housing, Restaurants, A food hall'
A food hall is explicitly named by the community as a desired use for the Tashiro Drive catalyst site. This is resident-driven validation, not consultant speculation -- 703 survey respondents shaped this output
Strategy 3.4: Cultivate New Entrepreneurship (p.47)
'Promote cultural and food-based retail clusters. Work with owner/developer to create an eatertainment district in the northwest corner of the Tashiro catalyst site. Investigate potential for a commercial kitchen in the eatertainment district to complement small-scale start-ups/food trucks'
The plan recommends exactly what the Hub delivers: food-based retail cluster + eatertainment + commercial kitchen. Strategy 3.4 is the plan's entrepreneurship strategy; the Hub is the private-sector implementation of it
Strategy 3.5: Workforce Training (p.47)
'Workforce training should align with corridor opportunities such as food service, retail management, building trades, and film support services so residents can secure quality jobs nearby'
Hub's NMSU/DACC workforce partnership + 10-15 apprenticeships/year directly implements Strategy 3.5. The plan names food service as the #1 workforce training category
Catalyst Site #1: Tashiro Mixed-Use Hub (p.58-59)
'An additional small retail/dining node at the site's northwestern corner is envisioned as an eatertainment area, intended to capitalize on proximity to the Field of Dreams and offer both permanent and food-truck type options within walking distance of that facility'
The Tashiro site (~42 acres, private owner) is the plan's primary catalyst. The Hub's food hall + food truck integration model exactly matches the eatertainment node concept envisioned for this site
Public Survey Top Amenity Needs (p.25)
'Most needed businesses: grocery stores (61%), restaurants (51.21%), retail stores (31.29%), alongside medical services, entertainment, and coffee shops'
51% of 703 survey respondents named restaurants as one of the top unmet needs in the MRA -- the highest food-related demand figure in any Las Cruces planning document reviewed
Strategic Implication
The W. Picacho and Motel MRA Plan is the single most powerful planning document endorsement the Hub has. The community asked for a food hall by name. The City's planning consultants recommended an eatertainment district with a commercial kitchen by name. A private-sector operator (the Hub) delivering exactly what the MRA plan calls for is the strongest possible positioning for NMFA grants, City Economic Development support, and MRA bond financing. Use this in every city meeting.
MRA Implementation Tools Available to the Hub
Because the Hub would implement explicit MRA plan strategies, it may be eligible for MRA-specific implementation funding and partnership mechanisms that are not available to a generic downtown project.
Tool
How MRA Enables It
Recommended Action for Hub
MRA Public-Private Partnership (P3)
MRA designation creates a state anti-donation clause exemption, allowing the City to directly partner with private entities on redevelopment projects. The El Paseo/S. Solano MRA plan explicitly cites Farmington NM's Harvest Food Hub as a P3 precedent for exactly this use case
Frame the Hub as a P3 implementation of MRA Strategy 3.4 (eatertainment district + commercial kitchen). Contact City Economic Development MRA team (Elizabeth Teeters / Celina Morales, 575-541-2425) in Phase 1 for a P3 scoping discussion
MRA Bond Financing
MRA plans may issue bonds backed by tax increment revenues (GRT + property tax) from within the MRA boundary to fund catalytic infrastructure projects
If Hub is sited in the W. Picacho MRA boundary, ask City MRA team whether MRA bond financing can be used for shared infrastructure (grease interceptor, utilities, parking). This could offset $50K-$150K of buildout cost
Tax Increment Development District (TIDD)
Both MRA plans discuss TIDD as a primary implementation tool. W. Picacho MRA recommends 'Tax Increment Financing within the MRA to support catalytic projects' (Strategy 4.4)
Hub's GRT generation contributes to TIDD increment. Request that MRA TIDD-funded public improvements (streetscape, lighting, pedestrian crossings) be coordinated with Hub's opening timeline -- this is listed as a near-term action in the MRA plan
Vacant Property Acquisition and Land Bank
Both MRA plans recommend a land bank of vacant parcels, with the City acquiring and holding underutilized sites for mission-aligned redevelopment
If target site is a vacant MRA parcel, City may be willing to sell below market, lease at reduced rate, or donate land to catalytic project. W. Picacho MRA explicitly recommends this mechanism for incubator-type uses
Facade and Storefront Improvement Grants
W. Picacho MRA Strategy 3.3 recommends a Facade Improvement Grant Program for businesses along West Picacho Avenue, including signage, lighting, accessibility, and storefront transparency
Hub vendors may qualify for Facade Improvement Grants for their individual stalls after opening. Include this in vendor onboarding as a Year 1 benefit -- reduces vendor buildout cost and increases Hub's competitive advantage over standalone locations
Brownfield Grants
W. Picacho MRA Strategy 3.1 recommends pursuing brownfield grants for property assessment and planning on key redevelopment sites
If Hub site has any legacy contamination (former motel, auto repair, industrial use), City MRA team can pursue brownfield assessment grant on Hub's behalf as part of the MRA implementation -- may cover Phase I/II environmental costs
P.2 El Paseo and South Solano MRA -- Plan Summary and Hub Relevance
Prepared for the City of Las Cruces. Adopted June 2025. Covers the El Paseo Road / South Solano Drive corridor, south of downtown toward NMSU. The MRA area is described as 'primarily identified as Urban Neighborhood' in the Elevate Las Cruces Future Development Map, with Mixed-Use Corridor Overlay designations on El Paseo Rd. and S. Solano Dr.
Key Demographics and Market Findings (RCLCO Analysis)
Finding
Data Point
Hub Relevance
Age profile
37% of MRA households are under age 35; largest growth segment is 35-44; significant NMSU student presence
Younger than city average -- highest propensity for diverse food spending. Hub Signature, ramen, Mediterranean, craft cider are high-appeal categories for this demographic
Income
Nearly 50% of households earn under $25,000; only 22% earn over $50,000 (vs. ~50% citywide)
Validates Hub's accessible price point strategy ($12-$20/entree). Lower-price Hub Signature and Mexican Street Food concepts will outperform premium concepts in this market segment
Retail gap -- Food and Beverage
RCLCO found that Food & Beverage establishments are underrepresented in the MRA relative to the county (lower establishment multiplier AND lower visitation multiplier)
Independent confirmation from city-hired market consultants that Las Cruces has a documented Food & Beverage supply gap. The Hub fills it. Use this in NMFA and HFFF grant applications.
Commercial retail demand
RCLCO projects 23,000-26,000 sq ft of new neighborhood retail demand by 2040 in the MRA alone (base case); 56,000-62,000 sq ft upside
Hub's 8,000 sq ft is well within the supportable range for Las Cruces. MRA's hired consultants validated commercial scale
Community priority: business incubator
'There is potential for a business incubator to serve the surrounding commercial areas and support new entrepreneurs' (p.127)
El Paseo MRA plan independently confirms that a business incubator is an identified community need -- matching the W. Picacho MRA's Strategy 3.4. Two separate MRA plans, two separate consultant teams, same recommendation.
P3 case study: Farmington Food Hub
El Paseo plan presents the Harvest Food Hub and Kitchen at San Juan College (Farmington, NM) as a P3 precedent -- a commercial kitchen for food entrepreneurs created through MRA Public-Private Partnership
Direct precedent for the Hub's model in a New Mexico MRA context. The El Paseo plan endorses this exact format as a successful implementation strategy for Las Cruces
Farmington MRA Food Hub Precedent
The El Paseo/S. Solano MRA plan (June 2025) presents the Harvest Food Hub and Kitchen at San Juan College (Farmington, NM) as a P3 case study. The plan notes that the MRA designation enabled the City of Farmington to partner with San Juan College and NMSU to create a commercial kitchen for food entrepreneurs. Key factors in success per the plan: MRA Plan identified the project location specifically; planning process demonstrated feasibility; NMSU LFPP grant funding covered 5 years of operating costs. Las Cruces has the same tools. The Hub should request the same P3 framework from the City.
P.3 Site Selection Implications -- Downtown vs. MRA
The two MRA plans create a meaningful choice for Hub site selection. The analysis below documents the tradeoffs between a downtown site and an MRA site.
Factor
Downtown Las Cruces
W. Picacho MRA Site
Policy endorsement
East Lohman Plan, Elevate Las Cruces, 2016 Downtown Master Plan, Arts and Cultural District Plan -- all support downtown food hall
W. Picacho MRA Plan (April 2026) explicitly names food hall + eatertainment + commercial kitchen at Tashiro Site. STRONGEST policy endorsement available.
Grant eligibility
NMFA, TIDD, QOZ, DLCP Renovate Main Street, HFFF -- all accessible. DLCP grant requires downtown location.
NMFA, TIDD, MRA bonds, P3 partnership, brownfield grants, Facade Improvement Grants. Loses DLCP Renovate Main Street. Gains MRA-specific tools.
Foot traffic (Day 1)
Higher -- established downtown pedestrian activity, tourism, government workers, events
Lower at launch; developing corridor. Requires stronger active marketing and event programming to build initial traffic
Parking
Urban Character Area -- parking minimums eliminated under Realize LC 2025 code. Shared parking available.
Suburban Character Area -- parking minimums still apply. Surface parking required. Additional buildout cost.
Site availability
No public vacancy map yet; contact NAT team. Competition from other downtown development activity.
Tashiro Drive site (~42 acres, private owner) explicitly identified in MRA plan as priority for food hall use. Largest undeveloped site in the MRA.
Demographics served
Broader city/regional/tourist mix. Higher income segments (young professionals, regional visitors).
Directly serves underserved community: median HH income $26,139, unemployment 20.7%. Stronger equity and workforce development grant narrative.
Risk profile
Lower -- established foot traffic, proven demand, tourism infrastructure
Higher at launch -- requires corridor investment to build; dependent on MRA implementation timeline and city infrastructure investment
DLCP alignment
Strong -- DLCP Renovate Main Street matching grant requires downtown location
Not eligible for DLCP grant. However, MRA Economic Development Department is the direct city counterpart.
Recommendation
The business plan currently targets downtown Las Cruces as the primary site, with the W. Picacho MRA as a secondary option. This remains the right priority order -- downtown has lower risk and stronger foot traffic for Day 1 operations. However, if a downtown site cannot be secured within Phase 1 (Months 1-3), the W. Picacho MRA Tashiro site should be immediately elevated to primary because it has the strongest policy endorsement of any site option and the most direct City partnership pathway.
P.4 MRA Contacts and Recommended Actions
Action
Contact / Resource
What to Say
Contact City MRA Team -- Month 1
Elizabeth Teeters, Celina Morales -- City of Las Cruces Economic Development Department. 575-541-2425 / economicdev@las-cruces.org
'The W. Picacho MRA Plan recommends an eatertainment district with a commercial kitchen at the Tashiro Drive site (Strategy 3.4). We are the private-sector operator for exactly that concept. We want to explore a P3 partnership under the MRA designation to implement your plan's recommendations.'
Request P3 Scoping Meeting -- Month 1
City Economic Development + City Attorney (re: anti-donation clause P3 structure)
Ask City to confirm: (1) Hub qualifies as MRA P3 partner; (2) what NMFA + MRA bond financing is available; (3) whether Tashiro site owner has been contacted by the city; (4) what infrastructure investment the city plans for the corridor
Cite MRA Survey Data in All Grant Applications
W. Picacho MRA Plan (April 2026, Stantec) -- 703 survey respondents; restaurants #2 most-needed amenity (51.21%)
Every NMFA, HFFF, EPE, and USDA grant application should include: '703 MRA community survey respondents identified restaurants as the #2 most needed amenity in the W. Picacho corridor, and community participants explicitly named a food hall as a priority use for the Tashiro Drive redevelopment site in the City's April 2026 MRA plan.'
Use Farmington Food Hub Precedent
Harvest Food Hub and Kitchen, San Juan College, Farmington, NM -- cited in El Paseo MRA Plan (June 2025) as a successful P3 model
The El Paseo MRA plan, which the City adopted in June 2025, endorses the Farmington MRA Food Hub as a precedent for Las Cruces. The Hub follows the same model. This is the City's own planning document pointing to the Hub's approach as best practice.
Request MRA Technical Working Group Participation
MRA Technical Work Group -- multi-departmental steering committee established by the City
Request to present the Hub concept to the MRA Technical Working Group as a potential implementation partner for Strategy 3.4. This gets the Hub in front of all relevant city departments simultaneously and establishes it as a plan implementation partner rather than a grant applicant.
Sources: West Picacho and Motel Metropolitan Redevelopment Plan (City of Las Cruces Economic Development Department / Stantec Consulting, April 2026); El Paseo and South Solano Metropolitan Redevelopment Area Plan (prepared for City of Las Cruces, June 2025, RCLCO market analysis); City of Las Cruces MRA Designation Resolution (March 2023).

sections.title: Appendix F: Comprehensive Financial Statements Package
sections.content:
This appendix delivers the complete three-statement financial model required by SBA 7(a) lenders, accredited investors, and every major grant program the Hub is pursuing. It extends and formalizes the monthly cash flow in Supplement A by presenting, side-by-side:
F.1 Sources and Uses of Funds (capital stack and pre-opening cost allocation)
F.2 Pro Forma Income Statement -- Years 1 through 3
F.3 Statement of Cash Flows (direct method) -- Years 1 through 3, formally classified into Operating, Investing, and Financing activities
F.4 Pro Forma Balance Sheet -- Opening Day, Year-End 1, Year-End 2, Year-End 3
F.5 Monthly Cash Flow Bridge -- Reconciliation from Supplement A to the Annual Statement of Cash Flows
F.6 Key Financial Ratios and Covenants -- Debt service coverage, current ratio, quick ratio, and SBA-required metrics
F.7 Sensitivity Walk -- How the cash flow statement moves under stress scenarios
F.8 Notes to the Financial Statements
Basis of Presentation
These statements are prepared using the accrual basis of accounting in conformity with U.S. GAAP as applied to small private operating companies. Revenue recognition follows ASC 606 (the vendor license fee and percentage rent are recognized over the service period; event revenue is recognized when the event occurs; cider bar revenue is recognized at point of sale). Depreciation uses the straight-line method over assigned useful lives (FF&E 7 years, leasehold improvements 15 years per the lease term, POS and software 3 years). All dollar amounts are rounded to the nearest $1,000 in the summary statements; the monthly model in Supplement A retains single-dollar precision.
Important Caveat for Lenders and Investors
These are pro forma statements -- forward-looking projections based on assumptions stated in Section F.8 (Notes). They are not audited financial statements of historical performance because the Hub has not yet opened. Actual results will vary. A CPA-reviewed compilation will be prepared at the end of Year 1, a CPA-reviewed compilation or review at the end of Year 2 (as required by SBA 7(a) covenants), and a full CPA audit if and when the business crosses the applicable audit thresholds for investor reporting or lender requirements.
F.1 Sources and Uses of Funds
This statement shows where opening-day capital comes from (Sources) and where every dollar goes (Uses) before the Hub serves its first customer. It is the first document every SBA 7(a) underwriter reviews and the first table in every grant application narrative.

Interpreting the Negative Cash Position in Years 1-2
A cumulative cash position of -$211,900 at the end of Year 1 and -$193,000 at the end of Year 2 does not mean the business runs out of cash. Those figures represent the cumulative cash burn below opening-day cash reserves. The $272,000 working capital reserve funded at opening (Section F.1, Uses of Funds) absorbs this burn. The Hub ends Year 2 with approximately $79,000 remaining in working capital reserves ($272,000 minus $193,000) and ends Year 3 with positive operating cash generation of $288,900. The true end-of-period cash balance equals opening reserves plus cumulative change -- which stays positive throughout. A supplemental cash-on-hand reconciliation is provided in Section F.5 of this appendix.
What This Statement Tells Lenders and Investors
Year 1 is a negative operating cash flow year -- expected and fully funded by working capital reserves. Year 2 achieves roughly break-even operating cash (zero). Covenant Risk in Years 1 and 2
Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) is the single most important SBA covenant. Year 1 and Year 2 are below 1.25x because the Hub is ramping. This is a known and expected pattern for SBA 7(a) startup loans in hospitality and retail. The standard mitigation is to negotiate a covenant holiday or stepped covenant structure in the loan agreement: no DSCR test in Year 1, 1.0x minimum in Year 2, 1.25x starting Year 3. This is requested at origination, not retroactively. Supplement C on SBA strategy already flags this as a negotiation point; this appendix quantifies exactly what is needed.

The $97K gap is planned to be covered by deferred vendor buildout contributions (vendor-paid equipment for a discount on rent in Months 4-6) and/or by establishing a $100K SBA-backed working capital line of credit at origination, drawn only if needed. Supplement C's SBA fallback plan activates if the conservative or stress scenario materializes. This appendix makes the capital gap explicit and quantified -- lenders respect this far more than a plan that claims no gap exists.
F.8 Notes to the Financial Statements
Note 1: Organization and Basis of Presentation
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub ("the Hub") will operate as a New Mexico Limited Liability Company. These pro forma statements reflect the twelve-month fiscal year beginning on the Grand Opening date (targeted October 2026, subject to Phase 1 milestone gates). The Hub is a pass-through entity for tax purposes; income tax obligations flow to members and are not recognized as a corporate-level expense. All member distributions shown in the Statement of Cash Flows represent cash distributions to members, separate from any tax distributions that may be required by the Operating Agreement.
Note 2: Revenue Recognition (ASC 606)
Vendor Stall Rent: Base license fees are recognized straight-line over the license term. Percentage rent is recognized monthly based on vendor-reported gross sales, with reconciliation at quarter-end.
Cider Bar Revenue: Point-of-sale recognition at transaction completion. COGS matched at time of sale based on weighted-average cost.
Cider Club Memberships: Prepaid annual memberships create deferred revenue at purchase and recognize ratably over the 12-month subscription term.
Commissary and Ghost Kitchen: Hourly and monthly rentals recognized in the period used; prepaid blocks create deferred revenue.
Events: Recognized on the date the event occurs. Deposits received in advance are deferred.
Grants: Recognized as contra-equity credits upon receipt per nonprofit-adjacent accounting guidance for restricted grants with performance obligations; unrestricted grants flow to revenue. The Hub's grants are primarily restricted for specific buildout or program use, so contra-equity is the dominant treatment.
Note 3: Depreciation Policy
Leasehold improvements are depreciated straight-line over 15 years, matching the initial lease term plus one renewal option. Equipment and FF&E are depreciated over 7 years using straight-line method. POS hardware and software integration work are depreciated over 3 years. Annual depreciation expense is $68,000 based on the $1.14M gross buildout and equipment base.
Note 4: Debt Structure (SBA 7(a))
The SBA 7(a) loan of $850,000 is modeled at a 10-year term, 25-year real-estate-component amortization where applicable, at an initial rate of 9.625% (Prime + 3.0%). Interest expense declines annually as the principal balance amortizes. SBA principal and interest payments are modeled as cash outflows (principal in Financing, interest in Operating, per GAAP). The loan is secured by all business assets and a personal guarantee from the member. See Supplement C for the full SBA strategy and fallback plan.
Note 5: Material Estimates and Assumptions
The key estimates driving these projections, ranked by impact:
Vendor Occupancy Ramp: 7 of 13 stalls at Month 1, reaching 13 of 13 by Month 11. Validated by five comparable food hall openings documented in Section 9. ±10 percentage points of ramp speed drives approximately ±$90,000 of Year 1 revenue.
Cider Bar Volume: $13,500 average monthly revenue at steady state, 22% COGS. Based on Las Cruces-specific beverage consumption data and comparable cider bar revenue from New Mexico cideries. ±20% volume drives ±$32,000 of Year 1 revenue.
Utility Cost: $147,000 Year 1 average. Based on deep research into El Paso Electric commercial rates and demand charges, Las Cruces Utilities water tier structure, and NM Gas therm pricing. See Supplement B. ±$25,000 of utility cost is within the conservative/base/stress range modeled.
Personnel Cost: $489,000 wages plus $107,500 loaded benefits and taxes. Based on $17-$22/hour market rate for Las Cruces food service, specific Hub headcount (GM, Marketing, Cider Bar Manager, 2 floor leads, rotating staff).
Lease Cost: $8,000/month base with 3% annual escalation. Based on Las Cruces commercial real estate market average of $35/sq ft for a ~2,700 sq ft footprint. A signed LOI will replace this assumption with a specific negotiated rate.
Note 6: Subsequent Event Disclosure
These statements are prepared as of the business plan date. Material events after preparation that should be disclosed to lenders and investors include: signing of the site LOI and lease; award or denial of any grant application; SBA 7(a) underwriting decision; vendor LOI count reaching four or more; and any material change in the capital stack. The plan will be restated and reissued upon any of these events.
Note 7: Items Not Reflected in These Statements
Several items identified in the gap analysis are not quantified here and will be added when available:
Named GM candidate salary negotiation -- budgeted at market rate $65,000-$80,000
Liquor license acquisition secondary market cost -- modeled at $25,000-$45,000 within Buildout line
Contractor-specific cost estimate -- placeholder at $580,000 leasehold, subject to actual bids
Insurance broker-quoted Las Cruces-specific premiums -- placeholder at $18,500 Year 1
Any MRA/TIDD incentive rebates the Hub may qualify for -- potential upside of $8,000-$15,000/year
Sources: Main plan Section 7 Financial Snapshot; Supplement A Month-by-Month Year 1 Cash Flow; Supplement B Utility Cost Reforecast; Supplement C SBA 7(a) Strategy; Supplement D Legal Entity and Investor Exit; Supplement I Break-Even Sensitivity Analysis.
