N.1 Local Economic Development Act (NMFA)
Official Program Summary
NOTE: NMFA was removed from this grant strategy per NM EDD guidance (David White, April 2026): NMFA is not a viable avenue for this project structure. NMFA programs are the recommended state financing alternative. NMFA (nmfa.nets to Local Governments (Municipality and/or County) to assist expanding or relocating businesses that are Qualified Entities that will stimulate economic development and produce public benefits. All NMFA grants are funded on a strictly reimbursement basis — the Hub spends money first, then submits for reimbursement after project milestones are verified.
N.1.1 Qualifying Entity Analysis
NMFA offers small-business loans, credit-enhancement programs, and sector-specific funds that are more accessible and affordable than traditional lending per NM EDD guidance. Contact NMFA at nmfa.net to walk through available prograre, syndicate, association, or other person that meets one or a combination of:
An industry for the manufacturing, processing, or assembling of agricultural or manufactured products
A commercial enterprise for storing, warehousing, distributing, or selling products of agriculture, mining, or manufactured goods
An 'Economic Base Employer' — an employer deemed eligible for in-plant training assistance by NMEDD's Job Training Incentive Program (JWIOA)
NMFA Program Fit
Does the Hub Qualify?
Analysis
Manufacturing/processing/assembling agricultural or manufactured products
Partial — arguable
The Hub's commissary kitchen and ghost kitchen bays process and package food products for distribution. The cider bar distributes New Mexico-produced cider. The incubator stalls produce food for retail sale. A careful framing of the commissary and ghost kitchen as food processing operations could qualify under this category. This is the strongest argument.
Commercial enterprise storing/warehousing/distributing products of agriculture or manufactured goods
Partial — arguable
The Hub stores, distributes, and sells food products of New Mexico agriculture (NM chile, NM-produced cider, local farm produce featured in stalls). The cider bar specifically curates and distributes NM-origin craft cider. This framing is viable but secondary.
Economic Base Employer (eligible for JWIOA)
Most likely YES
The Hub creates new, permanent, wage-paying jobs in Las Cruces that generate gross receipts taxes and produce measurable economic multiplier effects. If the Hub qualifies for WIOA (analyzed in N.3), it automatically qualifies as an Economic Base Employer for NMFA purposes. WIOA and NMFA eligibility are explicitly linked. This is the cleanest path to NMFA qualification.

N.1.3 Reimbursement Basis — What NMFA Will and Will Not Fund
Because NMFA is strictly reimbursement-based, the Hub must spend money first, then document and submit for reimbursement. This has two operational implications:
Cash Flow Timing: NMFA financing proceeds are available at or after closing based on program terms. Consult NMFA directly for disbursement schedules. What Gets Reimbursed: NMFA programs typically cover capital expenses including equipment, leasehold improvementsements, land (if applicable), and infrastructure. GRIP is offered by the City of Las Cruces. Businesses create infrastructure in exchange for up to 75% of GRT generated over the term of the planned infrastructure build-out. Eligibility requires meeting or exceeding $5,000,000 per year in sales volume after three years of operation.

GRIP: Not Applicable at Current Hub Scale
The Hub does not qualify for GRIP. The $5M annual sales minimum is approximately 3x the Hub's Year 3 revenue projection. Do not reference GRIP in grant applications — doing so signals to City reviewers that the applicant does not understand the program, which undermines credibility for the programs the Hub DOES qualify for. GRIP is noted here for completeness and to document the deliberate decision not to pursue it.
Strategic Alternative: The Hub should instead pursue GRT-adjacent benefits through the Metropolitan Redevelopment Area (MRA) TIDD mechanism (analyzed in Supplement K and Supplement L). N.4 Opportunity Zones
Official Program Summary
Opportunity Zones are an economic development tool to incentivize long-term private sector investment in low-income communities. The federal program provides: (1) temporary deferral of capital gains reinvested in a Qualified Opportunity Fund (until Dec 31, 2026 or disposition); (2) step-up in basis of 10% if held 5 years, additional 5% if held 7 years; (3) permanent exclusion from taxable income of capital gains from the sale of OZ investment if held 10+ years. Downtown Las Cruces/Amador Próximo is one of two designated Opportunity Zones in Las Cruces.
N.4.1 How Opportunity Zones Apply to the Hub
OZ Mechanism
What It Means for the Hub
Strategic Value
Qualified Opportunity Fund (QOF) investment
An investor who has capital gains from another source can roll those gains into a QOF that invests in the Hub's real estate or business improvements in the OZ
If the Hub's site is in the Downtown Las Cruces/Amador Próximo OZ, the operator can structure investor equity as a QOF investment — attracting a specific class of capital-gains investors who need OZ placements before 12/31/2026
Deferral until Dec 31, 2026 or disposition
An investor who rolls capital gains into a QOF by 12/31/2026 defers their tax bill until 12/31/2026 or until they sell their QOF interest
The Hub's October 2026 Grand Opening target puts it squarely in the final window for the federal OZ tax deferral benefit — a potential competitive advantage for attracting OZ-motivated investors now
Permanent exclusion on appreciation after 10 years
If the investor holds the QOF interest for 10+ years, ALL gains on the OZ investment itself are tax-free
For investors projecting a 10-year hold horizon in an appreciating downtown Las Cruces asset, this is a powerful wealth-building incentive on top of the Hub's projected 3x investor return
Equity investment (not grant)
OZ incentives do not provide a grant — they attract equity investors; the Hub must still offer return on investment
OZ is an investor-acquisition tool, not a capital-reduction tool. Use it to market to capital-gains investors, not as a substitute for grant funding.
N.4.2 Eligibility: Does the Hub's Site Fall in the Downtown Las Cruces OZ?
Verify OZ Boundary Before Using in Investor Materials
The Downtown Las Cruces/Amador Próximo Opportunity Zone is one of two OZ designations in Las Cruces. Before marketing the Hub as an OZ investment, the exact parcel must be confirmed within the OZ census tract boundary. The City of Las Cruces Economic Development Department and the NMEDD Opportunity Zone office (economicdev@las-cruces.org) can provide tract confirmation. A specific site address (from the pending LOI) is required to verify OZ eligibility with certainty.
N.4.3 Operational Recommendation: OZ as Investor Marketing Tool
Once site confirmation is obtained, add an 'Opportunity Zone Investment' section to the Investor Tear Sheet (Supplement M) and pitch deck. The OZ framing is particularly compelling for:
Investors with recent capital gains from real estate sales, stock liquidations, or business sales who need to deploy into a QOF before 12/31/2026
Local Las Cruces investors who want community impact + tax benefit in a single vehicle
Regional family offices or high-net-worth individuals in El Paso and Albuquerque who are actively seeking OZ placements in qualifying markets
Angel investors who want a permanent exclusion horizon on a 10-year food hall appreciation story

Correction to Existing Plan Documents
The funding strategy in Section 11 lists Renovate Main Street as providing '$25,000–$75,000.' This is incorrect. Per the official program documentation, the maximum award is $25,000. There is no pathway to $75,000 from this program. The Section 11 funding table must be revised. The Hub's total confirmed grant capacity is reduced by $50,000 from the previously stated range.

Renovate Main Street is a building improvement matching grant program to incentivize private investment in downtown and encourage economic development growth. The program provides financial reimbursement of up to $25,000 for the improvement and rehabilitation of Main Street properties intended as storefronts of retail, restaurant, and entertainment for-profit businesses.

Renovate Main Street applications are assessed primarily on the quality of the improvement documentation. Required materials typically include:

This ensures all documentation is available and the application is complete at first submission. sections.title: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
sections.content:
Q.1 Purpose of This Supplement
This supplement documents the regional tourism context that supports the Hub’s visitor demand assumptions. It draws from two primary sources: (1) the Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument Economic Impact Report (BBC Research & Consulting, August 2023), prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling; and (2) the BLM Las Cruces District Office Annual Manager’s Report for FY2024. Together, these documents establish that the Las Cruces gateway economy already receives substantial visitor traffic that generates meaningful food-and-beverage demand — and that the market’s existing programming infrastructure successfully converts visitor attention into downtown commercial activity.
Q.2 OMDPNM Economic Impact — Key Figures (2022)
The following figures are drawn from BBC Research & Consulting (2023), “A Decade of Opportunity: How the Designation of Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument is Boosting Southern New Mexico’s Economy,” using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling for Doña Ana and Luna Counties:
Total annual economic impact (2022): $35.0 million, including direct and secondary effects
Total non-local visitor spending (2022): $29.9 million within 50 miles of the Monument
Restaurant spending by non-local visitors (2022): $6.2 million (calculated from Figure 8 spending category breakdown: day visitors $257,589; overnight non-facility $441,606; overnight commercial $2,582,440; overnight non-participating $2,930,621)
Jobs supported in Doña Ana and Luna Counties (2022): 305
Tax revenues generated (2022): $1.9 million for local, county, and state governments
Total cumulative economic impact since designation (2014–2022): $234 million
Annual visitation trend: 183,900 (2012, pre-designation) → 612,781 (2022) → 613,645 (FY2024, BLM) — more than tripling and holding steady, exceeding original predictions by 51%
73% of non-local visitors cited OMDPNM as the primary reason for their visit to the Las Cruces area
Q.3 Hub Implications
The OMDPNM data establishes three facts directly relevant to the Hub’s demand case:
Visitor restaurant spending is already $6.2 million annually from monument visitors alone, before accounting for the 2.5 million total out-of-market visitors documented by Placer. This is not speculative demand — it is documented, recurring restaurant revenue from people already in the Las Cruces market who have no dedicated destination dining venue to visit.
Las Cruces responds to programmed experiences. The BLM FY2024 Manager’s Report documents 19 guided hikes, an archaeological fair, a 10th-anniversary celebration with 948 attendees, a girls’ outdoor camp, and social media reach of over half a million people. Visit Las Cruces has built “Monuments to Main Street” to channel this engagement into local business activity. The Hub’s weekly events, monthly cultural festivals, and quarterly signature events are the commercial counterpart of this proven community engagement model.
The economic multiplier is real. OMDPNM’s $29.9 million in direct non-local visitor spending generated $35.0 million in total economic impact — a 1.17x multiplier. The Hub operates at the direct-spending layer of this same economy. Every dollar captured at the Hub from monument visitors, I-10 travelers, or regional day-trippers represents new money to the Las Cruces economy, not a reallocation from an existing restaurant.
Q.4 Marketing Partnership Opportunity
The Hub should pursue a formal co-marketing relationship with Visit Las Cruces’ Monuments to Main Street (M2M) program, which already routes monument visitors into downtown businesses. Tactical actions: (1) apply for inclusion in the M2M business directory before Grand Opening; (2) propose a “Trails to Tables” promotion that pairs monument hiking events with Hub dining reservations; (3) schedule Hub cultural events during peak monument visitation periods (May anniversary, holiday weekend hikes); (4) co-brand the Hub cider bar’s NM craft cider program with the local outdoor identity — “Hike the monument, drink the cider.”

sections.title: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
sections.content:
Concept and Strategic Purpose
The Hub will include a dedicated gift shop and retail merchandising area positioned near the main exit or along the primary circulation path. Rather than a generic souvenir space, it functions as a curated retail extension of the Hub’s culinary identity — allowing guests to take home signature flavors, branded products, local pantry goods, and meal kits inspired by the vendors inside. It is treated as a formal ancillary profit center, not a side amenity.
The retail program supports the Hub's business model in four concrete ways: it diversifies revenue alongside stall license fees, commissary income, beverage sales, and event programming; it deepens guest engagement by allowing customers to continue interacting with Hub brands at home; it strengthens destination appeal for tourists and regional visitors seeking New Mexico food products and locally rooted culinary gifts; and it creates a legally managed retail incubator shelf for vendor-tested packaged products under the vendor license agreement.
Retail Product Mix — Five Categories
1. Vendor-Branded Experience Kits
The signature retail category: branded kits tied to the Hub’s core restaurant concepts that recreate a vendor’s signature flavor profile at home. Each kit includes a marinade pouch, sauce, seasoning blend, recipe card, and one or two supporting pantry items. These kits give the Hub a distinct retail identity, create strong gifting and repeat-purchase opportunities, and extend brand loyalty beyond the dining visit. Examples include a Hub Signature wings kit, a Southern BBQ dry rub set, a green chile seasoning kit, and a NM cider pairing box.
2. Vendor Washout and Graduate Alumni Products
The gift shop serves a dual incubator function. For vendors who exit the incubator before graduation, the shop provides a structured outlet for remaining branded or shelf-stable inventory, recovering value that would otherwise be lost. For successful graduates who move into independent restaurants, the shop becomes a permanent “Hub Alumni” showcase — graduates can continue selling packaged sauces, spice blends, baking mixes, and signature pantry items under a dedicated alumni designation. This reinforces the incubator’s credibility, keeps successful brands visible in the ecosystem, and allows the Hub to participate in the economic upside of its graduate brands after they leave physical stall space.
3. Local and Regional New Mexico Pantry Goods
A curated selection of NM and borderland pantry staples that align naturally with the Hub’s culinary identity and tourism profile: Hatch chile products, local hot sauces, honey, biscochito mixes, piñon coffee, prickly pear goods, and regional apple products from the Sacramento Mountains and Velarde orchards (consistent with the cider bar’s heritage storytelling). This category strengthens community positioning and creates cross-promotional opportunities with regional producers — many of whom will already be supplying the Hub’s vendor stalls.
4. Bottled Sauces, Marinades, and Spice Blends
Smaller-format, high-turn retail items — bottled sauces, spice blends, dry rubs, and marinade pouches — inspired by individual vendor concepts. Marinade-in-a-bag formats are familiar to customers, easy to merchandise near point of exit, and naturally tied to the food experiences inside the hall. These create a low-barrier impulse purchase for first-time buyers and strong repeat-purchase behavior for regulars.
5. Branded Merchandise and Kitchen Tools
A modest, carefully edited selection of practical branded merchandise: aprons, tote bags, mugs, recipe booklets, and simple cooking tools. These should not dominate the assortment but contribute to average transaction size and create additional branding opportunities for event attendees, tourists, and Cider Club members. Merchandise should carry the Hub’s branding and reflect the culinary identity — not generic promotional items.
Operating Model
The gift shop is compact, curated, and low-labor. Positioned near the main exit along the primary circulation path, it captures impulse purchases from guests who have already formed a strong flavor memory during their visit. The assortment launches deliberately limited — the most distinctive, highest-margin, and easiest-to-explain items first — and expands as vendor relationships deepen and sales data confirms winners. Branded kits and pantry items can be assembled in the Hub’s commissary or back-of-house prep space; locally sourced packaged goods are purchased wholesale from regional suppliers. Inventory is reviewed quarterly to maintain freshness, protect margins, and avoid SKU complexity.
The retail program does not cannibalize stall-level food sales because it serves different use occasions — gifting, home cooking, pantry stocking, and tourism purchases — rather than competing for the same immediate dining decision. When properly merchandised, it adds revenue without adding the labor and infrastructure burden of another full restaurant stall.
Revenue Projections
At conservative assumptions — 30% of daily visitors purchasing one gift shop item at an average of $18 — and an estimated 200 visits/day in Year 1, the gift shop generates approximately $18,000–$35,000 in gross retail revenue annually. At Year 2 volume (300 visits/day, higher tourist penetration from OMDPNM and M2M co-marketing), the program scales to $30,000–$55,000/year. At 50–65% gross margins on branded kits and pantry goods, net contribution is meaningfully positive with minimal incremental labor. These figures are included in the financial model as a discrete revenue line under “Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising.”

sections.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
sections.title: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
sections.content:
Strategic Purpose
The Hub’s Tabski POS handles the back-end of multi-vendor ordering — automated percentage-rent collection, per-stall KDS routing, and unified sales reporting. The mobile ordering platform is the consumer-facing layer on top of that infrastructure: a guest app that allows customers to browse all vendor menus, place pickup and to-go orders from multiple stalls in a single digital transaction, and manage loyalty rewards — all before or during their visit. The two systems work together. Tabski handles vendor-side operations; the app handles the guest relationship.
The platform is treated as core operating infrastructure, not a convenience feature. It materially expands the Hub’s revenue capture, improves throughput, and strengthens the long-term customer relationship in ways that a counter-only ordering model cannot replicate.
Operational Benefits
Throughput: Pre-queued digital orders reduce counter congestion during lunch rushes and weekend peaks. Vendors receive orders via KDS before guests arrive, allowing preparation to begin immediately. For a 13-stall hall with simultaneous peak demand, this meaningfully improves throughput and perceived wait time without adding staff.
Order Accuracy: Digital orders eliminate verbal miscommunication at the counter. Modifications, allergen flags, and special instructions are captured in writing and routed directly to the stall’s kitchen display screen, reducing waste and remakes.
Forecasting and Labor: Digital order history creates reliable demand data for vendors: which items sell by day, time, and weather; when to prep more; when to reduce. This data is valuable for coaching conversations during monthly P&L reviews and for optimizing labor scheduling across peak and off-peak periods.
Revenue Impact
Off-Premise Expansion: Pickup and to-go ordering captures revenue from customers who prefer not to dine in — NMSU students ordering between classes, downtown office workers on compressed lunch breaks, families with young children, and El Paso day-trippers who want to grab food before heading home on I-10. These customers represent genuine demand that a walk-up counter alone cannot efficiently serve.
Higher Average Ticket: Digital ordering naturally supports upsells, combo suggestions, and add-ons (“Add a cider flight? Add a gift shop item to your pickup?”) that counter staff cannot consistently execute during busy periods. Industry data across multi-vendor food halls consistently shows 12–18% higher average ticket on digital vs. counter orders.
Direct Revenue from Platform: A modest convenience fee on digital orders (e.g., $0.50–$1.00 per transaction) generates direct Hub revenue. At 30–50 digital orders per day in Year 1 (15–25% of estimated daily transactions), this produces $5,000–$15,000 annually — a small but incremental contribution that scales with volume.
Cross-Category Integration
The platform’s value compounds across the Hub’s other revenue streams. It can sell gift shop products (Section 5.5) for add-on or standalone retail pickup. It can manage event pre-sales and Cider Club member early access. It can push targeted promotions tied to seasonal vendor menus, new incubator launches, and OMDPNM-tied tourism campaigns (e.g., “Order ahead for your post-hike lunch”). This cross-category capability makes the app a unified customer engagement platform, not a single-function ordering utility.
Loyalty and Retention
The app creates a durable post-visit relationship through loyalty rewards, digital offers, and push notifications tied to events, seasonal menus, and new vendor launches. Unlike a walk-up customer who leaves no data, an app user creates an identifiable profile that the Hub can engage repeatedly. For a destination food hall in a smaller metro like Las Cruces, converting a first-time visitor into a regular depends on staying top of mind between visits — and a loyalty-linked app is the most cost-effective tool available for that job.
Tabski Integration Note
Tabski’s native multi-vendor architecture supports third-party app integrations and online ordering modules. Before finalizing the digital commerce vendor selection, confirm with Tabski whether their online ordering layer natively supports the Hub’s multi-vendor checkout model, or whether a third-party platform (e.g., Olo, Lunchbox, or a white-label food hall app) integrates via Tabski’s API. The commissary kitchen component uses The Food Corridor for scheduling — the mobile ordering platform applies only to the food hall vendor stalls and retail programs. Full technical evaluation is recommended in Phase 2 (Months 4–7) as part of the Tabski implementation scope. See Supplement F for the full POS comparison and cost model.

sections.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
sections.title: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
sections.content:
Q.1 Purpose of This Supplement
This supplement documents the regional tourism context that supports the Hub’s visitor demand assumptions. It draws from two primary sources: (1) the Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument Economic Impact Report (BBC Research & Consulting, August 2023), prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling; and (2) the BLM Las Cruces District Office Annual Manager’s Report for FY2024. Together, these documents establish that the Las Cruces gateway economy already receives substantial visitor traffic that generates meaningful food-and-beverage demand — and that the market’s existing programming infrastructure successfully converts visitor attention into downtown commercial activity.
Q.2 OMDPNM Economic Impact — Key Figures (2022)
The following figures are drawn from BBC Research & Consulting (2023), “A Decade of Opportunity: How the Designation of Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument is Boosting Southern New Mexico’s Economy,” using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling for Doña Ana and Luna Counties:
Total annual economic impact (2022): $35.0 million, including direct and secondary effects
Total non-local visitor spending (2022): $29.9 million within 50 miles of the Monument
Restaurant spending by non-local visitors (2022): $6.2 million (calculated from Figure 8 spending category breakdown: day visitors $257,589; overnight non-facility $441,606; overnight commercial $2,582,440; overnight non-participating $2,930,621)
Jobs supported in Doña Ana and Luna Counties (2022): 305
Tax revenues generated (2022): $1.9 million for local, county, and state governments
Total cumulative economic impact since designation (2014–2022): $234 million
Annual visitation trend: 183,900 (2012, pre-designation) → 612,781 (2022) → 613,645 (FY2024, BLM) — more than tripling and holding steady, exceeding original predictions by 51%
73% of non-local visitors cited OMDPNM as the primary reason for their visit to the Las Cruces area
Q.3 Hub Implications
The OMDPNM data establishes three facts directly relevant to the Hub’s demand case:
Visitor restaurant spending is already $6.2 million annually from monument visitors alone, before accounting for the 2.5 million total out-of-market visitors documented by Placer. This is not speculative demand — it is documented, recurring restaurant revenue from people already in the Las Cruces market who have no dedicated destination dining venue to visit.
Las Cruces responds to programmed experiences. The BLM FY2024 Manager’s Report documents 19 guided hikes, an archaeological fair, a 10th-anniversary celebration with 948 attendees, a girls’ outdoor camp, and social media reach of over half a million people. Visit Las Cruces has built “Monuments to Main Street” to channel this engagement into local business activity. The Hub’s weekly events, monthly cultural festivals, and quarterly signature events are the commercial counterpart of this proven community engagement model.
The economic multiplier is real. OMDPNM’s $29.9 million in direct non-local visitor spending generated $35.0 million in total economic impact — a 1.17x multiplier. The Hub operates at the direct-spending layer of this same economy. Every dollar captured at the Hub from monument visitors, I-10 travelers, or regional day-trippers represents new money to the Las Cruces economy, not a reallocation from an existing restaurant.
Q.4 Marketing Partnership Opportunity
The Hub should pursue a formal co-marketing relationship with Visit Las Cruces’ Monuments to Main Street (M2M) program, which already routes monument visitors into downtown businesses. Tactical actions: (1) apply for inclusion in the M2M business directory before Grand Opening; (2) propose a “Trails to Tables” promotion that pairs monument hiking events with Hub dining reservations; (3) schedule Hub cultural events during peak monument visitation periods (May anniversary, holiday weekend hikes); (4) co-brand the Hub cider bar’s NM craft cider program with the local outdoor identity — “Hike the monument, drink the cider.”
Sources: BBC Research & Consulting (August 2023), “A Decade of Opportunity: How the Designation of Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument is Boosting Southern New Mexico’s Economy,” prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce; BLM Las Cruces District Office, “2024 Annual Manager’s Report: Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument”; Placer out-of-market visitor data compiled by Visit Las Cruces, April 7, 2026.
Sources: BBC Research & Consulting (August 2023), “A Decade of Opportunity: How the Designation of Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument is Boosting Southern New Mexico’s Economy,” prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce; BLM Las Cruces District Office, “2024 Annual Manager’s Report: Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument”; Placer out-of-market visitor data compiled by Visit Las Cruces, April 7, 2026.

Food Hall Incubator Operations Playbook - Concept to Graduation
Full operating system with New Mexico compliance planning context

Program Use Guide
This playbook is for the founder, operations director, incubator director, hall manager, vendor operators, program partners, funders, lenders, and consultants. It explains how the food hall incubator recruits vendors, screens readiness, launches stalls, supports operators, manages daily hall operations, tracks performance, and graduates businesses.

New Mexico Compliance Note
This food hall incubator operations playbook is an operations and planning document, not legal advice. New Mexico Environment Department, City of Las Cruces, fire/building officials, New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department Alcoholic Beverage Control Division, New Mexico Taxation and Revenue, employment agencies, insurers, and applicable professional advisers control final requirements.
The Las Cruces Culinary Hub should treat every regulatory item below as a verification prompt. Exact permit class, plan-review scope, alcohol license pathway, packaged-food approval, zoning status, fees, timelines, and inspection requirements must be confirmed before launch and whenever the facility, menu, production method, retail channel, or event model changes.
Compliance Area
Planning Requirement
Operating Impact
NMED food permits
Confirm permit class for each food establishment, shared kitchen, food processor, mobile unit, temporary food event, and vendor stall as applicable.
Do not open or expand food operations until the permit path and inspection requirements are confirmed.
Food code / 7.6.2 NMAC
New Mexico uses state food rules that incorporate the 2017 FDA Food Code with modifications.
Maintain logs, active managerial control, food protection practices, and inspection readiness.
Food handler / CFPM
Maintain food handler cards or approved training records and Certified Food Protection Manager records where required.
Training files must be available for inspection and vendor onboarding.
Las Cruces business / zoning / building
Confirm CRS/business tax registration, city business registration, parcel zoning, building permits, fire review, and development approvals.
Site selection and buildout cannot rely on generic food-hall assumptions.
Alcohol/cider
Confirm ABC/RLD license class, server requirements, event permissions, and whether winegrower/restaurant/dispenser pathways apply.
Cider/bar service must be planned separately from food permits.
Packaged retail / gift shop
Confirm manufactured-food, labeling, storage, sales-tax, and vendor product responsibilities.
Retail shelf products require documentation, labels, inventory control, and vendor license terms.
1. Concept and Program Overview
A food hall incubator is a multi-vendor, customer-facing food business platform that combines stalls, shared infrastructure, business coaching, performance tracking, community programming, and graduation support. It is not simply a food court, and it is not only a back-of-house commissary. The operating model must balance mission and margin: vendors need a lower-risk path, while the hall needs predictable revenue, compliance, quality, and customer draw.
Model
Primary Purpose
What It Does Not Provide by Itself
Standard food hall
Curated dining destination with multiple food vendors and shared seating.
May not provide structured training, coaching, or graduation pathways.
Shared commissary
Licensed production space for caterers, packaged-food makers, trucks, or prep users.
Usually does not provide daily customer-facing retail traffic.
Food hall incubator
Customer-facing launch platform plus shared infrastructure, coaching, KPIs, and business graduation.
Requires stronger governance, vendor support, and performance management than a passive lease model.
Program Goal
Measurement
Support first-time entrepreneurs
Number admitted, trained, launched, retained, and graduated.
De-risk startup costs
Startup cost avoided versus standalone restaurant buildout.
Generate sustainable NOI
Occupancy, license revenue, percentage rent, bar/events/retail revenue, expense control.
Create community impact
Jobs, apprenticeships, minority/veteran/immigrant participation, local sourcing, public events.
Build a durable pipeline
Qualified vendor waitlist, academy graduates, alumni businesses, backfill speed.

sections.title: 1.1 New Mexico Incubator Benchmark - SVEDC
sections.content:
The South Valley Economic Development Center (SVEDC) in Albuquerque is a useful New Mexico benchmark for the Las Cruces Culinary Hub because it combines economic development, commercial kitchen access, food-business incubation, business advising, partner networks, and measurable community outcomes. SVEDC is an initiative of the Rio Grande Community Development Corporation, a 501(c)(3), and was created through a public-private partnership with Bernalillo County. Its public materials describe support for healthy economic development in the South Valley since 2005.
SVEDC's food business incubation structure is especially relevant because it separates early concept validation from later-stage incubation. Its incubation programs are described as a safe environment for new and emerging entrepreneurs, supported by experienced mentors, partner organizations, staff guidance, and facility amenities. Its two named program pathways are Semilla for early-stage entrepreneurs and Mariposa for food-industry businesses that are ready to scale with facility, equipment, and guidance support.
SVEDC Detail
Application to Las Cruces Culinary Hub
Economic development mission
Frame the Hub as both an operating business and a community economic-development platform.

Two-stage incubation model

Commercial kitchen access for product testing
Use the Hub commissary for testing, pop-ups, packaged-product pilots, and academy assignments before full vendor launch.
Mentors, partner organizations, and staff guidance
Build a formal advisor bench rather than relying only on informal founder coaching.
Business directory / local product support

3.3A SVEDC-Informed Academy Option
SVEDC's Semilla Program provides a more intensive benchmark than a short pre-incubator course. Public materials describe Semilla as a 6-month, approximately 24-week pathway built around the sequence Validate, Verify, Launch. It combines one-on-one support, online reference guides, videos, readings, practical worksheets, cohort networking, mentorship opportunities, and clear benchmarks. SVEDC states that participants either validate and launch or gain enough clarity to make a low-cost decision not to proceed.
For the Las Cruces Culinary Hub, the Food Entrepreneur Academy can operate in two tiers: an 8-12 week launch-readiness version for vendors close to stall placement, and a deeper 24-week concept-validation version for early-stage entrepreneurs who need more time before taking on food hall operating obligations.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual - Full Workflow
Full SOP framework with New Mexico compliance planning context
Prepared for founder planning, investor/lender review, operations build-out, staff onboarding, and consultant handoff.
Manual Use Guide
This manual is designed for the owner, operations director, kitchen manager, Person in Charge, vendor operators, staff trainers, consultants, lenders, and inspectors who need to understand how the kitchen will operate. It should be reviewed before design finalization, before permit submission, before staff onboarding, before soft opening, and after any major menu, equipment, ownership, or facility change.
User
How to Use This Manual
Review Cadence
Founder / Owner
Use as the operating blueprint for budget, staffing, compliance planning, and lender/investor explanation.
Monthly during buildout; quarterly after launch.
Operations Director
Translate workflows into SOPs, training plans, job descriptions, and audit checklists.
Weekly during launch; monthly after stabilization.
Kitchen Manager / PIC
Run opening/closing, food safety, prep, service, sanitation, corrective action, and inspection readiness.
Daily use; weekly log review.
Vendor Operators
Understand shared-use rules, storage, cleaning, scheduling, receiving, labeling, and compliance boundaries.
Before onboarding and each policy update.
Consultants / Designers
Validate layout, equipment, workflow, utility loads, clean/dirty flow, and compliance-file needs.
During design and plan review.
New Mexico Compliance Note
This commercial kitchen operations manual is an operations and planning document, not legal advice. New Mexico Environment Department, City of Las Cruces, fire/building officials, New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department Alcoholic Beverage Control Division, New Mexico Taxation and Revenue, employment agencies, insurers, and applicable professional advisers control final requirements.
The Las Cruces Culinary Hub should treat every regulatory item below as a verification prompt. Exact permit class, plan-review scope, alcohol license pathway, packaged-food approval, zoning status, fees, timelines, and inspection requirements must be confirmed before launch and whenever the facility, menu, production method, retail channel, or event model changes.
Compliance Area
Planning Requirement
Operating Impact
NMED food permits
Confirm permit class for each food establishment, shared kitchen, food processor, mobile unit, temporary food event, and vendor stall as applicable.
Do not open or expand food operations until the permit path and inspection requirements are confirmed.
Food code / 7.6.2 NMAC
New Mexico uses state food rules that incorporate the 2017 FDA Food Code with modifications.
Maintain logs, active managerial control, food protection practices, and inspection readiness.
Food handler / CFPM
Maintain food handler cards or approved training records and Certified Food Protection Manager records where required.
Training files must be available for inspection and vendor onboarding.
Las Cruces business / zoning / building
Confirm CRS/business tax registration, city business registration, parcel zoning, building permits, fire review, and development approvals.
Site selection and buildout cannot rely on generic food-hall assumptions.
Alcohol/cider
Confirm ABC/RLD license class, server requirements, event permissions, and whether winegrower/restaurant/dispenser pathways apply.
Cider/bar service must be planned separately from food permits.
Packaged retail / gift shop
Confirm manufactured-food, labeling, storage, sales-tax, and vendor product responsibilities.
Retail shelf products require documentation, labels, inventory control, and vendor license terms.
1. Overview and Purpose
A commercial kitchen is a licensed food-production environment designed to prepare, cook, cool, hold, package, serve, or distribute food under controlled sanitary conditions. In a shared-use kitchen, multiple operators may use the facility under assigned schedules and rules. In a restaurant-style kitchen, one operating team may support several menu lines, service periods, catering orders, retail products, and events.
The operating goals are food safety, consistency, efficiency, compliance, accountability, and scalability. Every workflow should identify the responsible person, required records, dependencies, and critical control points. The kitchen should be able to prove not only that food was produced, but that it was produced under a controlled system.
Operating Goal
Required System
Evidence
Food safety
Active managerial control, training, temperature control, separation, sanitation, corrective action.
Logs, inspection reports, training files, incident reports.
Consistency
Standard recipes, prep sheets, batch controls, portion tools, plate/package standards.
Recipe cards, batch sheets, manager line checks.
Efficiency
Logical layout, station readiness, accurate par levels, clear ticket/service flow, maintenance planning.
Prep lists, production schedules, shift notes, KPI review.
Compliance
Permit files, plan review, food handler/CFPM records, local business approvals, alcohol/retail files where applicable.
Compliance binder and digital backup.
Shared-use accountability
User agreements, storage assignments, schedules, cleaning verification, damage/incident reporting.
Vendor files, access logs, cleaning logs, chargebacks if applicable.
2. Physical Layout and Workflow
The preferred flow is receiving -> storage -> prep -> cooking -> cooling/reheating/holding -> plating/service/packaging -> dishwashing/cleaning. Layout decisions should reduce cross-traffic, backtracking, and ambiguity. Raw food, ready-to-eat food, allergens, chemicals, dirty wares, waste, and clean equipment should have clearly separated paths whenever feasible.
Zone
Purpose
Dependencies
Critical Control Points
Receiving
Accept or reject deliveries, verify supplier, condition, temperature, labels, and count.
Dock/entry access, thermometer, receiving log, purchase order.
Temperature checks, package integrity, allergen identity, rapid storage.
Dry storage
Hold shelf-stable food, disposables, smallwares, and non-food supplies.
Shelving, labels, pest control, chemical separation.
Food off floor, FIFO, allergen segregation, date/owner labels.
Cold/frozen storage
Hold TCS ingredients, proteins, dairy, produce, prepped foods, frozen goods.
Thermometers, storage map, raw/RTE hierarchy, backup plan.
Cold-holding range, covered containers, thawing control, raw below RTE.
Prep
Wash, cut, mix, portion, thaw, marinate, assemble, label, and stage mise en place.
Hand sink, prep sinks where required, sanitized tools, recipe cards.
Handwashing, surface sanitation, allergen control, time out of temperature control.
Cooking
Cook products to approved standards and recipe specifications.
Hood, fire suppression, calibrated thermometer, trained station staff.
Cooking temperatures, hot equipment safety, batch traceability.
Cooling/reheating
Safely cool cooked foods for later use and reheat for service.
Shallow pans, blast/chill capacity if used, cooling log, timer.
Time/temperature monitoring and corrective action.
Holding/service/packaging
Maintain food safety and quality until served, plated, packed, or transferred.
Hot/cold holding, expo, packaging, allergen communication.
Holding temperatures, time marking, final quality check.
Dish/cleaning
Wash, rinse, sanitize, air dry, store clean wares; clean facility.
Dish machine/3-compartment sink, chemicals, drying racks.
Sanitizer concentration, dirty-to-clean flow, chemical safety.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 2.1 Layout and Adjacency Principles
sections.content:
Receiving should connect quickly to storage without routing deliveries through active plating or customer-facing service.
Raw animal protein prep should be physically or procedurally separated from ready-to-eat prep, bakery, packaging, and allergen-sensitive work.
Clean wares should exit dishwashing into protected storage, not into the dirty dish return path.
Chemicals and maintenance supplies must be stored away from food, food-contact surfaces, single-service items, and retail products.
Shared-use kitchens need visible storage assignments, user-specific labels, and scheduling rules to prevent operators from using one another's ingredients or tools.
Allergen-sensitive production should be scheduled, tooled, labeled, and cleaned with extra control; where possible, produce allergen-sensitive batches before allergen-heavy batches.
Staff circulation should not force cooks to cross dish return, trash, or mop-sink areas while carrying finished food.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 2.2 New Mexico Shared-Kitchen Benchmark - The Kitchen Table Santa Fe
sections.content:
The Kitchen Table Santa Fe provides a practical New Mexico benchmark for shared commercial kitchen planning. Its public materials describe an accessible, affordable commercial kitchen for food entrepreneurs with 2,500 square feet of cooking and prep space, 14 rentable workstations, 24-hour/7-day access, a hot kitchen, two prep kitchens, dry storage lockers, walk-in refrigeration, walk-in freezer storage, personal lockers, dishwashing, freeze dryers, and event/pop-up dining capacity. The facility opened in May 2023 and reports 34 current members.
For the Las Cruces Culinary Hub, the useful lesson is not to copy Santa Fe pricing or site design exactly. The transferable operating model is the combination of membership onboarding, required compliance documents, flexible storage add-ons, 24/7 scheduling controls, commercial-grade equipment, on-site management, security monitoring, deep cleaning, waste/grease handling, recycling/composting, and event-space integration.
KTSF Benchmark Detail
Operational Use for Las Cruces Culinary Hub
Membership model with monthly included hours and add-on hours
Use member tiers or vendor usage plans to control access, forecast labor/utilities, and prevent informal kitchen use.
Required member agreement and security deposit
Require a signed kitchen use agreement, rules acknowledgment, and deposit before access is granted.
Food Manager certificate requirement
Keep manager-level food safety certification records in each vendor/operator file.
CRS number requirement
Require New Mexico business tax registration evidence before commercial kitchen use.
Health department food permit requirement
Do not allow public food production until the operator's permit path is confirmed.
Commercial general liability insurance with additional insured requirement
Collect certificates of insurance and additional insured language before facility access.
Local business license requirement
Require Las Cruces or applicable municipal business registration before regular operations.
24-hour access, video-monitored security, and scheduling via The Food Corridor
Use controlled access, scheduling software, and camera/security policies for shared-use accountability.
A la carte dry, refrigerated, freezer, and reach-in storage
Price and assign storage separately from kitchen time; label all storage by operator.
Event space and pop-up dining room
Design the kitchen to support classes, pop-ups, tastings, vendor showcases, and sponsor/community events.
Commercial Kitchen Equipment Planning Notes From KTSF
KTSF's published equipment list is useful as a planning reference for a shared kitchen that supports diverse operators. Relevant categories include mixers, tilting kettle, tilting skillet/braising pan, ice machines, worktop refrigeration, walk-in refrigerator, walk-in freezer, low-temperature dishwasher with pre-rinse, three-compartment and two-compartment sinks, hand sinks, stainless work tables, double convection ovens, gas ranges, charbroiler, utility carts, mop sink area, and freeze dryers.
The Hub should treat this as a benchmark equipment palette, then right-size equipment by menu mix, vendor count, production volume, utility capacity, ventilation, cleaning load, and NMED/plan-review requirements. Specialty equipment such as freeze dryers should be justified by vendor demand, retail product strategy, training value, and maintenance cost.
3. Regulatory Compliance and Food Safety
New Mexico food operations should confirm permit class, plan-review expectations, inspection requirements, food handler/manager records, and operational rules with NMED or the applicable local authority before opening. This manual uses FDA Food Code and HACCP concepts as operating standards, but New Mexico rules and local permit conditions control.
Compliance Topic
New Mexico Planning Claim
Operational Requirement
Food establishment permit
Retail food establishments and related food operations generally require NMED/local permit review under New Mexico food rules.
Confirm permit class before buildout; maintain permit and inspection records.
Food code basis

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 7.6.2.8 NMAC incorporates the 2017 FDA Food Code with New Mexico modifications.
sections.content:
Train to local requirements, not generic national assumptions.
Certified Food Protection Manager
New Mexico rules address CFPM expectations for covered establishments, subject to exceptions/agency interpretation.
At least one supervisory food-safety manager should maintain current certification before opening.
Food handler records
Food handler cards or approved training records must be maintained where required and available for inspection.
Collect records before staff or vendor users work in the kitchen.
Mobile or temporary food
Mobile units and temporary food events have separate rule considerations.
Do not use food truck/pop-up operations without confirming permit path.
Manufactured/packaged food
Packaged or processed foods may trigger manufactured-food/labeling requirements.
Gift shop products need approval, labels, records, and vendor responsibility terms.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 3.1 Active Managerial Control
sections.content:
Active managerial control means the facility anticipates food safety risks and controls them before inspection or complaint. The Person in Charge should be able to explain what hazards exist, how they are controlled, where the records are, and what corrective action occurs when a standard is missed.
Maintain current permit, inspection, training, and log records in a compliance file.
Review logs during each shift rather than filing them unread.
Train staff to stop production and notify a manager when temperatures, sanitation, illness, allergen, pest, or equipment standards fail.
Use corrective action records to show what happened, who was notified, what food was retained/discarded, and how recurrence will be prevented.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 3.2 HACCP-Style Control System
sections.content:
Principle
Implementation in This Kitchen
Hazard analysis
Evaluate biological, chemical, physical, and allergen hazards for each menu item, process, and retail product.
Critical control points
Identify receiving, cold holding, cooking, cooling, reheating, hot holding, packaging, and sanitation points where loss of control matters.
Critical limits
Use local code, approved process, validated recipe, or manufacturer instructions for time/temperature and sanitation limits.
Monitoring
Assign who checks, when they check, what tool they use, and where the result is recorded.
Corrective action
Define discard, reheat, rapid cool, relabel, stop sale, retrain, repair, or notify authority steps.
Verification
Manager reviews records, observes behavior, calibrates thermometers, and validates corrective actions.
Recordkeeping
Keep logs long enough to satisfy agency, insurance, grant, and internal quality needs.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 3.3 Employee Health, Allergen, and Inspection Readiness
sections.content:
Employee health: staff must know when symptoms, diagnoses, or exposure risks must be reported to the Person in Charge under applicable food code rules.
Allergens: menu, prep, service, and packaging systems must identify major allergens and prevent accidental cross-contact where allergen claims are made.
Thermometers: each critical station should have an accurate, clean, calibrated thermometer or assigned temperature device.
Sanitizer: sanitizer concentration must be verified with the correct test strips or device at setup and during use.
Inspection readiness: permits, CFPM/food handler records, logs, pest records, cleaning schedules, and corrective actions should be available without delay.
4. Daily Operations Workflow

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 4.1 Opening Workflow
sections.content:
Person in Charge performs facility walk-through: security, odors, pests, leaks, refrigeration alarms, standing water, utility status, and equipment condition.
Log refrigeration/freezer temperatures before food is moved or deliveries are accepted.
Set hand sinks, sanitizer stations, prep surfaces, dish machine/three-sink setup, and waste stations.
Start equipment only according to manufacturer and safety instructions; confirm hood/ventilation before heat-producing equipment is used.
Review schedule, operator bookings, prep lists, special events, allergens, maintenance notes, and expected deliveries.
Assign staff by station and identify the manager authorized to make food safety corrective decisions.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 4.2 Receiving Workflow
sections.content:
Receiver matches delivery to order guide and approved supplier list.
Inspect vehicle and packaging condition where practical; prioritize refrigerated, frozen, and hot-held items.
Measure and record temperatures for TCS items using a clean thermometer or approved method.
Reject unsafe temperature, damaged packaging, spoilage, pest evidence, unapproved substitution, missing label, or questionable product.
Label accepted goods with date received, owner/operator, use-by date where applicable, and allergen note if needed.
Move cold/frozen products immediately to assigned storage; do not allow deliveries to sit in prep aisles.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 4.3 Storage Workflow
sections.content:
Use FIFO and visible date labels; shorter shelf-life products move first even if received later.
Store raw animal products below ready-to-eat foods and separate by cooking risk hierarchy.
Keep allergen-heavy ingredients and chemicals from contaminating common prep or retail products.
Shared-use operators may use only assigned storage unless management approves temporary overflow.
Unlabeled, expired, leaking, or unassigned product is documented and discarded or quarantined under policy.

sections.title: 4.4 Prep, Cooking, Cooling, Reheating, and Holding
sections.content:
Step
Required Practice
Critical Control Point
Prep
Work from approved prep list and recipe; sanitize surfaces; label all batches.
Time out of temperature control, allergen cross-contact, tool sanitation.
Cooking
Cook to approved internal standard and recipe specification; verify with thermometer where required.
Critical cooking limit and corrective action if not met.
Cooling
Use shallow pans, small batches, ice baths, blast chillers if available, and active monitoring.
Cooling time/temperature and log completion.
Reheating
Reheat rapidly to approved standard before hot holding unless local rule/process says otherwise.
Reheat limit and time control.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 4.5 Dishwashing, Cleaning, Closing, and Manager Handoff
sections.content:
Separate dirty return from clean storage and food production; scrape and pre-rinse only in assigned areas.
Wash, rinse, sanitize, and air dry; do not towel-dry food-contact items unless approved by procedure.
Clean food-contact surfaces first, then non-food-contact surfaces, then floors, drains, trash, and mop areas.
Store retained food safely with complete labels; discard food that lacks safe time/temperature or identity control.
Manager verifies logs, trash, grease, chemicals, refrigeration, security, and next-day prep notes.
Handoff report records shortages, maintenance needs, incidents, rejected deliveries, waste, and corrective actions.

sections.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
sections.title: 6.1 Utility and Equipment Failure Response
sections.content:
Power outage: keep cold storage closed, start time tracking, protect food, and follow local authority/insurance guidance before reopening.
Refrigeration failure: move food to verified alternate cold holding, log temperatures, quarantine questionable product, call service vendor.
Hood/fire suppression issue: stop heat-producing equipment under the affected hood until safe operation is confirmed.
Water interruption: stop operations that require handwashing, warewashing, produce washing, cooking water, or sanitation until approved alternate procedures are in place.
Grease interceptor issue: stop operations contributing to overflow or backup; protect food areas and call service provider.

chunks.text:
One-Page Investor Tear Sheet
1. Executive Summary
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub is a food hall-style marketplace built for the Las Cruces resident who loves their city but has run out of choices. In a market dominated by Mexican, New Mexican, and fast food, tens of thousands of residents -- families, students, professionals, military community members, and visitors -- are actively seeking something different: global cuisine variety — Mediterranean, Southern BBQ, ramen, plant-forward cuisine, and flavors they have never had locally. The Hub is where they find it.
It combines a tightly curated mix of globally diverse food concepts -- global flavors — Mediterranean, Southern BBQ, Asian fusion, and more -- alongside New Mexican and Mexican anchors that keep the menu grounded in local culture. Add a small number of rotating incubator stalls, a shared commissary kitchen, two ghost-kitchen bays, and the region's only specialty craft cider bar -- all under one 8,000 sq ft indoor, climate-controlled roof in downtown Las Cruces.
Founder Capital and Funding Status Disclosure
Founder cash available for startup capital is $0. Project launch therefore depends on a layered funding strategy built from grants, investor equity, lender financing, sponsorships, and, if necessary, a lower-capital phased opening before full indoor buildout.
This disclosure is intentional. The plan does not assume hidden owner cash or guaranteed awards. Grants, sponsorships, and investors are treated as targeted and pending until formal commitments are received; SBA or other lender financing is positioned as strongest after equity-equivalent grants, investor commitments, vendor deposits, and sponsor-backed buildout support are documented.
Sponsor outreach has already begun with organizations that may support specific buildout packages such as the training kitchen, incubator stalls, cider/event pad, gift shop, workforce programming, and community event infrastructure.
The Core Premise

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: Supplement M
chunks.text:
Residents drive 45+ minutes to Albuquerque and El Paso for Thai, Japanese, Mediterranean, and other global cuisines completely absent locally -- documented, recurring dining dollar leakage from a 300,000–350,000+ regional draw (Doña Ana County: 219,561; Las Cruces city: ~115,000). Las Cruces attracted 2.5M out-of-market visitors in 2025 (Placer data, Visit Las Cruces April 2026), with full-service restaurant gross receipts of $178.7M (NMTR RP-80). Top visitor origins: El Paso TX, Maricopa AZ, Bernalillo NM. The adjacent Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument generated $35.0M in total economic impact in 2022 (BBC Research & Consulting), including $6.2M in restaurant spending by non-local visitors alone — a direct demand signal for destination dining in the Las Cruces gateway economy Confirmed also by the West Picacho MRA community survey (703 respondents, 2025): 51% of residents identified restaurants as the #1 most needed business type; 60% regularly leave the area for shopping and services
Zero dedicated craft cider bars in southern NM -- completely open niche with 400+ years of NM apple-growing heritage to anchor it
No structured culinary incubator in the region -- food entrepreneurs face $250,000-$500,000 barriers to entry with no lower-risk pathway
NMSU enrollment growth, downtown Las Cruces revitalization, Fort Bliss military community expansion, and an AI data center workforce influx -- all bringing more residents who have experienced diverse dining elsewhere and expect it here
Elevate Las Cruces (Feb 2020), East Lohman Development Plan (Sept 2021), W. Picacho and Motel MRA Plan (April 2026), and El Paseo/S. Solano MRA Plan (June 2025) have all established explicit policy frameworks for exactly this type of project -- the Hub is a direct implementation of four adopted city planning documents, not a request for new policy support
2. Market and Cultural Context

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: Supplement M
chunks.text:
Las Cruces and Dona Ana County have a thriving Mexican and New Mexican restaurant culture -- and a large, documented population that is hungry for something beyond it. With 15+ traditional NM restaurants competing for the same customer base, residents seeking Thai, Mediterranean, Japanese, Southern BBQ, Vietnamese, or other global cuisines have almost nowhere to go locally. They drive to Albuquerque. They order fast food out of resignation. Or they cook at home and wish they had more options. The Hub exists for them.
The Central Strategic Decision
The Hub leads with the craving for variety -- the genuine, documented frustration of living in a city where dining out too often means choosing between the same options. Residents do not need to be convinced that diverse food is worth trying. They are already driving 45 minutes to Albuquerque to get it. The Hub makes the case simple: all of it, right here, without leaving Las Cruces. New Mexican and Mexican anchors remain in the mix because they belong and they draw traffic -- but they are no longer the headline. Variety is the headline.
The primary audience for the Hub is direct to describe: Las Cruces residents who are tired of eating Mexican or New Mexican food — or fast food — as their default dining option every time they go out. This is not a rejection of local culinary heritage. It is a community that loves what it has and is hungry for more. These residents want variety, new flavors, and a genuinely exciting place to bring their families on a Friday night or a Sunday morning. They are already spending those dining dollars — in Albuquerque, in El Paso, or simply staying home. The Hub’s core job is to give them a reason to spend those dollars in Las Cruces.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 2.1 Primary Market -- Las Cruces Metro
chunks.text:
Full-service restaurant gross receipts (NAICS 722511) for Las Cruces were $190.4M in 2023, $171.8M in 2024, and $178.7M in 2025 (New Mexico Taxation and Revenue RP-80). Per-visitor-plus-resident spending on full-service restaurants calculates to $65.37 per person per year in 2023, $63.29 in 2024, and $68.32 in 2025. These figures establish a documented baseline for the Hub’s revenue assumptions: each incremental visitor or new resident dining occasion captured represents meaningful, sourced demand.
The Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument (OMDPNM), located immediately east of Las Cruces, is a direct feeder of food-and-beverage demand to the city. According to “A Decade of Opportunity” (BBC Research & Consulting, August 2023), OMDPNM generated $35.0 million in total annual economic impact in 2022 and supported 305 jobs in Doña Ana and Luna Counties. Of the $29.9 million in non-local visitor spending that year, $6.2 million went directly to restaurants. Visitation to the Monument has more than tripled since 2012 — from 183,900 visits to 612,781 in 2022 — and held at 613,645 in FY2024 (BLM Annual Manager’s Report). Of non-local visitors, 73 percent stated the Monument was the primary reason for their visit to the area, meaning the Las Cruces dining economy benefits from a substantial and growing base of visitors specifically drawn to the region — not passing through it.
Data sources: Placer (out-of-market visitor counts); NM Taxation and Revenue RP-80 (gross receipts NAICS 722511); US Census 5-Year Table S0101 (population). Compiled by Visit Las Cruces in response to a feasibility data request, April 7, 2026. Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument economic impact data: BBC Research & Consulting (2023), “A Decade of Opportunity,” prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce, using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling. BLM Annual Manager’s Report 2024.

chunks.heading: 3.3 Programming as Core Infrastructure
chunks.text:
This approach is validated by regional data. The Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument, Las Cruces’ most significant regional attractor, demonstrates that Las Cruces-area residents and visitors respond strongly to programmed experiences. The BLM Annual Manager’s Report (FY2024) documents 613,645 monument visits, 19 guided docent hikes, an archaeological fair that drew regional attendance, a week-long girls’ outdoor camp, and a 10th-anniversary celebration that drew 948 attendees to organized events with over 4,000 social media reactions reaching more than half a million people. Visit Las Cruces has leveraged monument programming through its “Monuments to Main Street” (M2M) initiative to drive visitors from monument experiences into downtown restaurants, shops, and entertainment. The Hub’s programming strategy is designed as the urban counterpart to this model: create events that give people a reason to show up, then convert that attention into dining revenue and repeat visits.
Weekly rituals and seasonal festivals are treated as operational infrastructure from Day 1 -- not amenities added once doors are open. Consistent programming is essential for customer habit-building (repeat visits), grant-funded community outcomes, and Cider Club member engagement.

4. Vendor and Incubator Model
Vendors participate through license agreements rather than traditional leases -- a structure recommended by food hall legal analysts (ArentFox Schiff, 2024) for its flexibility, faster vendor transition capability, and reduced litigation risk. Licenses give the Hub exclusive right to manage shared spaces and allows rapid transition if a concept underperforms, without the burden of formal eviction proceedings.
Smallman Galley Lesson -- Applied from Day 1
Pittsburgh's Smallman Galley incubator food hall learned the hard way: when all vendor licenses expire simultaneously, the entire cohort departs at once, creating revenue collapse and customer disorientation. The Las Cruces Hub staggers all incubator license start dates by 3-6 months from the outset. No more than one stall turns over at any given time. Combined with 7-8 permanent stalls on rolling 2+ year commitments, revenue continuity is structurally protected regardless of incubator rotation activity.

Before vendors enter an incubator stall, the Hub may operate an 8-12 week Food Entrepreneur Academy to prepare operators for customer-facing retail service. The academy gives funders a clear, measurable training pipeline and gives vendors a lower-risk path before signing a stall license.

chunks.heading: 4.7 Vendor Failure Protocol
chunks.text:
Vendor underperformance is managed as an operating risk, not as a surprise. If a vendor misses agreed standards, the Hub uses a stepwise response: coaching, documented improvement plan, menu/pricing correction, temporary shift into pop-up or ghost-kitchen format, and replacement from the waitlist if performance does not recover.
This protects the revenue base while still supporting entrepreneurs. Permanent anchors and staggered incubator start dates keep no single vendor departure from destabilizing the food hall.

5. Specialty Craft Cider Bar
The specialty craft cider bar is the Hub's most visible point of differentiation and its primary community-building engine. It fills a completely open niche in southern New Mexico by highlighting regional cider makers, New Mexico heritage apple orchards, and the 400+ year history of apple growing in Velarde, Los Ranchos, Cloudcroft, and the Sacramento Mountains.
Because cider is naturally lower-ABV than many spirits and beers, it fits well with customers who want a social drink that feels lighter, more sessionable, and more food-pairing-friendly. It also anchors the Hub's evening programming: live music, trivia, themed cultural nights, and educational tastings build naturally around the cider bar as the social gravitational center of the facility.
