chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 5.4 NM Liquor License -- Critical Path Item
chunks.heading: 5.4 NM Liquor License -- Critical Path Item
chunks.text:
The cider bar's liquor license is the most time-sensitive regulatory item in the entire project timeline. The NM Dispenser's License application process takes 30-120 days through the NM Regulation and Licensing Department's ABC Division, and requires a 30-day public notice posting on premises. This application must be initiated in Month 1 -- simultaneously with site lease execution -- or the Grand Opening timeline is at risk.
Two licensing paths exist for the cider bar. The standard route is the NM Dispenser’s License ($1,050–$1,300/year), which operates under a quota system that may require purchasing a secondary-market license ($5,000–$50,000+) if the Las Cruces quota is full. The lower-cost alternative is the NM Winegrower’s License (NMSA §60-6A-11), which costs only $25/year and permits both production and retail sale of cider under 5,000 gallons annually — bypassing the quota system entirely. The Winegrower’s path is also the appropriate federal trigger: any on-site cider production additionally requires a free TTB (Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau) Winery Permit or Brewer’s Notice, with a 60–120 day processing time at ttb.gov. If the Hub pours only pre-produced ciders from licensed NM producers with no on-site blending or production, no TTB permit is needed. The correct license class must be confirmed with a New Mexico alcohol licensing attorney before any application is filed — the two paths have different eligibility requirements and different implications for the Hub’s operating model.
Month 1 Action Required
Check Las Cruces Dispenser license quota availability at rld.nm.gov/abc immediately. If the quota is full, a secondary-market license purchase may be required ($5,000-$50,000+). Budget this contingency into the capital stack. Also obtain NM CRS Tax Registration first -- it is a prerequisite for the liquor license application.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 5.4 NM Liquor License -- Critical Path Item
chunks.heading: 5.4 NM Liquor License -- Critical Path Item
chunks.text:
ALTERNATIVE LICENSING PATH — NM Winegrower’s License (NMSA 60-6A-11): The Winegrower’s License costs $25/year and permits production AND retail sale of wine and cider under 5,000 gallons annually. This may be the correct primary license for the Hub’s cider bar if it pours producer-supplied NM ciders at retail and does not exceed the volume threshold. Confirm with NM RLD ABC whether the Hub’s specific operating model qualifies — this path avoids the Dispenser quota system entirely.
FEDERAL REQUIREMENT — TTB Permit: Any on-site cider production or blending also requires a federal Alcohol and Tobacco Tax and Trade Bureau (TTB) Brewer’s Notice or Winery Permit (ttb.gov). TTB applications are free but take 60–120 days to process. If the Hub intends any in-house production or custom blending of NM ciders, initiate the TTB application in Month 1 concurrently with the NM license application. If the Hub pours only pre-produced ciders from licensed NM producers with no on-site production, no TTB federal permit is required — only the NM retail license applies. Consult an NM alcohol licensing attorney before filing to confirm which path applies.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
chunks.text:
Concept and Strategic Purpose
The Hub will include a dedicated gift shop and retail merchandising area positioned near the main exit or along the primary circulation path. Rather than a generic souvenir space, it functions as a curated retail extension of the Hub’s culinary identity — allowing guests to take home signature flavors, branded products, local pantry goods, and meal kits inspired by the vendors inside. It is treated as a formal ancillary profit center, not a side amenity.
The retail program supports the Hub's business model in four concrete ways: it diversifies revenue alongside stall license fees, commissary income, beverage sales, and event programming; it deepens guest engagement by allowing customers to continue interacting with Hub brands at home; it strengthens destination appeal for tourists and regional visitors seeking New Mexico food products and locally rooted culinary gifts; and it creates a legally managed retail incubator shelf for vendor-tested packaged products under the vendor license agreement.
Retail Product Mix — Five Categories
1. Vendor-Branded Experience Kits
The signature retail category: branded kits tied to the Hub’s core restaurant concepts that recreate a vendor’s signature flavor profile at home. Each kit includes a marinade pouch, sauce, seasoning blend, recipe card, and one or two supporting pantry items. These kits give the Hub a distinct retail identity, create strong gifting and repeat-purchase opportunities, and extend brand loyalty beyond the dining visit. Examples include a Hub Signature wings kit, a Southern BBQ dry rub set, a green chile seasoning kit, and a NM cider pairing box.
2. Vendor Washout and Graduate Alumni Products

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
chunks.text:
The gift shop serves a dual incubator function. For vendors who exit the incubator before graduation, the shop provides a structured outlet for remaining branded or shelf-stable inventory, recovering value that would otherwise be lost. For successful graduates who move into independent restaurants, the shop becomes a permanent “Hub Alumni” showcase — graduates can continue selling packaged sauces, spice blends, baking mixes, and signature pantry items under a dedicated alumni designation. This reinforces the incubator’s credibility, keeps successful brands visible in the ecosystem, and allows the Hub to participate in the economic upside of its graduate brands after they leave physical stall space.
3. Local and Regional New Mexico Pantry Goods
A curated selection of NM and borderland pantry staples that align naturally with the Hub’s culinary identity and tourism profile: Hatch chile products, local hot sauces, honey, biscochito mixes, piñon coffee, prickly pear goods, and regional apple products from the Sacramento Mountains and Velarde orchards (consistent with the cider bar’s heritage storytelling). This category strengthens community positioning and creates cross-promotional opportunities with regional producers — many of whom will already be supplying the Hub’s vendor stalls.
4. Bottled Sauces, Marinades, and Spice Blends
Smaller-format, high-turn retail items — bottled sauces, spice blends, dry rubs, and marinade pouches — inspired by individual vendor concepts. Marinade-in-a-bag formats are familiar to customers, easy to merchandise near point of exit, and naturally tied to the food experiences inside the hall. These create a low-barrier impulse purchase for first-time buyers and strong repeat-purchase behavior for regulars.
5. Branded Merchandise and Kitchen Tools

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
chunks.text:
A modest, carefully edited selection of practical branded merchandise: aprons, tote bags, mugs, recipe booklets, and simple cooking tools. These should not dominate the assortment but contribute to average transaction size and create additional branding opportunities for event attendees, tourists, and Cider Club members. Merchandise should carry the Hub’s branding and reflect the culinary identity — not generic promotional items.
Operating Model
The gift shop is compact, curated, and low-labor. Positioned near the main exit along the primary circulation path, it captures impulse purchases from guests who have already formed a strong flavor memory during their visit. The assortment launches deliberately limited — the most distinctive, highest-margin, and easiest-to-explain items first — and expands as vendor relationships deepen and sales data confirms winners. Branded kits and pantry items can be assembled in the Hub’s commissary or back-of-house prep space; locally sourced packaged goods are purchased wholesale from regional suppliers. Inventory is reviewed quarterly to maintain freshness, protect margins, and avoid SKU complexity.
The retail program does not cannibalize stall-level food sales because it serves different use occasions — gifting, home cooking, pantry stocking, and tourism purchases — rather than competing for the same immediate dining decision. When properly merchandised, it adds revenue without adding the labor and infrastructure burden of another full restaurant stall.
Revenue Projections
At conservative assumptions — 30% of daily visitors purchasing one gift shop item at an average of $18 — and an estimated 200 visits/day in Year 1, the gift shop generates approximately $18,000–$35,000 in gross retail revenue annually. At Year 2 volume (300 visits/day, higher tourist penetration from OMDPNM and M2M co-marketing), the program scales to $30,000–$55,000/year. At 50–65% gross margins on branded kits and pantry goods, net contribution is meaningfully positive with minimal incremental labor. These figures are included in the financial model as a discrete revenue line under “Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising.”

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.6 Retail Incubator Shelf
chunks.text:
The gift shop will also function as a retail incubator shelf where vendors can test shelf-stable sauces, spice blends, baked goods, meal kits, pantry goods, branded merchandise, and local producer products before investing in wholesale or e-commerce expansion.
Participation will be governed by the vendor license agreement so retail activity is legally managed rather than informal. This creates a cohesive visitor experience while giving vendors another path to revenue and brand recognition.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 5.7 Regional Theme Nights and Signature Festival
chunks.heading: 5.7 Regional Theme Nights and Signature Festival
chunks.text:
The Hub's event calendar will include rotating regional theme nights that create repeat-visit behavior and sponsor-friendly programming: Hatch chile nights, borderlands BBQ, Indigenous foods, Sonoran food events, New Mexican heritage nights, and global student nights.
The annual Taste of Southern New Mexico festival will be positioned as the signature event for sponsors, tourism partners, local producers, and media. It can combine vendor booths, cider tastings, chef demonstrations, retail products, live music, and workforce program storytelling.
6. Operations and Licensing
The Hub is structured to be operationally clear, NMED-compliant, and regulatory-sound from Day 1. Each stall has its own dedicated kitchen and is permitted as its own food establishment through the NM Environment Department -- which isolates any health-code issues to individual operators and maintains quality accountability. A unified POS system supports multi-vendor ordering so guests check out once across multiple stalls.

chunks.heading: 6.3 Key Operational Systems and Standards
chunks.text:
Unified POS Platform: Hub-wide multi-vendor ordering system; guests can check out once across multiple stalls; hub receives unified reporting for percentage-rent calculation accuracy
Quality Gate Protocol: 4.0+ Google rating standard; removal trigger below 3.5 for 8+ consecutive weeks; weekly spot-check tastings by founder/CEO; monthly P&L review with hub management; 60-day notice for removal per license agreement
Allergen Compliance: All 9 FDA-recognized allergens (including newly added sesame) displayed on compliant posters at all required points; verified monthly in quality gate protocol
Insurance Verification: Each vendor's commercial general liability insurance verified as a condition of license execution; hub maintains umbrella policy covering all common areas and hub-level operations
Staggered Scheduling: Incubator license start dates offset by 3-6 months; permanent stall renewal dates also staggered; prevents any simultaneous mass departure scenario
Hours of Operation: Sunday-Thursday 11am-9pm; Friday-Saturday 11am-10pm; 365 days/year; climate-controlled indoor operation eliminates weather dependency entirely
Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce: Guest-facing mobile ordering platform for pickup and to-go orders across all vendor stalls in one digital experience. Reduces counter congestion, supports off-premise sales, enables loyalty rewards and push notifications, and expands Hub reach to NMSU students, downtown office workers, families, and El Paso day-trippers. Integrates with Tabski POS for live order routing per stall KDS. Also supports gift shop retail, event pre-sales, and vendor promotions. See Section 6.4 for full platform strategy.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.heading: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.text:
Strategic Purpose
The Hub’s Tabski POS handles the back-end of multi-vendor ordering — automated percentage-rent collection, per-stall KDS routing, and unified sales reporting. The mobile ordering platform is the consumer-facing layer on top of that infrastructure: a guest app that allows customers to browse all vendor menus, place pickup and to-go orders from multiple stalls in a single digital transaction, and manage loyalty rewards — all before or during their visit. The two systems work together. Tabski handles vendor-side operations; the app handles the guest relationship.
The platform is treated as core operating infrastructure, not a convenience feature. It materially expands the Hub’s revenue capture, improves throughput, and strengthens the long-term customer relationship in ways that a counter-only ordering model cannot replicate.
Operational Benefits
Throughput: Pre-queued digital orders reduce counter congestion during lunch rushes and weekend peaks. Vendors receive orders via KDS before guests arrive, allowing preparation to begin immediately. For a 13-stall hall with simultaneous peak demand, this meaningfully improves throughput and perceived wait time without adding staff.
Order Accuracy: Digital orders eliminate verbal miscommunication at the counter. Modifications, allergen flags, and special instructions are captured in writing and routed directly to the stall’s kitchen display screen, reducing waste and remakes.
Forecasting and Labor: Digital order history creates reliable demand data for vendors: which items sell by day, time, and weather; when to prep more; when to reduce. This data is valuable for coaching conversations during monthly P&L reviews and for optimizing labor scheduling across peak and off-peak periods.
Revenue Impact
Off-Premise Expansion: Pickup and to-go ordering captures revenue from customers who prefer not to dine in — NMSU students ordering between classes, downtown office workers on compressed lunch breaks, families with young children, and El Paso day-trippers who want to grab food before heading home on I-10. These customers represent genuine demand that a walk-up counter alone cannot efficiently serve.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.heading: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.text:
Higher Average Ticket: Digital ordering naturally supports upsells, combo suggestions, and add-ons (“Add a cider flight? Add a gift shop item to your pickup?”) that counter staff cannot consistently execute during busy periods. Industry data across multi-vendor food halls consistently shows 12–18% higher average ticket on digital vs. counter orders.
Direct Revenue from Platform: A modest convenience fee on digital orders (e.g., $0.50–$1.00 per transaction) generates direct Hub revenue. At 30–50 digital orders per day in Year 1 (15–25% of estimated daily transactions), this produces $5,000–$15,000 annually — a small but incremental contribution that scales with volume.
Cross-Category Integration
The platform’s value compounds across the Hub’s other revenue streams. It can sell gift shop products (Section 5.5) for add-on or standalone retail pickup. It can manage event pre-sales and Cider Club member early access. It can push targeted promotions tied to seasonal vendor menus, new incubator launches, and OMDPNM-tied tourism campaigns (e.g., “Order ahead for your post-hike lunch”). This cross-category capability makes the app a unified customer engagement platform, not a single-function ordering utility.
Loyalty and Retention
The app creates a durable post-visit relationship through loyalty rewards, digital offers, and push notifications tied to events, seasonal menus, and new vendor launches. Unlike a walk-up customer who leaves no data, an app user creates an identifiable profile that the Hub can engage repeatedly. For a destination food hall in a smaller metro like Las Cruces, converting a first-time visitor into a regular depends on staying top of mind between visits — and a loyalty-linked app is the most cost-effective tool available for that job.
Tabski Integration Note

chunks.sectionTitle: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.heading: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.text: Tabski’s native multi-vendor architecture supports third-party app integrations and online ordering modules. Before finalizing the digital commerce vendor selection, confirm with Tabski whether their online ordering layer natively supports the Hub’s multi-vendor checkout model, or whether a third-party platform (e.g., Olo, Lunchbox, or a white-label food hall app) integrates via Tabski’s API. The commissary kitchen component uses The Food Corridor for scheduling — the mobile ordering platform applies only to the food hall vendor stalls and retail programs. Full technical evaluation is recommended in Phase 2 (Months 4–7) as part of the Tabski implementation scope. See Supplement F for the full POS comparison and cost model.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 6.5 Membership Eligibility and Requirements
chunks.text:
The Hub’s shared kitchen and incubator facilities operate in a highly regulated environment. To protect public health, maintain strong relationships with the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED) and the City of Las Cruces, and manage risk for grantors and investors, every kitchen user must meet a standardized set of membership requirements prior to accessing the facility. These requirements mirror best-practice New Mexico commercial kitchens, specifically The Kitchen Table Santa Fe (313 Camino Alire, Santa Fe — 2023 Santa Fe Chamber Business of the Year, 2024 Edible Magazine Local Hero Award) and the SVEDC Mixing Bowl program in Albuquerque’s South Valley.
Each member business must:
Sign a Hub Membership Agreement and provide a refundable security deposit of $200 (benchmarked to The Kitchen Table Santa Fe’s standard deposit), payable at the time of signing.
Designate at least one person with a valid Food Manager’s certificate recognized by the State of New Mexico (e.g., National Registry of Food Safety Professionals, ServSafe, or NM Restaurant Association courses).
Maintain a current New Mexico Combined Reporting System (CRS) tax registration number issued by the New Mexico Department of Taxation and Revenue.
Hold an active New Mexico Environment Department food permit appropriate to their operation (fixed stall, ghost kitchen, or mobile unit). The Hub provides templates and technical assistance modeled on The Kitchen Table Santa Fe’s permit support process.
Carry a commercial general liability insurance policy with a minimum coverage of $1,000,000 per occurrence and list the Hub’s operating entity as an additional insured for the duration of facility use — consistent with The Kitchen Table Santa Fe’s standard.
Maintain a valid local business license from the City of Las Cruces (or the member’s home municipality, as applicable) — mirroring the City of Santa Fe business license requirement at The Kitchen Table.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 6.5 Membership Eligibility and Requirements
chunks.text:
By standardizing these requirements at the point of entry, the Hub ensures that every operator in the building is fully licensed, insured, and inspection-ready before they ever turn on a burner. This reduces regulatory risk, streamlines health department inspections, and creates a predictable, professional operating environment for all vendors. The checklist approach translates complex regulatory requirements into a clear, repeatable process — the same approach already proven at The Kitchen Table Santa Fe and the SVEDC Mixing Bowl in New Mexico.
NM Precedent Note: New Mexico already supports multiple shared commercial kitchens that provide structured on-ramps for food entrepreneurs. In Albuquerque’s South Valley, the SVEDC Mixing Bowl offers a nonprofit kitchen incubator model. In Santa Fe, The Kitchen Table Santa Fe (opened May 2023) operates under exactly this membership framework — and launched with 15 businesses pre-signed, now serving 34 members. These precedents validate both the demand for and the regulatory feasibility of shared commercial kitchen infrastructure in New Mexico. The Hub adapts and extends these proven elements to southern New Mexico, combining a full food hall, shared commissary kitchen, and structured incubation pathway under the same rigorous compliance framework.
7. Financial Snapshot
Financial targets are intentionally conservative and built around everyday Las Cruces price points rather than big-city assumptions. The model treats Year 1 as a ramp-up year with realistic occupancy expectations and a gradual build in bar and event revenue as the programming calendar matures.
Conservative Design Principle
The model does not assume tourist pricing or best-case traffic. Vendor license fees and percentage rent provide the steady revenue base. Cider bar and events contribute meaningfully but not dominantly in Year 1. The objective is a resilient, diversified base that reaches breakeven without depending on optimistic scenarios -- leaving upside if demand is stronger than projected.

9. Comparable Market Analysis
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub's model has been validated against directly comparable food hall and incubator concepts at both the regional and national level. The following analysis incorporates research into Sawmill Market and Park Square Market (Albuquerque, NM), Smallman Galley (Pittsburgh, PA), One Eleven Food Hall (Chicago, IL), and Durham Food Hall (Durham, NC).

Park Square Market opened June 2025 in Albuquerque's Uptown district as Heritage Cos.'s second food hall. Key data points for the Las Cruces Hub:

chunks.sectionTitle: 9.3 The Kitchen Table Santa Fe -- New Mexico In-State Commissary Precedent
chunks.heading: 9.3 The Kitchen Table Santa Fe -- New Mexico In-State Commissary Precedent
chunks.text:
The Kitchen Table Santa Fe (KTSF, 313 Camino Alire, Santa Fe, NM; thekitchentablesantafe.com) opened in May 2023 and is the closest in-state New Mexico comparable for the Hub's commissary kitchen component. Founded by chef and entrepreneur Andrea Abedi (Culinary Institute of America, Johnson and Wales, formerly Charlie Trotter's Chicago), KTSF is a fully equipped 24/7 commercial kitchen operating on a membership model. It opened with 15 pre-signed members and has grown to 34 active members within two years of opening. In 2023 it was named Business of the Year by the Santa Fe Chamber of Commerce, and in 2024 it received Edible Magazine's Local Hero Award for Innovation and Education -- New Mexico's food industry recognition for exactly the entrepreneurship infrastructure model the Hub is building.
Key lessons and applications:

Las Cruces is 2.5x larger with NMSU campus, Fort Bliss, and military community -- commissary kitchen addressable market is demonstrably stronger

Hub commissary targets 8-12 monthly members at $25-$35/hr; KTSF's ramp from 15 to 34 members in ~2 years validates this growth trajectory

Additionally, the Farmington, NM Harvest Food Hub and Kitchen at San Juan College -- cited as a successful MRA case study in the Las Cruces El Paseo and S Solano MRA Plan (April 2026) -- provides a directly comparable NM precedent for the Hub's commissary kitchen component. The El Paseo MRA plan's explicit citation of this project as a model reinforces the Hub's case for USDA LFPP and NMSU partnership funding. The relevant benchmarks apply specifically to the Hub's commissary kitchen component ($25-$35/hour rentals; monthly members; value-added food processing). The Hub's dedicated vendor stall model -- which KTSF does not replicate -- remains differentiated.

11. Funding Strategy and Capital Stack
The Hub's capital requirements are met through a deliberately diversified blended stack combining investor equity, SBA or other lender financing, pre-opening grants serving as equity-equivalent capital where allowable, sponsor-backed buildout packages, vendor deposits, pre-sales, and ongoing economic development grants. Founder cash contribution = $0. This structure is transparent about the founder's current capital position while showing funders how the project can still be capitalized through documented commitments, phased launch discipline, and non-dilutive support.

chunks.heading: 11.4 Risk-Adjusted Return
chunks.text:
Investor returns should be evaluated against milestone execution, not best-case launch assumptions. The GAAP ramp-year view may show a Year 1 operating loss while vendors onboard, events mature, and customer habits form; the plan therefore requires working capital reserve coverage before full buildout obligations are accepted.
Risk-adjusted upside comes from proving demand before committing all fixed costs. Phased launch options, sponsor-backed buildout packages, vendor deposits, Cider Club and event pre-sales, gift shop retail tests, and pop-up proof events all reduce the amount of speculative capital exposed before the model is validated.
The investor story is strongest when each funding release is tied to evidence: site control, grant status, sponsor commitments, vendor LOIs, proof-event sales, lender progress, and reserve coverage. This approach protects credibility with lenders and makes the return case more disciplined for investors.

chunks.heading: 11.4 Investor Exit and Return Scenarios
chunks.text:
Investor return mechanics will be finalized with legal and tax counsel, but the plan supports several practical pathways: preferred return from cash flow after stabilization, founder or company buyback, refinance after stabilized operating history, real estate appreciation if the project controls property, long-term profit participation, or conversion into a project-specific preferred equity position.
Because founder cash is $0, investor security and priority must be described clearly before funds are accepted. Potential protections include use-of-funds controls, milestone-based release of funds, preferred return rights, collateral or lien position where legally available, reporting covenants, and defined remedies if the project does not reach funding milestones.

Before full buildout, the Hub should run 2-3 pop-up proof events with local vendors. Each event should document attendance, gross sales, average ticket, customer feedback, email signups, vendor performance, sponsor interest, media reach, and lessons for the permanent operating model.
These proof events give grant reviewers, lenders, sponsors, and investors concrete evidence of demand while allowing the Hub to test menus, pricing, event operations, retail products, and bilingual vendor support before committing full capital.
The implementation is structured in four phases across 10+ months to Grand Opening in Q1–Q2 2027 (February–April 2027 target), with explicit dependency management, licensing timeline buffers, and contingency triggers built into the schedule.

13. Risk Management
TIER-1 RISK DISCLOSURE — Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR)
Per Appendix F.6, the Hub’s DSCR is projected to fall below the SBA standard 1.25x covenant in Years 1 and 2 (Year 1: approximately 2.38 on interest-only basis, but below 1.25x on full P&I basis; Year 2 DSCR approximately 0.44 on full P&I). This is a known and disclosed risk. It is the direct result of the Year 1 operating loss during vendor ramp-up — not a structural deficiency in the business model. Mitigation strategy: (1) negotiate a lender-committed stepped-covenant agreement with the SBA 7(a) lender prior to underwriting submission — deferring full DSCR covenant testing to Year 3 when the Appendix F.2 model shows $317,000 EBITDA and a passing ratio; (2) present the $272,000 working capital reserve as evidence that debt service will be met from reserves during the ramp period even if EBITDA is negative; (3) document any committed interest-only period in the loan structure. This plan must not be distributed to SBA underwriters without a committed lender step-covenant agreement or alternative DSCR mitigation documented in writing.
Risk management in this plan reflects genuine failure-mode analysis, not pro forma disclosure. Each risk below has a specific, designed mitigation -- not just an acknowledgment. The engineering background of the founder means risk identification and mitigation design are core competencies, not afterthoughts.

15. Founder Profile: The Person Behind the Plan
Investors and grantmakers don't just fund ideas -- they fund people. The founder of the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub is not a first-time dreamer hoping food halls are a good idea. This is a trained engineer, an advanced degree holder in engineering management, a proven business operator, and a genuine food lover with deep roots in the community this Hub is designed to serve.
What makes this combination rare and genuinely compelling is that a food hall is not fundamentally a culinary challenge -- it is a systems-engineering and management challenge wrapped inside a hospitality business. It demands process discipline, capacity planning, vendor coordination, quality control, multi-unit scheduling, regulatory compliance, and financial modeling just as much as it demands good recipes and community energy. The founder brings all of it.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 15.1 Engineering Foundation -- Systems Thinking Applied to Food
chunks.heading: 15.1 Engineering Foundation -- Systems Thinking Applied to Food
chunks.text:
The Engineering Lens
Most food businesses fail not because the food is bad -- they fail because the systems are broken. Inconsistent service, poor kitchen workflows, vendor conflicts, cost overruns, compliance gaps, scheduling breakdowns. A trained general engineer looks at a food hall and sees exactly what it is: a complex, multi-unit operations system requiring disciplined design to function reliably at scale. That is the founder's native professional language.
Systems Thinking: Every element of the Hub -- stall layouts, shared utilities, POS integration, NMED permitting per stall, vendor cohort scheduling, grease trap connections, HVAC capacity -- has been mapped as an interconnected system. Problems in one subsystem propagate. A general engineer designs to contain and isolate failure.
Process Standardization: The Hub's quality gate protocol, monthly P&L reviews, taste-testing schedules, allergen compliance checklists, and vendor onboarding sequence are all standardized processes. Not because bureaucracy is good, but because variance in execution is the primary enemy of a multi-vendor food operation.
Capacity Planning: The 8,000 sq ft floor plan, stall kitchen sizing, shared utility load calculations, HVAC capacity for 60-80 covers, and parking requirements have all been evaluated against realistic demand scenarios -- not optimistic ones. Note: the Realize Las Cruces 2025 Zoning Code eliminates auto parking minimums in Urban Character Areas (which includes downtown Las Cruces). This is a material cost advantage -- surface parking construction runs $5,000-$15,000 per space. If the Hub site is in an Urban Character Area, confirm parking-minimum elimination with City Planning before committing to any parking provision in the buildout budget. Engineers plan for load, not just average use.
Risk Identification and Mitigation Design: The risk management section of this plan is not a formality. It reflects genuine failure-mode analysis. The staggered cohort structure (Smallman Galley lesson), liquor license timeline buffer, insurance verification requirement, and funding source diversification are all designed risk controls.

Industrial engineering is the discipline of optimizing complex systems involving people, processes, materials, information, and equipment. The engineering management concentration extends that into leadership, financial management, organizational design, and strategic decision-making under uncertainty.
In practical terms, this academic background means:

chunks.text: A Master of Science in Industrial Engineering with an Engineering Management concentration is, in many ways, the ideal academic preparation for running a complex multi-unit food business. The degree teaches you to see systems, manage constraints, model uncertainty, lead teams, and make decisions under resource pressure -- all of which describe daily operations in a food hall.

chunks.heading: 15.3 Engineering Management Degree -- Leadership Backed by Technical Discipline
chunks.text:
Engineering management bridges the analytical precision of engineering with the human dimensions of leadership: financial management, organizational behavior, strategic planning, and stakeholder communication. Graduates are trained to be effective in exactly the situation the Las Cruces Hub represents: a technically complex project with significant financial stakes, multiple stakeholders, regulatory constraints, and a team that must function reliably under pressure.
Engineering Management Competency
How It Manifests in This Project
Financial Management and Capital Budgeting
The blended capital stack (equity + SBA + six grant categories) was assembled using rigorous financial modeling. Conservative projections are stress-tested at 60-70% occupancy -- not built on best-case assumptions.
Multi-Stakeholder Management
The Hub simultaneously serves investors, 12+ vendors, six grant agency categories, city partners (DLCP, MVEDA, Visit Las Cruces), apprenticeship partners (NMSU, DACC), and four distinct customer segments. Engineering management teaches tracking and serving all of them simultaneously.
Strategic Planning Under Uncertainty
The four-phase roadmap with explicit contingencies (liquor license fallback, funding delay response, vendor departure protocol, revenue shortfall stress test) reflects the engineering management emphasis on planning for variance, not just the expected case.
Technology and Systems Integration
Unified POS selection; NMED per-stall permitting structure; multi-vendor ordering platform; hub-wide reporting dashboard; insurance verification systems -- all requiring simultaneous technical and organizational judgment.
Cross-Functional Team Leadership
The Hub's leadership team spans restaurant management (GM), operations (Operations Manager), beverage curation (Beverage Director), customer experience (FOH Supervisor), and marketing -- a genuinely cross-functional team requiring bridging leadership.

chunks.text:
Beyond formal education, the founder is a proven multi-year business operator. This matters enormously because the most common failure mode in food and hospitality businesses is not lack of passion or capital -- it is lack of operational discipline and business management competence.
Profit and Loss Management: Sustained multi-year business operations with consistent financial management, cost control, and revenue optimization. The financial projections in this plan are not guesses -- they are built by someone who has actually managed a business's P&L across multiple reporting cycles.
Staff Coordination and Team Leadership: Experience building and managing teams, setting performance expectations, and maintaining operational standards under real-world conditions -- not just academic preparation.
Supplier and Vendor Relationships: Negotiating and managing supplier relationships, quality standards, and contract terms in an operational context translates directly to vendor management at the Hub level across 12+ independent operators.
Customer Experience Ownership: Understanding that customer satisfaction is not an abstract goal but a measurable operational outcome requiring active daily management -- exactly the mindset behind the Hub's quality gate protocol and weekly spot-check tasting program.
Regulatory Compliance Navigation: Comfort with permit requirements, government agency relationships, and compliance frameworks -- experience that now extends to NM ABC liquor licensing, NMED food establishment permitting, and city building compliance across 10 simultaneous permits.

chunks.sectionTitle: 15.6 The Food Passion -- Why This Is Personal, Not Just Professional
chunks.heading: 15.6 The Food Passion -- Why This Is Personal, Not Just Professional
chunks.text:
A business plan built entirely on engineering credentials would be unconvincing in a food and hospitality context. The equally important truth about the founder is a deep, long-standing, genuine love of food -- of cooking, of eating, of the cultural stories that live in dishes, and of the community that forms around a shared meal.
The Personal Investment
The founder does not just understand food intellectually -- this is someone who spends weekends at the smoker, who has developed real craft in meat preparation and flavor development, who moves through Las Cruces and southern New Mexico experiencing the food landscape with genuine curiosity and personal passion. The 'honestly curated' promise at the heart of the Hub's brand is not a marketing slogan. It is a personal commitment backed by real food knowledge and genuine taste.
Smoking and Grilling Expertise: Years of hands-on experience with smoked and grilled meat preparation -- developing palate through technique, understanding flavor development from wood to plate, building the food credibility that makes vendor taste-testing meaningful rather than performative. This is the founder's culinary native language and the inspiration behind pursuing Southern BBQ as a priority permanent anchor stall.
Diversified Food Curiosity: A genuine interest in global cuisines, regional cooking traditions, flavor pairing, and culinary innovation. This is what enables the Hub's curation to be authentic: the founder knows what distinguishes excellent global cuisine, what distinguishes excellent New Mexican cuisine, what makes a Spanish Basque cider pairing with Mediterranean mezze work, and what a perfectly smoked brisket demands.
Las Cruces Culinary Culture Connection: Deep familiarity with Las Cruces's specific dining landscape -- the family restaurants, the taco trucks, the chile culture, the community gatherings that form around food. This cultural fluency is what ensures the Hub won't feel like a transplant from Austin or Denver. It will feel like it grew out of Las Cruces because it was designed from inside it.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 15.6 The Food Passion -- Why This Is Personal, Not Just Professional
chunks.heading: 15.6 The Food Passion -- Why This Is Personal, Not Just Professional
chunks.text: Community Pride and Ownership: The founder is building this in Las Cruces because Las Cruces deserves it. This is not a business concept that could be dropped interchangeably into any mid-sized city. It is designed for this specific market, this specific culture, this specific community's food identity -- and that intentionality is visible throughout every section of this plan.

chunks.sectionTitle: 15.7 The Rare Combination -- Why It Matters to Investors and Grantmakers
chunks.heading: 15.7 The Rare Combination -- Why It Matters to Investors and Grantmakers
chunks.text:
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub requires a founder who can simultaneously accomplish six things that are rarely found in one person:
Design and manage complex multi-unit operational systems -- general engineering and industrial engineering training
Lead a diverse cross-functional team across technical and non-technical disciplines -- engineering management degree
Navigate government funding, compliance, and regulatory environments with competence -- engineering training and professional business operations experience
Manage a real business's P&L with discipline and documented foresight -- proven multi-year business operator
Curate food and beverage quality with genuine personal credibility and palate -- deep food passion, smoking and grilling expertise, diverse culinary knowledge
Connect authentically with the Las Cruces community and its specific culinary and cultural identity -- local roots, genuine cultural fluency, building for this community specifically
Most food hall and incubator projects are led either by hospitality veterans who lack the operational systems discipline, or by business operators who lack the food credibility. The founder of the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub has both -- backed by formal engineering and management training, a federal government career, a real business operation track record, and a genuine love of the food and the community this Hub is designed to serve.
For Investors and Grantmakers
This is not a passion project seeking validation. This is a disciplined, systems-designed, research-validated economic development platform built by someone with the formal training, operational experience, regulatory familiarity, and personal food investment to execute it at the highest level. The engineering background ensures the plan is realistic and the systems are sound. The food passion ensures the curation is authentic and the community connection is real. Together, they make this venture both operationally credible on paper and emotionally credible in Las Cruces.

Las Cruces is ready for this. The research confirms it. The demand is documented and frustrated: residents are already driving 45 minutes to find what the Hub will offer locally. The market gaps are documented. The city support programs are active and funded. The model is nationally proven. The licensing path is mapped. The financial projections are conservative and stress-tested. The team structure is defined. And the person leading it has the rare combination of engineering discipline, management training, federal regulatory experience, business operation track record, and genuine food passion to execute it well.

Why This Section Exists
This section documents a formally designated City of Las Cruces Metropolitan Redevelopment Area that directly intersects with the Hub's site selection process, financial incentive stack, and grant application strategy. The W. Picacho and Motel Boulevard MRA was adopted December 1, 2025 and received GRT increment financing approval March 16, 2026 -- events that occurred after the initial drafting of this business plan. This section ensures investors, lenders, and grant reviewers have complete information about this opportunity and John's deliberate approach to evaluating it.

chunks.sectionTitle: 17.1 What the W. Picacho MRA Is
chunks.heading: 17.1 What the W. Picacho MRA Is
chunks.text:
A Metropolitan Redevelopment Area (MRA) is a zone formally designated by a city government under New Mexico statute where the city identifies underutilized or blighted conditions and unlocks a specific set of public investment tools to catalyze private development. The MRA designation does not mandate any particular use -- it creates the legal and financial infrastructure for the city and private developers to partner on revitalization projects that the market alone would not fund.
The West Picacho and Motel Boulevard MRA covers a 1.5-mile corridor bounded by Tashiro Drive and McClure Road to the north, the BNSF Railroad tracks to the east, West Hadley Avenue to the south, and the Rio Grande to the west. This corridor was chosen by the City because it contains significant commercial potential that is underperforming relative to its location -- high vehicle traffic on West Picacho Avenue (18,000-19,000 vehicles per day by traffic count), an existing commercial base, and immediate adjacency to established residential neighborhoods, but fragmented development that has not fulfilled the corridor's economic potential.
MRA Timeline Event
Date
Significance
West Picacho MRA plan publicly developed with community input
2024-2025
City engaged residents and business owners through small group meetings, pop-up events, and public hearings to shape the plan
MRA boundary extension and plan adoption
December 1, 2025
Las Cruces City Council unanimously adopted the W. Picacho and Motel Boulevard MRA plan and boundary -- making it fully legally operative
GRT increment financing approved
March 16, 2026
City Council unanimously approved GRT (Gross Receipts Tax) increment financing for the MRA -- the mechanism that allows tax revenue growth generated within the MRA to be reinvested back into corridor improvements for up to 20 years
GRT baseline established
March 16, 2026
Baseline set at approximately $42,000/month; any GRT revenue above this baseline generated by new or growing businesses within the MRA is eligible for 75% reinvestment back into the corridor
City actively seeking catalytic private developers
April 2026 (ongoing)

chunks.sectionTitle: 17.2 The Shoto Catalytic Site -- The Hub's Specific Opportunity
chunks.heading: 17.2 The Shoto Catalytic Site -- The Hub's Specific Opportunity
chunks.text:
The MRA plan identifies three catalytic project sites. Catalyst Site 1: the Tashiro Mixed-Use Hub -- approximately 42 acres at the southeast corner of Tashiro and Valley Drives, private ownership -- is the site most directly relevant to the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub. The MRA plan's own language (Strategy 3.4) directs the City to 'work with owner/developer to create an eatertainment district in the northwest corner of the Tashiro catalyst site' with 'both permanent and food-truck type options within walking distance of the Field of Dreams sports facility.' Strategy 3.5 further directs the City to 'investigate potential for a commercial kitchen in the eatertainment district to complement small-scale start-ups/food trucks.' The Hub is the exact operator the city is actively seeking for this site. The plan notes the city expects to provide development incentives and active recruitment support for desired uses at Tashiro.
For the Hub, this creates a rare opportunity: rather than leasing space in a building designed for a different purpose and adapting it to food hall use, the Hub could anchor a purpose-built mixed-use development on a city-identified catalytic site, with the city as an active partner in permitting, infrastructure, and incentive delivery. Purpose-built food halls consistently outperform adaptive reuse conversions on buildout efficiency, kitchen layout precision, and long-term operating cost.
Shoto Site Characteristic

Far more than the Hub's 8,000-12,000 sq ft footprint; Hub would be one anchor among several uses -- residential, retail, parking -- in a mixed-use development. Requires either a development partner for the broader site or a ground lease for the Hub's specific footprint.

City staff are actively looking for exactly this type of private developer conversation. Early engagement with Blairre Flores at Economic Development gives John first-mover access to this conversation before any other food-related developer.

Designing from a blank canvas eliminates the most common adaptive reuse risks: asbestos in older buildings, undersized electrical service for heavy kitchen loads, non-standard plumbing requiring major rerouting. Each of the 13 kitchen stalls can be laid out optimally rather than fitted into existing space.
Parking is fully solvable
A 42-acre site accommodates the 80-120 surface parking spaces a food hall of this scale requires without shared parking arrangements, paid structures, or the 300-foot proximity constraints that downtown locations face.
Residential adjacency built into the plan
The MRA plan includes affordable and multi-family housing components adjacent to the commercial hub. Residents of this development become regular Hub customers by default -- a built-in daily foot traffic source that downtown locations do not automatically have.

chunks.sectionTitle: 17.3 Financial Incentives Available Within the MRA
chunks.heading: 17.3 Financial Incentives Available Within the MRA
chunks.text:
Operating within the W. Picacho MRA boundary makes the Hub eligible for a defined stack of financial incentives that are not available to a downtown location. These incentives are grounded in New Mexico statute and established MRA implementation practice -- they are documented, not speculative.
Incentive
How It Works
Estimated Value to Hub (5 Years)
Status
Property tax deferral (up to 20 years)
Building rehabilitation and improvements within an MRA can qualify for property tax deferral under NM Metropolitan Redevelopment Code. For a tenant, this benefit flows through reduced rent from a landlord who receives the deferral on the improved property. For an owner-operator or ground lessee, the deferral applies directly.
$40,000-$125,000 depending on ownership structure and assessed improvement value
Established in NM law; applied in other NM MRAs
Development and permit fee waivers
MRA designation allows the City to waive or reduce development fees and building permit fees for projects aligned with MRA plan goals. The W. Picacho plan explicitly calls for pedestrian-friendly commercial spaces and culturally rich landmarks -- a food hall and culinary incubator is a direct match.
$15,000-$40,000 (one-time at buildout); fee waiver is negotiable with City Economic Development
Requires negotiation; not automatic -- but city staff are actively seeking projects like the Hub
Expedited plan review
MRA projects receive priority review by City Planning and Building, reducing the standard 2-4 week commercial plan review cycle. For a project with 13 separate NMED stall permit applications requiring coordination, weeks of schedule acceleration translate directly to reduced holding costs.
$15,000-$45,000 in avoided carrying costs during construction (lease payments, interest accrual on construction financing)
Standard MRA benefit; applied consistently across Las Cruces MRAs
GRT increment reinvestment

chunks.sectionTitle: 17.3 Financial Incentives Available Within the MRA
chunks.heading: 17.3 Financial Incentives Available Within the MRA
chunks.text:
The Hub operating at $1M+ in annual food sales generates approximately $83,900/year in GRT at the Las Cruces 8.39% rate. Up to 75% of the GRT growth above the $42,000/month baseline generated within the MRA is reinvested in corridor streetscape, parking, lighting, and infrastructure improvements. These improvements directly benefit the Hub's site over time.
$20,000-$50,000/year in corridor infrastructure funded by the Hub's own GRT growth -- improving the site environment without additional Hub capital outlay
Approved by City Council March 16, 2026; legally operative
Enhanced grant program eligibility
MVEDA lists 'Business in a Metropolitan Redevelopment Area' as an explicit qualifying category for the EPE Economic Development Fund. MRA location also strengthens NMFA, USDA LFPP, and HFFF applications by adding an equity and corridor revitalization narrative that downtown-located businesses cannot claim.
$50,000-$150,000 in incremental grant awards due to stronger eligibility positioning across multiple programs
Requires application; MRA location is a qualifying factor, not a guarantee
Total Incentive Package Estimate
Combining property tax deferral, permit fee waivers, expedited review savings, GRT reinvestment, and enhanced grant eligibility, the W. Picacho MRA offers the Hub an estimated $140,000-$360,000 in total value over five years. This range reflects the difference between a owner-operator model — which the Hub IS pursuing, meaning the Hub captures the full deferral value directly rather than indirectly through a reduced-rent negotiation with a landlord. At the midpoint estimate of $250,000, the MRA incentive package reduces effective project cost by approximately 15-18% -- a material financial advantage.

Traffic: Higher Than Most Successful Food Hall Locations
West Picacho Avenue carries 18,000-19,000 vehicles per day through the MRA corridor, confirmed by Mesilla Valley MPO traffic count data. This is a through-traffic arterial, not a destination-only street -- it generates continuous drive-by exposure throughout the day, seven days a week. By comparison, downtown Las Cruces Main Street functions primarily as a destination corridor with lower daily vehicle throughput.
At 18,500 daily vehicles, even a 0.5% conversion rate (92 vehicles/day stopping) at a $20 average spend generates $672,000/year in traffic-capture revenue before a single destination visit is counted. This traffic base is self-renewing -- it does not depend on the Hub building a brand reputation before customers discover it.
Behavioral Evidence: The Format Already Works Here
Las Cruces residents already demonstrate strong appetite for multi-vendor food experiences:
The Farmers & Crafts Market of Las Cruces, recognized by Visit Las Cruces as one of the top-rated farmers markets in the country, draws consistent crowds who move between multiple food vendors in a shared outdoor format.

chunks.text:
The Borderland Car Show & Food Truck Festival drew 25 food trucks and an estimated 5,000-10,000 attendees, proving that curated multi-vendor food events generate mass attendance when properly promoted.
Active food truck clusters operate throughout the city. Facebook community groups document residents actively seeking out informal multi-truck food gatherings in parking lots -- demonstrating demand that lacks permanent infrastructure to serve it.
No purpose-built, permanent food hall or structured food truck park currently exists anywhere in Las Cruces, confirming that the Hub would be establishing a new category with no direct competition.

Lower corridor lease costs and the availability of larger parcels allow the Hub to open Phase 1 as an outdoor-first food truck and cider pad format, validate demand with operating history, and then deploy Phase 2 enclosed stall capital backed by real revenue data.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: Phase 2 SBA Loan Advantage
chunks.text: A startup SBA 7(a) application with no operating history faces a 40-50% approval rate and maximum lender scrutiny. A Phase 2 SBA application submitted after 12 months of Phase 1 operations -- with documented monthly revenue, vendor performance data, GRT tax history, and a proven customer base -- is a fundamentally different application. Industry lenders treat food service businesses with 12+ months of operating history significantly more favorably than pre-revenue startups. The phased model does not reduce total capital invested; it sequences the capital deployment to match evidence of demand.

The One Risk the MRA Scenario Cannot Eliminate
The W. Picacho corridor is an MRA precisely because it is underinvested. The city's own economic development coordinator acknowledged the revitalization timeline runs 'immediate to 20 years' -- meaning no city commitment to surrounding improvements on a fixed schedule. The Hub must be financially modeled to generate its own foot traffic and revenue regardless of whether the city's corridor improvements materialize on any particular schedule. MRA improvements are modeled as upside in Years 2-5, not as a baseline assumption in Year 1 projections.

chunks.sectionTitle: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.heading: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.text:
This appendix provides a comprehensive regulatory analysis of seating area requirements as they apply to standalone food truck operations versus organized food truck parks, with specific attention to New Mexico state law, national regulatory benchmarks, and the direct strategic implications for the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub. Understanding these distinctions is critical both for competitive positioning and for compliance planning when the Hub's commissary kitchen or event spaces interact with mobile food vendor regulations.
Why This Matters for the Hub
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub is a fixed indoor food hall -- not a food truck or a food truck park. However, understanding the regulatory gap between mobile food truck seating (severely restricted) and food truck park seating (moderately regulated with structured requirements) directly demonstrates why the Hub's indoor, permitted, climate-controlled format is the superior model for Las Cruces. This appendix also informs how the Hub's commissary kitchen program relates to food truck operators who use it as their servicing area.
D.1 New Mexico State Law Governing Mobile Food Establishments
All food trucks operating in New Mexico are governed by Title 7, Chapter 6, Part 2 of the New Mexico Administrative Code (7.6.2 NMAC) -- the Food Service and Food Processing Regulations administered by the New Mexico Environment Department (NMED). This code was last substantively updated in December 2018 and is based on the 2017 FDA Model Food Code.
The Enclosure Rule -- The Single Most Important NM Food Truck Seating Constraint
NM Admin. Code Section 7.6.2.9(G) states explicitly:
"The operation of mobile food establishments shall be conducted within the enclosure of the permitted unit. During a single event or celebration, certain operations (e.g., additional covered storage, additional food preparation area, outdoor serving counter) may be conducted outside of the enclosure, when approved. If approved, an additional temporary food establishment permit shall be required."

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.heading: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.text:
This single provision has profound implications for seating. The law requires all mobile food operations to occur within the physical enclosure of the truck itself. Any outdoor activity -- including an outdoor serving counter -- requires separate approval and a temporary food establishment permit. The regulation says nothing about customer seating areas because, under the strict reading of NM law, mobile food establishments are not expected to have them at all under standard operating conditions.
NM Code Provision
Regulatory Text (Summary)
Seating Implication
7.6.2.9(G) -- Enclosure Rule
All operations shall be conducted within the permitted unit's enclosure; outdoor operations at events require additional temporary permit
Customer seating is not addressed because standard food truck operation contemplates no seating; any outdoor serving arrangement requires separate NMED approval and temporary permit
7.6.2.9(H) -- Single-Service Articles
Mobile food establishments shall provide only single-service articles (disposable) for consumers
No reusable dishware, glassware, or table service -- operationally consistent with take-away service, not seated dining
7.6.2.9(I) -- Self-Contained Requirements
Self-contained units must accomplish all food preparation and warewashing within the enclosure
No built-in provision for table service or seated-dining support infrastructure such as bus tubs, dishwashing stations for table items, etc.
7.6.2.9(J) -- Servicing Area Agreement
Non-self-contained units require a formal servicing area agreement specifying days, hours, and support services
The servicing area (commissary) is the food truck's regulatory home base -- this is where the Hub's commissary kitchen program intersects with food truck operators
The Servicing Area Relationship -- How This Connects to the Hub's Commissary Kitchen
NM 7.6.2.9(J) requires all non-self-contained mobile food units to maintain a formal agreement with a licensed servicing area (commissary kitchen). That agreement must document the days and hours of use and the extent of support services provided. The servicing area itself must hold its own NMED food permit.

chunks.heading: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.text:
This means the Hub's shared commissary kitchen, when used by food truck operators as their licensed servicing area, creates a formal regulatory relationship between the Hub and those operators. The Hub's commissary kitchen permits must remain current and the servicing area agreement must be properly documented for each food truck client. This is manageable and is built into the Hub's commissary kitchen rental agreement framework.
D.2 Standalone Food Truck Seating -- The National Regulatory Picture
Across the United States, the regulatory treatment of seating areas for standalone food trucks -- those operating on streets, public property, or private lots without a designated park structure -- varies significantly by municipality. However, several consistent patterns emerge from national research that are directly instructive for Las Cruces.
Pattern 1: Many Jurisdictions Prohibit Standalone Food Truck Seating Entirely
The Town of Cary, North Carolina's food truck ordinance is representative of one end of the regulatory spectrum. It states explicitly: 'Outdoor seating areas for dining associated with a food truck, including but not limited to tables, chairs, booths, bar stools, benches, and standup counters, are not permitted.' This is not an uncommon approach -- many municipalities treat mobile food vendors as purely transactional operations with no seating infrastructure permitted.
The rationale is straightforward: standalone food trucks are mobile vendors, not restaurants. Permitting seating would effectively convert a mobile food vendor into a semi-permanent outdoor restaurant, which carries different zoning, health, ADA, and public safety obligations than a mobile permit covers.
Pattern 2: Where Seating Is Permitted, Lot Size Is the Primary Limiting Factor

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.heading: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.text:
In jurisdictions that do permit food truck seating, the permission is typically tied to minimum lot size requirements. The City of Raleigh's food truck regulations, for example, specify that outdoor seating associated with a food truck is only permitted on lots of at least two acres in size. This threshold effectively excludes most urban street locations, small parking lots, and sidewalk vending positions from seating eligibility.
Pattern 3: Distance Requirements from Existing Restaurants Create Seating Zone Conflicts
Most food truck ordinances require trucks to maintain 50 to 150 feet of distance from existing restaurants and their outdoor dining areas. In downtown Las Cruces, where the Hub is located, these distance requirements would make it practically impossible for any standalone food truck to legally set up customer seating nearby without conflicting with the Hub's own outdoor event areas or neighboring restaurant seating.

chunks.heading: Appendix D: Food Truck Seating Regulations vs. Food Truck Park Seating -- Research Analysis
chunks.text:
Pattern 5: Restroom Access Is the Regulatory Trigger That Changes Everything
Urban planning research consistently identifies restroom access as the single most significant operational constraint for food trucks with seating. As urban planner publications note, if food trucks are 'allowed to stand for many hours a day, the issue of restrooms for employees and customers should be addressed. If public restrooms are not available, there should be assurance that food truck employees have access to other facilities.' When seating is provided, the practical expectation of restroom access shifts from 'helpful' to 'effectively required' -- and providing permanent restroom facilities almost always triggers commercial building permit requirements that a mobile food vendor cannot satisfy.
D.3 Food Truck Parks -- A Fundamentally Different Regulatory Category
A food truck park is legally and operationally distinct from a standalone food truck operation. Once an operator establishes a permanent or semi-permanent location with organized seating, sanitary facilities, and multiple vendor operations, most jurisdictions reclassify the operation from 'mobile food vendor' to 'food truck park' or 'outdoor food establishment' -- and an entirely different set of zoning, building, health, and safety regulations apply.
Defining Characteristic
The key distinction is permanence and infrastructure. A food truck park is defined by permanent on-site seating, sanitary facilities, and organized amenities. Once these elements are present, the regulatory framework shifts from mobile food vendor codes toward commercial restaurant and outdoor dining codes.

Zoning Classification for Food Truck Parks
Food truck parks are typically regulated as a distinct land use category in zoning codes -- neither 'restaurant' nor 'mobile food vendor' but a hybrid requiring its own use permit. Key zoning considerations relevant to Las Cruces include:
Food truck parks are typically allowed by right or special exception in commercial and mixed-use zones -- consistent with the C-2 or equivalent zoning where the Hub operates
Residential adjacency buffers are common: food truck parks adjacent to residential zones typically require landscaping buffers and have noise and hours-of-operation restrictions
Many codes require a detailed site plan showing vendor locations, seating areas, dumpster placement, service vehicle access, fire lane locations, and ADA paths before a food truck park use permit is issued
Las Cruces adopted a new 'Realize Las Cruces' character-based zoning code passed February 2025 -- the first major zoning overhaul in 25 years. The new code organizes all parcels by character (Rural, Suburban, Urban) and zoning district (NH-1 residential, NH-2 mixed residential/commercial, NH-3 transitional retail/office/housing, Commercial Retail, Mixed-Use Overlay, Town Centers). Food hall/restaurant use is permitted in Commercial Retail zones and available in varying degrees in NH-3, Mixed-Use, and Town Center designations. The downtown Urban Character Area eliminates most parking minimums -- a significant cost advantage. This new code should be reviewed specifically for food truck park definitions and outdoor dining regulations before any outdoor food truck seating is planned

The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) applies to any public dining area regardless of whether it is associated with a mobile vendor, a food truck park, or a fixed restaurant. When customer seating is provided in any context -- even outdoors adjacent to a food truck -- ADA accessibility requirements are triggered.
ADA Requirement
Standard
Application to Food Truck Seating
Accessible seating percentage
Minimum 5% of total seating must be wheelchair accessible; minimum one accessible table required even if total seating is very small
Any food truck or food truck park with customer seating must provide at least one ADA-compliant table; more as seating grows

28-34 inches high; 27+ inches of knee clearance; 19+ inches under-table knee clearance depth; labeled as accessible
Applies to outdoor seating tables at food trucks and food truck parks; standard folding and picnic table designs often fail this requirement

The Hub's shared commissary kitchen serves food truck operators as their required NM servicing area. Understanding the seating regulatory landscape clarifies both the Hub's obligations and the competitive value it provides to these clients.

chunks.heading: Appendix E: The City Commercial Kitchen -- Competitive Landscape Analysis and Strategic Response
chunks.text:
This appendix directly addresses the emerging competitive landscape created by the City of Las Cruces's plans to open a commercial kitchen, as well as the existing El Calvario Commercial Kitchen Incubator already operating in downtown Las Cruces. Understanding both developments is essential to refining the Hub's positioning, identifying genuine threats, and -- more importantly -- identifying the significant opportunities this landscape creates for partnership, differentiation, and market capture.
The Strategic Frame
The city opening a commercial kitchen is simultaneously a competitive challenge and a strong validating signal. It confirms that civic and philanthropic leaders in Las Cruces see genuine market demand for food entrepreneurship infrastructure. The question is not whether the Hub can survive alongside it -- the Hub's model is fundamentally different. The question is how to position the two as complementary while ensuring the Hub occupies the specific niche that a city-operated facility cannot.
E.1 What Already Exists: El Calvario Commercial Kitchen Incubator
Before addressing the city's planned commercial kitchen, it is important to understand the facility that already exists in Las Cruces. El Calvario United Methodist Church, located at the intersection of the Las Cruces Downtown Arts and Cultural District and the Mesquite Historic District, operates the El Calvario Commercial Kitchen Incubator -- which describes itself as the only 24/7 accessible nonprofit commercial kitchen in southwestern New Mexico.

Important Timing Note
El Calvario's $383,000 federal expansion is expected to complete by December 2026 -- the same window as the Hub's Grand Opening. This means the Las Cruces commercial kitchen landscape will have two new or expanded facilities launching within months of each other. This is not a problem; it is a confirmation that the market has reached critical mass. But it means the Hub's differentiation strategy must be sharp and clearly communicated from Day 1.
E.2 The City's Planned Commercial Kitchen: What We Know
The City of Las Cruces is planning to construct and open a brand-new, purpose-built commercial kitchen facility -- not a renovation of existing space but a newly built structure -- designed specifically to support local food entrepreneurs. The facility is expected to provide access to professional-grade equipment, offer educational workshops and business development resources, attract food-related businesses, and serve as a hub for culinary innovation and economic development in Las Cruces. City leadership has framed this initiative as a direct investment in the food sector, recognizing that food innovation is already underway in Las Cruces and that providing dedicated infrastructure will accelerate and formalize it.

Key point: the city's planned facility is a new construction project -- a purpose-built commercial kitchen -- rather than a renovation or lease of existing space. This is a significant investment signal. New construction means the facility will be designed to modern commercial kitchen standards from the ground up, likely with capacity that exceeds what El Calvario's leased and renovated space can offer. Specific details -- site, square footage, operational model, pricing structure, timeline, and managing entity -- are emerging and should be confirmed directly with the Las Cruces Economic Development Department (575-541-2425 or economicdev@las-cruces.org) as early as possible in Phase 1.
The New-Build Significance
The distinction between the city's plan and El Calvario's expansion is important: El Calvario is renovating and expanding leased space. The city is building a new facility from the ground up. New construction of a purpose-built commercial kitchen represents a larger capital commitment, a longer development timeline (typically 18-36 months from planning to opening for a municipal new-build project), and a facility designed with current commercial kitchen standards rather than adapted from a prior use. It also signals a stronger and longer-term institutional commitment to food entrepreneurship infrastructure than a leased space renovation would.
This timeline reality is strategically significant for the Hub: a new-build city commercial kitchen is unlikely to open before the Hub's Q1–Q2 2027 Grand Opening target. This means the Hub will be the first new food entrepreneurship infrastructure to come online in Las Cruces -- establishing its brand, vendor relationships, and community identity before the city facility opens. First-mover advantage in this market is meaningful.

E.4 The Opportunity: Complementary Positioning and Pipeline Partnership
The existence of both a city commercial kitchen and the El Calvario Kitchen Incubator in Las Cruces is not a threat to the Hub. Properly framed, it is one of the strongest arguments for the Hub's viability -- and one of its most valuable partnership opportunities.
The Las Cruces Food Entrepreneur Pipeline: A Three-Stage Ecosystem
When the city's commercial kitchen, El Calvario, the Hub, and the SVEDC (South Valley Economic Development Center, Albuquerque) are understood as stages in a food entrepreneur's development journey, they form a coherent regional ecosystem -- not a competitive landscape. New Mexico already has a proven model for Stage 1 food business incubation: SVEDC has operated its Semilla and Mariposa programs since 2005, serving up to 45 food businesses at a time in Albuquerque. Critically, SVEDC explicitly does not serve full-service restaurant concepts (NAICS 722511-722514) -- the exact category the Hub occupies. This means SVEDC graduates who want to open a food stall serving customers directly have nowhere local to go. The Hub fills that gap for Las Cruces. City and nonprofit kitchens are production facilities -- their users generate no customer revenue within the facility. Hub vendors serve customers directly from Day 1 in a retail food hall context. This is not a minor operational difference; it is the difference between making food and running a business.
Dedicated Private Kitchen Per Stall
City and shared kitchens, including El Calvario, operate on a time-share model. Multiple users share equipment and schedule around each other. The Hub provides every vendor with their own fully equipped, private kitchen -- permanently assigned, available 100% of operating hours. This is a fundamentally different operational experience.
Community Destination Identity
City kitchens are industrial production spaces invisible to the public. The Hub is a 60-80 seat indoor dining destination with a specialty craft cider bar, monthly cultural festivals, live music, and a community gathering identity. No city kitchen competes with this.
Structured Incubator Pipeline with Graduation
El Calvario and city kitchens provide access and basic support. The Hub provides a three-stage, milestone-driven incubator pipeline with monthly P&L coaching, quality gates, permanent stall promotion, and SBA loan graduation support. This is a materially different level of structured business development support.
The Cider Bar

chunks.sectionTitle: Appendix E: The City Commercial Kitchen -- Competitive Landscape Analysis and Strategic Response
chunks.heading: Appendix E: The City Commercial Kitchen -- Competitive Landscape Analysis and Strategic Response
chunks.text:
No city kitchen has a 20-25 tap specialty craft cider bar featuring 8-10 New Mexico cideries, a Cider Club Membership program, and quarterly pairing dinners. This is unique to the Hub and creates a distinct social identity and recurring revenue stream that no public or nonprofit kitchen facility can match.
E.6 The Validation Signal: What the City's Investment Tells Investors
For investors reviewing this business plan, the city's decision to invest in a commercial kitchen facility should be read as a strong validation signal, not a competitive red flag. Here is why:
Demand Validation: When a city government decides to invest public funds in food entrepreneurship infrastructure, it means elected officials and their economic development staff have concluded that there is documented, underserved demand for this type of resource. This is the same market demand the Hub is entering. The city's investment is a third-party confirmation of the Hub's market thesis.
Grant Ecosystem Confirmation: Cities invest in commercial kitchens because the grant landscape for food entrepreneurship infrastructure -- USDA Resilient Food Systems Infrastructure grants, workforce development grants, downtown revitalization funding -- is robust and accessible. The fact that El Calvario alone received $383,000 in federal USDA funding confirms that the grant sources the Hub is pursuing are real and funded. The city's entry confirms the funding environment, not just the market demand.
Talent Pipeline Activated: The city's commercial kitchen and El Calvario's expansion together mean that the Las Cruces food entrepreneur community will be more active, better trained, and more ready to take their concepts to the next level by the time the Hub opens. The Hub's incubator stalls benefit from an enlarged, better-prepared pipeline of potential vendor candidates who have already tested their concepts in a licensed commercial kitchen environment.

Ecosystem Legitimacy: A city that invests in food entrepreneurship infrastructure has already made the political and economic argument that the food sector deserves public investment. That institutional support makes the Hub's grant applications, city partnership requests, and media positioning dramatically easier than they would be in a city with no civic food infrastructure.
The Bottom Line for Investors
The city's commercial kitchen is not the competition. It is proof of market demand, confirmation of the grant funding landscape, and the first stage of the pipeline that feeds the Hub's incubator program. The Hub is what comes after the city kitchen -- where food entrepreneurs go when they are ready to serve customers, build a business, and become a permanent part of Las Cruces's culinary identity.
