The main financial model budgets $25,000/year for utilities in common areas. Deep research into Las Cruces-specific utility rates and the actual energy demand of a multi-kitchen food hall in a desert climate reveals this figure requires significant upward revision. This supplement presents the corrected utility cost model and explains the drivers.

An 8,000 sq ft indoor, climate-controlled facility with 10-13 commercial kitchen operations in Las Cruces will consume dramatically more energy than the $25,000/year estimate in the main model. Las Cruces summer temperatures exceed 100 degrees F for months at a time; commercial kitchen exhaust creates substantial heat load that HVAC must counteract; and El Paso Electric's commercial rate structure includes demand charges on top of consumption rates. The corrected annual utility budget is $120,000-$175,000 -- six to seven times higher than the original estimate.

The Las Cruces dining market is anchored by deeply entrenched, multi-generational family restaurants with fierce customer loyalty. Understanding these incumbents -- who they serve, at what price points, and on which dining occasions -- is essential to defining exactly where the Hub captures share versus where it competes head-on.
Strategic Context
The Hub does not compete with these restaurants for the same customers on the same occasions. It creates a new occasion: the multi-concept social food destination. Customers who visit Chope's for Sunday family dinner are not substituting the Hub for Chope's -- they are adding the Hub to their dining rotation for different occasions. The Hub's primary competition for share of dining occasions is the decision to eat at home, not the decision of which NM restaurant to visit.

F.1 Grease Interceptor and FOG Compliance Plan
Las Cruces Utilities administers the FOG (Fats, Oils, and Grease) program under Municipal Code Section 28-186 et seq. All food service establishments are required to install, use, and maintain a grease interceptor. With 10-13 commercial kitchen stalls each generating significant grease discharge, this is a major infrastructure and ongoing compliance item.
Sizing Requirement
Each kitchen stall generates approximately 24-29 Drainage Fixture Units (DFUs) from its 3-compartment sink, prep sink, floor drains, mop sink, and pre-rinse station. With 10-13 stalls producing 240-377 raw DFUs (effective 150-250 DFUs after diversity factors), NM Plumbing Code (UPC 2021 Table 1014.3.6) requires a system exceeding the standard 2,000-gallon threshold. The recommended configuration is a 2,000-3,000 gallon gravity grease interceptor (GGI), either as a single unit or two 1,500-gallon units for separate kitchen zones. A licensed professional engineer must seal the sizing calculations before permit submission.

F.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce — Tabski Integration Path
Tabski’s native POS architecture handles multi-vendor back-end operations. The consumer-facing mobile ordering layer — allowing guests to browse menus, pre-order pickup, and manage loyalty across all vendor stalls — requires a separate evaluation during Phase 2 (Months 4–7). Three integration paths exist:
Tabski Native Online Ordering: Confirm with Tabski whether their platform includes a guest-facing online ordering module with multi-vendor checkout, loyalty, and push notifications. If yes, this is the lowest-cost and simplest path — no third-party integration required. Evaluate during Phase 2 vendor selection conversations.
White-Label Food Hall App (Third-Party via Tabski API): Platforms such as Olo, Lunchbox, or purpose-built food hall app vendors integrate with Tabski via API, providing a branded guest experience while routing orders to Tabski’s KDS. These typically cost $200–$600/month plus setup. Strongest option if Tabski’s native ordering module is limited.
QR-Code Web Ordering (Launch Minimum): If a full app is not ready for Grand Opening, a QR-code-linked web ordering system (table QR codes, pickup station QR codes) provides immediate digital ordering capability at near-zero incremental cost while the full app is built. This is acceptable as a 90-day bridge, not a permanent solution.
Recommendation: Do not build a custom app from scratch. Evaluate Tabski’s native online ordering first. If insufficient, select a third-party food hall app with a proven Tabski integration. Budget $2,400–$7,200/year for the digital commerce layer, separate from Tabski’s base $11,280/year POS cost. See Section 6.4 for the full strategic rationale and customer experience design. chunks.text:
This sensitivity analysis shows how the Hub's cumulative break-even month shifts under four occupancy scenarios (60%, 70%, 80%, and 90%) crossed with three utility cost scenarios ($100K, $125K, and $175K per year). The base case -- 80% stabilized occupancy and $150K utilities -- projects break-even at Month 18-20, consistent with the main financial model. The tables and scenario narratives below give investors and lenders clear visibility into how key assumptions affect the timeline.
How to Read This Analysis
The break-even month shown is the first month in which the Hub's cumulative cash position (revenue minus all operating costs since soft opening) turns positive. A lower number is better. Color coding: Blue = base case zone (Month 18-22, in line with plan); Green = better than plan (Month 18 or earlier); Gold = moderately extended (Month 23-26); Red = significantly extended (Month 27+). All scenarios assume the same staggered vendor onboarding ramp (55% occupancy at Month 1, reaching the scenario occupancy ceiling by Month 9).

I.2 Scenario Narratives
Best Case: 90% Occupancy + $100K Utilities -- Break-Even Month 15
Achieved if vendor recruitment exceeds expectations (all 13 stalls filled rapidly), the Cider Club launches strongly (100+ members by Month 3), and utility costs are kept below $8,400/month through energy-efficient equipment choices and favorable summer HVAC performance. At this scenario, the Hub reaches cumulative break-even three to five months ahead of plan, and Year 2 EBITDA approaches $450,000. This is the scenario that justifies a higher valuation at Year 5 buyout.
Base Case: 80% Occupancy + $150K Utilities -- Break-Even Month 20
The primary financial model. Vendor occupancy reaches 80% stabilization (10-11 of 13 stalls) by Month 9, utility costs run $12,500/month consistent with the desert climate reforecast, and the Cider Club builds to 75 members by Year 1. Year 1 EBITDA of $114,000 reflects this scenario. This is the projection presented to SBA lenders and grant agencies.
Conservative Case: 70% Occupancy + $150K Utilities -- Break-Even Month 26
Vendor recruitment is slower than planned -- the Hub stabilizes at 9-10 of 13 stalls, reflecting one or two unfilled incubator slots and slower ghost kitchen revenue. Utilities remain at the desert reforecast baseline. Break-even extends to approximately Month 26. In this scenario, the $272,000 working capital reserve is fully consumed and an additional $60,000-$90,000 bridge may be needed. The mitigation is activating the Fallback Phase 1 plan from Supplement C: open fewer stalls, reduce staffing overhead, and pursue CDFI bridge financing.

The Hub's main financial model budgets $22,000 per year for insurance. This supplement validates that estimate against current market data, distinguishes between the FLIP vendor-level premiums referenced in the plan and the operator-level coverages the Hub actually requires, and provides a coverage-by-coverage cost model with a clear recommendation to obtain a formal broker quote before the SBA loan application is submitted.
Critical Distinction: Vendor Insurance vs. Hub Operator Insurance
FLIP (Food Liability Insurance Program) data shows food vendor premiums around $61/month ($732/year) -- this covers an individual food stall operator for general liability on their specific concept. This is the insurance each of the Hub's 13 vendors carries for their own stall operations. The Hub as the facility operator requires an entirely different, larger, and more complex insurance program covering the entire 8,000 sq ft facility, the craft cider bar with liquor service, all employees across all hub-level functions, and the capital assets of the buildout. These are two distinct insurance programs; both are required.
J.1 Required Coverage Types -- Hub Operator Level
As the Hub operator, five distinct coverage types are required. A sixth -- business interruption insurance -- is strongly recommended given the Hub's fixed cost structure and SBA debt service obligations. NM ABC requires proof of liquor liability insurance as a condition of the Dispenser license application, making that coverage non-optional.

chunks.sectionTitle: Supplement K: West Picacho & Motel Boulevard MRA -- Site Opportunity Analysis
chunks.heading: Supplement K: West Picacho & Motel Boulevard MRA -- Site Opportunity Analysis
chunks.text:
The City of Las Cruces adopted the West Picacho and Motel Boulevard Metropolitan Redevelopment Area (MRA) plan on December 1, 2025, and on March 16, 2026, the City Council unanimously approved GRT increment financing for the MRA -- one of six MRAs receiving this designation citywide. This supplement analyzes whether locating the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub within this MRA boundary represents a stronger strategic option than the currently planned downtown footprint, and what the financial and operational implications of each path are.
Bottom Line Up Front
The W. Picacho MRA offers a genuinely compelling financial incentive package -- property tax deferral, permit fee waivers, expedited review, and GRT increment reinvestment -- and the Shoto mixed-use catalytic site is a real opportunity. However, the MRA location trades the Hub's strongest asset (downtown walkability and destination identity) for financial savings. This is a viable alternative site worth serious investigation, but it is not a clear upgrade over downtown. The decision hinges on one question John should answer before proceeding: what is the rent differential between a downtown adaptive reuse building and a West Picacho corridor site? If the MRA incentives close that gap without sacrificing foot traffic, the MRA becomes the better option. If downtown is already competitively priced, the MRA savings may not offset the location risk.
K.1 What the MRA Is and What Was Just Approved
An MRA (Metropolitan Redevelopment Area) is a city-designated zone that unlocks public investment tools to stimulate private development in underutilized corridors. The W. Picacho and Motel Boulevard MRA covers approximately a 1.5-mile corridor bounded by Tashiro Drive/McClure Road to the north, the BNSF Railroad tracks to the east, West Hadley Avenue to the south, and the Rio Grande to the west -- as shown in the boundary map included with this supplement.

The March 16, 2026 City Council vote approved GRT increment financing for this MRA, establishing a baseline of approximately $42,000 per month in existing GRT revenue. Up to 75% of any GRT revenue generated above that baseline -- from new businesses opening or existing businesses growing within the MRA -- can be reinvested back into the MRA for up to 20 years. This does not increase anyone's tax rate. It means that economic growth generated by businesses like the Hub stays in the corridor that generated it.

K.2 Financial Incentives Available Inside the MRA
Operating within the MRA boundary makes the Hub eligible for a stack of incentives that are not available to a downtown location. These are real, documented, and available now -- not speculative future programs.

Property tax deferral (up to 20 years)
Building rehabilitation and improvements within an MRA can qualify for property tax deferral under NM Metropolitan Redevelopment Code. The tax is not forgiven -- it is deferred, meaning it becomes payable when the property transfers ownership or at the end of the deferral period. For a tenant/operator rather than property owner, the benefit flows through reduced rent from a landlord who receives the deferral.

Total Estimated Incentive Value
Combining property tax deferral, permit fee waivers, expedited review schedule savings, and GRT reinvestment, the total MRA incentive package for the Hub is estimated at $75,000-$150,000 over the first five years of operation. This is meaningful but not transformative -- it represents roughly 5-10% of total project cost. It is enough to shift the financial model from marginal to comfortable on certain cost lines, but not enough on its own to justify a location that underperforms on foot traffic.
K.3 The Shoto Mixed-Use Hub: The Catalytic Site Opportunity
The W. Picacho MRA plan identifies three catalytic projects. The Shoto mixed-use hub -- approximately 42 acres near Tashiro Drive -- is envisioned as a shopping center/plaza development and is the site most relevant to a food hall. The city is actively seeking private developers to anchor this vision.
For John, this creates a rare scenario: rather than leasing space in someone else's building, the Hub could potentially become the anchor tenant or co-developer of a purpose-built mixed-use development on the Shoto site, with the city as an active partner rather than a regulatory gatekeeper. Purpose-built food halls consistently outperform adaptive reuse conversions on buildout efficiency, kitchen layout flexibility, and long-term lease terms.

City staff are actively looking for private developers to bring this to life. John contacting Blairre Flores at Las Cruces Economic Development before any other developer claims this conversation is time-sensitive.
Purpose-built construction possible
A ground-up food hall designed for 13 kitchen stalls from the start eliminates most of the adaptive reuse risks: asbestos, undersized electrical service, non-standard plumbing. Buildout cost per stall decreases; timeline reliability increases.
Parking is solvable
42-acre site means parking is not a constraint. A food hall at this scale needs 80-120 surface parking spaces; the Shoto site can accommodate this without shared parking arrangements or structured parking costs.
Residential adjacency
The MRA plan includes affordable and multi-family housing components. Residential density adjacent to the Hub is a significant foot traffic driver -- residents of the development become regular Hub customers by default.
K.4 Honest Assessment: What the MRA Location Gives Up
The MRA opportunity is real. The incentives are documented. The Shoto site is a genuine opening. But a balanced analysis requires acknowledging the meaningful advantages the Hub would sacrifice by moving from downtown to the W. Picacho corridor.

Decision Implication
1. What is the actual rent differential between a downtown site and a W. Picacho corridor site?
Request quotes from NAI 1st Valley or SVN commercial brokers for comparable sq footage in both areas. Downtown adaptive reuse: $12-$18/sq ft NNN annually. W. Picacho corridor: likely $6-$10/sq ft NNN annually.
If downtown costs $12/sq ft ($96K/year) and W. Picacho costs $7/sq ft ($56K/year), the MRA saves $40,000/year before any incentives. At that level, the incentive package makes the MRA decisively superior financially. If rents are similar, the downtown foot traffic advantage wins.
2. Is public transit connecting the W. Picacho corridor to NMSU and downtown adequate?
Check RoadRUNNER Transit route maps. The 2 and 4 routes serve W. Picacho. Confirm stop proximity to the Shoto site specifically.
If transit connectivity to NMSU is within 0.5 miles of a stop, the student demographic accessibility concern is mitigated significantly.
3. Is the Shoto site truly available, and on what terms would the city partner with a private developer?
Contact Blairre Flores directly: (575) 541-2425 or economicdev@las-cruces.org. Ask specifically about the Shoto catalytic site, developer interest to date, and the city's vision for anchor tenant structure.
If the city is open to a ground lease or co-development arrangement with the Hub as anchor tenant, the Shoto site becomes the strongest possible option. If it requires John to buy 42 acres, it is not viable without a development partner.
4. Do the MRA incentives stack with the existing grant program?
Confirm with MVEDA and City Economic Development whether being in the MRA makes Hub MORE eligible for NMFA, EPE, and HFFF grants -- or whether it changes any eligibility criteria.
If MRA location strengthens grant eligibility AND provides incentives, the cumulative financial advantage could exceed $200,000 over five years -- a compelling case for the MRA.

chunks.text:
Supplement K analyzed the MRA financial incentives and site decision framework. This supplement incorporates newly available market research data to strengthen the quantitative case for the MRA location and introduces a phased development model that substantially de-risks the capital commitment. Together, Supplements K and L constitute the complete MRA opportunity analysis.
What This Supplement Adds to Supplement K
Supplement K answered: what are the MRA incentives, what does the Hub give up by leaving downtown, and what four questions should drive the site decision. This supplement answers: what does the market data actually say about demand at this specific location, how does a phased outdoor-first model change the financial risk profile, and how should the concept be positioned differently for the W. Picacho community versus downtown. These are the data gaps that remained after Supplement K.
L.1 Quantified Market Data: Who Is Actually in This Trade Area
The W. Picacho corridor serves a distinct demographic profile from downtown Las Cruces. This is not a weakness -- it is a different customer opportunity that requires a different positioning strategy. The data below is drawn from current census and traffic sources and should be used directly in Section 2 (Market Analysis) if the MRA site is selected.

One concern about the W. Picacho location is whether it has adequate drive-by visibility and vehicle access compared to downtown. Traffic count data resolves this concern directly.

Traffic Count Implication for the Business Plan
18,000-19,000 vehicles per day along W. Picacho is a stronger drive-by traffic base than most downtown Las Cruces streets. Combined with the residential density of the surrounding neighborhoods, this corridor offers a high-frequency customer base that visits for everyday occasions -- not just destination dining. A food hall that captures even 0.5% of daily pass-through traffic (90-95 vehicles converting to visitors) at $20 average spend generates $657,000/year in traffic-capture revenue alone, before any destination visits are counted.
Behavioral Evidence: Locals Already Show Up for Multi-Vendor Food
One of the strongest arguments against a food hall in a new location is the question of whether the local population will change its dining behavior. In the W. Picacho MRA trade area, the behavioral evidence says they already have:
Farmers & Crafts Market of Las Cruces, described by Visit Las Cruces as one of the top-rated farmers markets in the country, regularly draws crowds who move between multiple vendors in a shared outdoor format -- exactly the multi-vendor food experience the Hub provides in a permanent setting.

chunks.heading: Supplement L: W. Picacho MRA -- Market Data, Phasing Model, and Concept Refinement
chunks.text:
Food truck clusters operate throughout the city along Solano and Lohman, demonstrating comfort with ordering from non-traditional food service formats.
The Borderland Car Show & Food Truck Festival drew 25 food trucks and an estimated 5,000-10,000 attendees, proving that a curated, multi-vendor food event is not a foreign concept to Las Cruces residents -- it is already a proven draw when promoted.
Informal food truck park experiments in parking lots have emerged organically, showing market pull without any formal infrastructure. The Hub formalizes and upgrades what the market is already trying to create on its own.
What the Behavioral Evidence Does Not Prove
Event attendance at a festival or farmers market does not directly validate a permanent, year-round food hall at a specific address. The Borderland Car Show drew 5,000-10,000 for a single event; a permanent food hall needs 2,500-3,500 unique visitors per week sustained across 52 weeks. The behavioral evidence validates the format and the appetite -- it does not substitute for a pre-opening market survey or signed vendor LOIs as the primary demand validation tools.
Tourism Layer: The Hub as an Authentic Visitor Stop

For the W. Picacho MRA location, the Hub's positioning statement shifts from the downtown version. The following language is ready for insertion into Section 3 (Concept Overview) if the MRA site is selected:
Recommended Positioning Statement -- W. Picacho MRA Version
A year-round borderland food hub anchoring the W. Picacho corridor revitalization -- bringing together beloved New Mexican and Mexican vendors and complementary concepts in a safe, shaded, family-friendly setting with accessible price points for local residents, and an authentic one-stop taste of Las Cruces for visitors arriving from White Sands, the Organ Mountains, and I-10. Where Las Cruces families eat, gather, and celebrate food the way they always have -- just with a permanent home that's finally worthy of it.
This positioning deliberately frames the Hub as an upgrade to existing behavior rather than an imported concept. It leads with community identity, not culinary novelty. It names the MRA corridor explicitly, turning a location that investors might view as a risk into the story's central argument. And it speaks directly to the grant review criteria for NMFA, EPE, and equity-focused funders who want to see investment reaching the communities that need it most.
L.3 Phased Development Model: Prove Demand Before Committing Full Capital
The most significant new insight from this additional research is the phased development approach. The existing business plan commits to a full 8,000 sq ft indoor food hall buildout from Day 1 -- a $1.4M+ capital commitment before a single customer has visited. At the W. Picacho MRA location, a three-phase model allows the Hub to prove demand at lower capital risk before committing to the permanent enclosed structure.
Why Phasing Changes the Risk Profile

Phase 1 generates revenue and market validation data before Phase 2 capital is committed. This is the model that Smallman Galley (Pittsburgh), La Marqueta (New York), and other incubator food markets used successfully.

Phase 1 cash flow at conservative revenue ($16,400) vs. mid-cost ($30,000) = monthly deficit of $13,600. Phase 1 at growth revenue ($27,200) vs. mid-cost ($30,000) = near break-even monthly. Phase 1 does not generate profit -- it generates market validation data at a capital cost of $300,000-$500,000 vs. $1.4M for the full buildout. The working capital requirement for Phase 1 is approximately $80,000-$120,000 (4-6 months of deficit cover) rather than the $272,000 required by the full Phase 1 indoor model.
The Core Phasing Argument for Investors
The phased model asks investors and lenders to commit $300,000-$500,000 in Phase 1, generate 12 months of market validation data, then make the Phase 2 commitment of $600,000-$900,000 backed by actual operating history. Total capital deployed in Phases 1+2 ($900,000-$1,400,000) is comparable to the full downtown buildout, but the timing and risk profile are fundamentally different. The SBA loan application in Phase 2 is supported by 12 months of revenue, vendor performance data, and GRT generation history -- a dramatically stronger application than a startup with no operating history.

Supplement M.1 Investor FAQ
What happens if grants are not awarded? The project does not assume grants are guaranteed. If awards are delayed or declined, the Hub shifts to Plan B or Plan C: smaller phased launch, proof events, expanded sponsor outreach, investor LOIs, revised scope, and reapplication with stronger validation.
What happens if SBA financing is declined? The Hub will evaluate CDFI/community lender options, investor-led equity, a smaller first site, food truck park operations, cider/event pad activation, and commissary partnerships before committing to full indoor buildout.
Who owns or controls the real estate? The preferred structure is site control through purchase, ground lease, or long-term lease with protections adequate for buildout investment. Final structure will depend on site selection, grant eligibility, lender requirements, and investor terms.
What security or priority do investors receive? Investor security will be negotiated with counsel and may include preferred return, milestone-based funding release, reporting rights, defined use-of-funds controls, collateral where available, or project-level equity participation.
How does the project proceed with $0 founder cash? The plan proceeds only if grants, investors, sponsorships, lender financing, vendor commitments, pre-sales, or phased-launch savings create a credible capital base. Founder contribution is operational leadership, business planning, grant pursuit, sponsor outreach, vendor development, and project execution, not personal cash.
What milestones must be met before full buildout? Minimum milestones include site control, capital stack commitments, lender or investor approval, core permits pathway, vendor LOIs, sponsor package pipeline, proof-event results, and a working capital plan sufficient for the Year 1 ramp.

chunks.heading: Supplement N: Policy Alignment Analysis — Elevate Las Cruces (2020) and East Lohman Development Plan (2021)
chunks.text:
This supplement documents the Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub's alignment with two adopted city planning documents: Elevate Las Cruces (City Comprehensive Plan through 2045, adopted February 18, 2020) and the East Lohman Development Plan (subarea implementation plan, adopted September 20, 2021). Together, these documents create an explicit policy basis for the Hub that strengthens every grant application, every city partnership request, and every investor narrative. The Hub is not asking the City of Las Cruces to invent a new policy pathway. It is asking the city to fund and support a project that directly implements plans already adopted by City Council.
The Strategic Framing for Every City Meeting
Present the Hub not as a business seeking city support, but as a private implementation partner for adopted city policy. Elevate Las Cruces and the East Lohman Development Plan have already established the policy justification. The Hub delivers on it.
N.1 Elevate Las Cruces — The Comprehensive Plan Foundation
Elevate Las Cruces is the City's adopted comprehensive plan through 2045, organized around Community Prosperity, Community Livability, and Community Environment. It was produced through an 18-month public participation process including community-builder meetings, subcommittees, open houses, and three online surveys. Its findings represent the documented preferences of Las Cruces residents — and they align directly with what the Hub delivers.

When applying to NMFA, HFFF, EPE/MVEDA, DLCP, USDA, or any city-administered program: cite the specific Elevate Las Cruces survey scores above. Grant reviewers at the City of Las Cruces and MVEDA will recognize these as their own adopted priorities. Growth Scenario and Land Use Policy
Elevate Las Cruces adopted a Consensus Scenario for growth through 2045 that explicitly favors centers, corridors, infill, and mixed-use nodes over isolated, auto-dependent fringe development. The plan projects 1.607 million additional square feet of retail and 1.103 million additional square feet of office growth city-wide, with downtown treated as an existing, high-priority mixed-use center — not a speculative future growth area. This means public tools and incentives are already authorized and expected to flow toward downtown projects.

For the Hub, the key policy implication is that locating downtown is the city's preferred investment geography. A downtown Hub site activates the city's highest-policy-priority center, qualifies for the Downtown TIDD, sits within or adjacent to the Downtown-Amador Proximo Qualified Opportunity Zone, and aligns with the Arts and Cultural District Plan (2018) that links cultural programming to economic growth. These are not coincidental benefits — they are the direct result of choosing the location that city policy has already designated as the priority.

Sawmill Market — The City's Own Cited Precedent
The East Lohman plan explicitly reviews Sawmill Community Land Trust and Sawmill Market (Albuquerque) as a development precedent. It notes that the Sawmill Market food hall emerged from phased mixed-use investment and that subsidized housing and affordability-oriented development did not harm commercial viability, market-rate demand, or private investment in trendy retail and restaurant space. The plan specifically states: the food hall attracted private investment that followed, rather than preceded, mixed-income neighborhood building.
The Grant Application Implication
The Las Cruces City Council has already endorsed Sawmill Market as a positive precedent in an adopted planning document. When the Hub presents Sawmill Market as comparable market analysis and validation in Section 9 of the business plan — or in grant applications to the City of Las Cruces — it is citing the city's own adopted planning documents back to city staff. That is a far stronger position than citing an outside case study.

Shaded outdoor seating Elevate Las Cruces and the East Lohman plan both emphasize public gathering space with shade as a design priority in the desert climate. The Hub's outdoor seating area should include shade structures, landscape, and comfortable seating that functions as public space, not just overflow seating.
Active pedestrian frontage Both plans require commercial ground floors to present active, transparent frontages to the public right-of-way. The Hub's counter/serving window design and any storefront glazing should prioritize street presence over internal focus.
Event capacity and public programming The comprehensive plan's cultural district goals and the East Lohman neighborhood center concept both treat community events as integral to successful mixed-use places. The Hub's monthly cultural festivals and quarterly night markets directly advance this policy goal — document them as community programming commitments in permit applications and grant narratives.
Rear or screened parking Both plans prefer parking that does not dominate pedestrian frontages. Any Hub parking should be rear-located, screened, or shared with adjacent uses — not a surface lot fronting the street.
Bike access and wayfinding Downtown mobility plans include active transportation infrastructure. The Hub should provide secure bike parking and appear in downtown wayfinding signage as a cultural destination.

chunks.heading: Supplement O: Realize Las Cruces 2025 Zoning Code -- Site Selection Analysis
chunks.text:
Realize Las Cruces is the City's new character-based zoning code, passed by City Council in February 2025 and upheld after a public petition challenge in May 2025. It is the first major overhaul of Las Cruces land use regulations since 2001 -- a 24-year gap. The new code fundamentally changes how commercial and mixed-use development is classified, where food service uses are permitted, and what parking is required. This supplement documents the direct implications for the Hub's site selection, permitting strategy, and cost structure.
How to Access the Official Zoning Data
The City of Las Cruces maintains a public ArcGIS group layer called '2025 Zoning Code (Full Context Group)' containing four layers: (1) Owner Parcel -- most current parcel data from the County Assessor; (2) Overlays -- mixed-use overlay, town centers, urban/rural character; (3) 2025 Zoning Code -- primary layer with zoning district, character, town center, and mixed-use data per parcel; (4) Zoning District Underlay -- detail for Multi-Zoned Parcels (MZP). Access at: las-cruces.maps.arcgis.com (Item ID: d8afcd53b511453e91e8b09aa8221910). Note: a public parcel vacancy map is not yet available -- contact the City's NAT (Neighborhood Action Team) directly for parcel availability information.
O.1 The New Zoning Structure -- What It Means for the Hub
The 2025 code organizes all Las Cruces parcels along two axes: Character Area (how urban or rural the location is) and Zoning District (what uses and densities are permitted). A food hall with a cider bar and commercial kitchen sits primarily in the commercial use category, but the new code creates multiple viable zoning contexts beyond the old Commercial Retail designation.

O.3 Parking Minimum Elimination -- Cost Impact
One of the most financially significant provisions of the Realize Las Cruces code for the Hub is the elimination of auto parking minimums in Urban Character Areas. Under the old code, a food hall of 8,000 sq ft could have faced a parking requirement of 40-80 spaces (1 per 100-200 sq ft of dining area) -- at $5,000-$15,000 per surface space and $20,000-$50,000 per structured space. The 2025 code eliminates this requirement in Urban Character Areas.
Parking Cost Savings -- Urban Character Area Hub Site
If the Hub site is in a downtown Urban Character Area, parking minimums are eliminated under Realize Las Cruces. A 40-space surface lot requirement would have cost $200,000-$600,000. Elimination of this requirement directly reduces buildout cost and can free that budget for kitchen infrastructure, cider bar equipment, or working capital reserves. Confirm Urban Character designation for your specific parcel using the 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS layer before finalizing buildout cost projections.

Note: Even without a parking minimum, providing some customer parking remains a practical necessity in Las Cruces given the city's car-dependent transportation patterns. The goal is to negotiate shared parking agreements with adjacent properties or nearby public lots rather than building dedicated parking into the Hub buildout cost. The Realize Las Cruces code also allows up to 50% of any remaining parking requirements to be substituted with bicycle parking -- further reducing the surface parking footprint if any minimum remains applicable.
O.4 Multi-Zoned Parcels (MZP) -- What to Watch For
Some parcels in Las Cruces are classified as Multi-Zoned Parcels (MZP), meaning they contain multiple zoning districts. The 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS group includes a Zoning District Underlay layer specifically for these parcels, showing each zoning district within the parcel boundary. Character, mixed-use, and town center designations typically remain consistent across the parcel even if zoning districts differ.
For site due diligence: if a target parcel shows as MZP in the 2025 Zoning Code layer, review the Zoning District Underlay to confirm which zoning district covers the portion of the parcel where the Hub would be located. A parcel that is partly Commercial Retail and partly NH-2, for example, may have very different use permissions depending on where the Hub's footprint falls.

The West Picacho and Motel Boulevard MRA (analyzed in Supplements K and L) gains additional significance under the Realize Las Cruces code. Picacho MRA site parcels are designated as NH-3, Mixed-Use, or Commercial Retail in the 2025 Zoning Code layer, the Hub would have clear permitting pathways without needing any rezoning. The MRA's TIDD and other incentive tools are also explicitly linked to the new code's redevelopment priorities.

Picacho MRA: open the 2025 Zoning Code ArcGIS layer and check the specific parcels identified in the Shoto hub area (referenced in Supplement K) for their current zoning district and character designation. chunks.text:
Two Metropolitan Redevelopment Area plans have been adopted by the City of Las Cruces that directly affect the Hub's site strategy, grant positioning, and community mandate. The West Picacho and Motel MRA Plan (adopted November 2025; GRT increment financing approved March 2026) explicitly names a food hall, eatertainment district, and commercial kitchen as named community development priorities. The El Paseo and South Solano MRA Plan (adopted April 16, 2026) cites the Farmington, NM food hub/commercial kitchen as a successful MRA case study and calls for a business incubator along its corridors. Together, these two documents constitute the strongest available evidence that the City of Las Cruces has formally endorsed the Hub's model in two separate planning documents — before the Hub has even opened its doors.
P.1 West Picacho and Motel MRA Plan — Direct Site and Policy Alignment
The West Picacho and Motel MRA covers approximately the corridor from the BNSF Railroad tracks west along West Picacho Avenue to Valley Drive, including Motel Boulevard. It was created in March 2023 when City Council unanimously designated two MRA areas. The plan was produced by Stantec Consulting and adopted November 2025.
P.1.1 — The Food Hall and Eatertainment District Are Named in the Plan
Strategy 3.4 — Direct Quote from the Adopted MRA Plan
"Work with owner/developer to create an 'eatertainment' district in the northwest corner of the Tashiro catalyst site... Investigate potential for a commercial kitchen in the eatertainment district to complement small-scale start-ups/food trucks." Strategy 3.5 adds: "A shared commercial kitchen can help launch home businesses to food trucks to restaurants or catering." Community Big Ideas section: residents explicitly named 'a food hall' as a desired use for the Tashiro Drive vacant parcel. These are not general policy statements — they are named project recommendations in an adopted plan.

The El Paseo and South Solano MRA Plan (adopted April 16, 2026) covers approximately 1,200 acres between downtown Las Cruces and NMSU, centered on El Paseo Road and South Solano Drive. While the Hub is not currently targeting this corridor as a primary site, the plan contains three elements of direct relevance: a food incubator case study, an explicit business incubator recommendation, and the most detailed explanation of MRA financing tools available for any Las Cruces site.
P.2.1 — Farmington Food Hub: NM MRA Precedent Now Cited by Las Cruces
The Farmington Harvest Food Hub Case Study — Cited in Las Cruces' Own MRA Plan
The El Paseo MRA plan (April 2026) includes Farmington, NM's Harvest Food Hub and Kitchen at San Juan College as a successful case study for MRA-supported food entrepreneurship infrastructure. Key details: the project provided a commercial kitchen for entrepreneurs and a local food distribution center; the City of Farmington's MRA Plan identified the need and provided support for land acquisition and funding; NMSU's Local Food, Local Places grant covered operating costs for the first five years of programming and facility needs. This is the second NM MRA planning document in Las Cruces to identify food hub/commercial kitchen infrastructure as a city-endorsed development model. The Hub's commissary kitchen component is directly aligned with this precedent.
Application to the Hub: the Farmington model used NMSU as a primary program and funding partner. The Hub's commissary kitchen, combined with NMSU's existing food entrepreneurship curriculum at the Arrowhead Center, creates the same partnership structure. The USDA Local Food, Local Places grant that funded Farmington's operations for five years is a directly applicable funding mechanism the Hub should pursue in Phase 1.
P.2.2 — Business Incubator Explicitly Called For in El Paseo MRA Plan

MRA Implementation Tools Available to the Hub
Because the Hub would implement explicit MRA plan strategies, it may be eligible for MRA-specific implementation funding and partnership mechanisms that are not available to a generic downtown project.
Tool
How MRA Enables It

MRA Public-Private Partnership (P3)
MRA designation creates a state anti-donation clause exemption, allowing the City to directly partner with private entities on redevelopment projects. The El Paseo/S. Solano MRA plan explicitly cites Farmington NM's Harvest Food Hub as a P3 precedent for exactly this use case

MRA Bond Financing
MRA plans may issue bonds backed by tax increment revenues (GRT + property tax) from within the MRA boundary to fund catalytic infrastructure projects

This appendix delivers the complete three-statement financial model required by SBA 7(a) lenders, accredited investors, and every major grant program the Hub is pursuing. It extends and formalizes the monthly cash flow in Supplement A by presenting, side-by-side:
F.1 Sources and Uses of Funds (capital stack and pre-opening cost allocation)

F.6 Key Financial Ratios and Covenants -- Debt service coverage, current ratio, quick ratio, and SBA-required metrics
F.7 Sensitivity Walk -- How the cash flow statement moves under stress scenarios
F.8 Notes to the Financial Statements
Basis of Presentation
These statements are prepared using the accrual basis of accounting in conformity with U.S. GAAP as applied to small private operating companies. Revenue recognition follows ASC 606 (the vendor license fee and percentage rent are recognized over the service period; event revenue is recognized when the event occurs; cider bar revenue is recognized at point of sale). Depreciation uses the straight-line method over assigned useful lives (FF&E 7 years, leasehold improvements 15 years per the lease term, POS and software 3 years). All dollar amounts are rounded to the nearest $1,000 in the summary statements; the monthly model in Supplement A retains single-dollar precision.

It is prepared using the direct method, which shows actual cash receipts and cash payments by category (preferred by FASB and typically requested by SBA reviewers). The direct method is more transparent to lenders than the indirect method because every line is a literal cash movement.
Three activity categories govern the classification:
Operating Activities: Cash flows from core business operations -- collecting from vendors and customers, paying staff, suppliers, and operating costs.
Investing Activities: Cash flows related to long-term assets -- the initial buildout, FF&E purchases, and any subsequent capital improvements.
Financing Activities: Cash flows related to capital structure -- SBA loan proceeds, pre-opening grant awards (equity equivalent; owner cash $0), grant receipts, SBA principal repayments, and member distributions.

Interpreting the Negative Cash Position in Years 1-2
A cumulative cash position of -$211,900 at the end of Year 1 and -$193,000 at the end of Year 2 does not mean the business runs out of cash. Those figures represent the cumulative cash burn below opening-day cash reserves. The $272,000 working capital reserve funded at opening (Section F.1, Uses of Funds) absorbs this burn. The Hub ends Year 2 with approximately $79,000 remaining in working capital reserves ($272,000 minus $193,000) and ends Year 3 with positive operating cash generation of $288,900. The true end-of-period cash balance equals opening reserves plus cumulative change -- which stays positive throughout. A supplemental cash-on-hand reconciliation is provided in Section F.5 of this appendix.
What This Statement Tells Lenders and Investors
Year 1 is a negative operating cash flow year -- expected and fully funded by working capital reserves. Year 2 achieves roughly break-even operating cash (zero). Year 3 generates approximately $289,000 in positive operating cash flow -- sufficient to cover SBA principal payments ($56,500), begin member distributions ($50,000), and still retain cash for future capital needs. This is the classic food-hall ramp profile documented in Supplement A and validated by the comparable-market analysis in Section 9.

Covenant Risk in Years 1 and 2
Debt Service Coverage Ratio (DSCR) is the single most important SBA covenant. Year 1 and Year 2 are below 1.25x because the Hub is ramping. This is a known and expected pattern for SBA 7(a) startup loans in hospitality and retail. The standard mitigation is to negotiate a covenant holiday or stepped covenant structure in the loan agreement: no DSCR test in Year 1, 1.0x minimum in Year 2, 1.25x starting Year 3. This is requested at origination, not retroactively. Supplement C on SBA strategy already flags this as a negotiation point; this appendix quantifies exactly what is needed.

The base case Year 1 needs approximately $369K in operating cash support. The working capital reserve in Uses of Funds is $272K. The $97K gap is planned to be covered by deferred vendor buildout contributions (vendor-paid equipment for a discount on rent in Months 4-6) and/or by establishing a $100K SBA-backed working capital line of credit at origination, drawn only if needed. Supplement C's SBA fallback plan activates if the conservative or stress scenario materializes. This appendix makes the capital gap explicit and quantified -- lenders respect this far more than a plan that claims no gap exists.

Note 1: Organization and Basis of Presentation

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: Supplement A Monthly Figure
chunks.text:
The Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub ("the Hub") will operate as a New Mexico Limited Liability Company. These pro forma statements reflect the twelve-month fiscal year beginning on the Grand Opening date (targeted October 2026, subject to Phase 1 milestone gates). The Hub is a pass-through entity for tax purposes; income tax obligations flow to members and are not recognized as a corporate-level expense. All member distributions shown in the Statement of Cash Flows represent cash distributions to members, separate from any tax distributions that may be required by the Operating Agreement.
Note 2: Revenue Recognition (ASC 606)
Vendor Stall Rent: Base license fees are recognized straight-line over the license term. Percentage rent is recognized monthly based on vendor-reported gross sales, with reconciliation at quarter-end.
Cider Bar Revenue: Point-of-sale recognition at transaction completion. COGS matched at time of sale based on weighted-average cost.
Cider Club Memberships: Prepaid annual memberships create deferred revenue at purchase and recognize ratably over the 12-month subscription term.
Commissary and Ghost Kitchen: Hourly and monthly rentals recognized in the period used; prepaid blocks create deferred revenue.
Events: Recognized on the date the event occurs. Deposits received in advance are deferred.
Grants: Recognized as contra-equity credits upon receipt per nonprofit-adjacent accounting guidance for restricted grants with performance obligations; unrestricted grants flow to revenue. The Hub's grants are primarily restricted for specific buildout or program use, so contra-equity is the dominant treatment.
Note 3: Depreciation Policy
Leasehold improvements are depreciated straight-line over 15 years, matching the initial lease term plus one renewal option. Equipment and FF&E are depreciated over 7 years using straight-line method. POS hardware and software integration work are depreciated over 3 years. Annual depreciation expense is $68,000 based on the $1.14M gross buildout and equipment base.
Note 4: Debt Structure (SBA 7(a))

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: Supplement A Monthly Figure
chunks.text:
The SBA 7(a) loan of $850,000 is modeled at a 10-year term, 25-year real-estate-component amortization where applicable, at an initial rate of 9.625% (Prime + 3.0%). Interest expense declines annually as the principal balance amortizes. SBA principal and interest payments are modeled as cash outflows (principal in Financing, interest in Operating, per GAAP). The loan is secured by all business assets and a personal guarantee from the member. See Supplement C for the full SBA strategy and fallback plan.
Note 5: Material Estimates and Assumptions
The key estimates driving these projections, ranked by impact:
Vendor Occupancy Ramp: 7 of 13 stalls at Month 1, reaching 13 of 13 by Month 11. Validated by five comparable food hall openings documented in Section 9. ±10 percentage points of ramp speed drives approximately ±$90,000 of Year 1 revenue.
Cider Bar Volume: $13,500 average monthly revenue at steady state, 22% COGS. Based on Las Cruces-specific beverage consumption data and comparable cider bar revenue from New Mexico cideries. ±20% volume drives ±$32,000 of Year 1 revenue.
Utility Cost: $147,000 Year 1 average. Based on deep research into El Paso Electric commercial rates and demand charges, Las Cruces Utilities water tier structure, and NM Gas therm pricing. See Supplement B. ±$25,000 of utility cost is within the conservative/base/stress range modeled.
Personnel Cost: $489,000 wages plus $107,500 loaded benefits and taxes. Based on $17-$22/hour market rate for Las Cruces food service, specific Hub headcount (GM, Marketing, Cider Bar Manager, 2 floor leads, rotating staff).
Lease Cost: $8,000/month base with 3% annual escalation. Based on Las Cruces commercial real estate market average of $35/sq ft for a ~2,700 sq ft footprint. A signed LOI will replace this assumption with a specific negotiated rate.
Note 6: Subsequent Event Disclosure

N.4 Opportunity Zones
Official Program Summary
Opportunity Zones are an economic development tool to incentivize long-term private sector investment in low-income communities. The federal program provides: (1) temporary deferral of capital gains reinvested in a Qualified Opportunity Fund (until Dec 31, 2026 or disposition); (2) step-up in basis of 10% if held 5 years, additional 5% if held 7 years; (3) permanent exclusion from taxable income of capital gains from the sale of OZ investment if held 10+ years. Downtown Las Cruces/Amador Próximo is one of two designated Opportunity Zones in Las Cruces.

chunks.sectionTitle: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.heading: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.text:
Q.1 Purpose of This Supplement
This supplement documents the regional tourism context that supports the Hub’s visitor demand assumptions. It draws from two primary sources: (1) the Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument Economic Impact Report (BBC Research & Consulting, August 2023), prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling; and (2) the BLM Las Cruces District Office Annual Manager’s Report for FY2024. Together, these documents establish that the Las Cruces gateway economy already receives substantial visitor traffic that generates meaningful food-and-beverage demand — and that the market’s existing programming infrastructure successfully converts visitor attention into downtown commercial activity.
Q.2 OMDPNM Economic Impact — Key Figures (2022)
The following figures are drawn from BBC Research & Consulting (2023), “A Decade of Opportunity: How the Designation of Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument is Boosting Southern New Mexico’s Economy,” using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling for Doña Ana and Luna Counties:
Total annual economic impact (2022): $35.0 million, including direct and secondary effects
Total non-local visitor spending (2022): $29.9 million within 50 miles of the Monument
Restaurant spending by non-local visitors (2022): $6.2 million (calculated from Figure 8 spending category breakdown: day visitors $257,589; overnight non-facility $441,606; overnight commercial $2,582,440; overnight non-participating $2,930,621)
Jobs supported in Doña Ana and Luna Counties (2022): 305
Tax revenues generated (2022): $1.9 million for local, county, and state governments
Total cumulative economic impact since designation (2014–2022): $234 million
Annual visitation trend: 183,900 (2012, pre-designation) → 612,781 (2022) → 613,645 (FY2024, BLM) — more than tripling and holding steady, exceeding original predictions by 51%
73% of non-local visitors cited OMDPNM as the primary reason for their visit to the Las Cruces area
Q.3 Hub Implications
The OMDPNM data establishes three facts directly relevant to the Hub’s demand case:

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.heading: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.text:
Visitor restaurant spending is already $6.2 million annually from monument visitors alone, before accounting for the 2.5 million total out-of-market visitors documented by Placer. This is not speculative demand — it is documented, recurring restaurant revenue from people already in the Las Cruces market who have no dedicated destination dining venue to visit.
Las Cruces responds to programmed experiences. The BLM FY2024 Manager’s Report documents 19 guided hikes, an archaeological fair, a 10th-anniversary celebration with 948 attendees, a girls’ outdoor camp, and social media reach of over half a million people. Visit Las Cruces has built “Monuments to Main Street” to channel this engagement into local business activity. The Hub’s weekly events, monthly cultural festivals, and quarterly signature events are the commercial counterpart of this proven community engagement model.
The economic multiplier is real. OMDPNM’s $29.9 million in direct non-local visitor spending generated $35.0 million in total economic impact — a 1.17x multiplier. The Hub operates at the direct-spending layer of this same economy. Every dollar captured at the Hub from monument visitors, I-10 travelers, or regional day-trippers represents new money to the Las Cruces economy, not a reallocation from an existing restaurant.
Q.4 Marketing Partnership Opportunity
The Hub should pursue a formal co-marketing relationship with Visit Las Cruces’ Monuments to Main Street (M2M) program, which already routes monument visitors into downtown businesses. Tactical actions: (1) apply for inclusion in the M2M business directory before Grand Opening; (2) propose a “Trails to Tables” promotion that pairs monument hiking events with Hub dining reservations; (3) schedule Hub cultural events during peak monument visitation periods (May anniversary, holiday weekend hikes); (4) co-brand the Hub cider bar’s NM craft cider program with the local outdoor identity — “Hike the monument, drink the cider.”

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
chunks.text:
Concept and Strategic Purpose
The Hub will include a dedicated gift shop and retail merchandising area positioned near the main exit or along the primary circulation path. Rather than a generic souvenir space, it functions as a curated retail extension of the Hub’s culinary identity — allowing guests to take home signature flavors, branded products, local pantry goods, and meal kits inspired by the vendors inside. It is treated as a formal ancillary profit center, not a side amenity.
The retail program supports the Hub's business model in four concrete ways: it diversifies revenue alongside stall license fees, commissary income, beverage sales, and event programming; it deepens guest engagement by allowing customers to continue interacting with Hub brands at home; it strengthens destination appeal for tourists and regional visitors seeking New Mexico food products and locally rooted culinary gifts; and it creates a legally managed retail incubator shelf for vendor-tested packaged products under the vendor license agreement.
Retail Product Mix — Five Categories
1. Vendor-Branded Experience Kits
The signature retail category: branded kits tied to the Hub’s core restaurant concepts that recreate a vendor’s signature flavor profile at home. Each kit includes a marinade pouch, sauce, seasoning blend, recipe card, and one or two supporting pantry items. These kits give the Hub a distinct retail identity, create strong gifting and repeat-purchase opportunities, and extend brand loyalty beyond the dining visit. Examples include a Hub Signature wings kit, a Southern BBQ dry rub set, a green chile seasoning kit, and a NM cider pairing box.
2. Vendor Washout and Graduate Alumni Products

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
chunks.text:
The gift shop serves a dual incubator function. For vendors who exit the incubator before graduation, the shop provides a structured outlet for remaining branded or shelf-stable inventory, recovering value that would otherwise be lost. For successful graduates who move into independent restaurants, the shop becomes a permanent “Hub Alumni” showcase — graduates can continue selling packaged sauces, spice blends, baking mixes, and signature pantry items under a dedicated alumni designation. This reinforces the incubator’s credibility, keeps successful brands visible in the ecosystem, and allows the Hub to participate in the economic upside of its graduate brands after they leave physical stall space.
3. Local and Regional New Mexico Pantry Goods
A curated selection of NM and borderland pantry staples that align naturally with the Hub’s culinary identity and tourism profile: Hatch chile products, local hot sauces, honey, biscochito mixes, piñon coffee, prickly pear goods, and regional apple products from the Sacramento Mountains and Velarde orchards (consistent with the cider bar’s heritage storytelling). This category strengthens community positioning and creates cross-promotional opportunities with regional producers — many of whom will already be supplying the Hub’s vendor stalls.
4. Bottled Sauces, Marinades, and Spice Blends
Smaller-format, high-turn retail items — bottled sauces, spice blends, dry rubs, and marinade pouches — inspired by individual vendor concepts. Marinade-in-a-bag formats are familiar to customers, easy to merchandise near point of exit, and naturally tied to the food experiences inside the hall. These create a low-barrier impulse purchase for first-time buyers and strong repeat-purchase behavior for regulars.
5. Branded Merchandise and Kitchen Tools

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.heading: 5.5 Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising
chunks.text:
A modest, carefully edited selection of practical branded merchandise: aprons, tote bags, mugs, recipe booklets, and simple cooking tools. These should not dominate the assortment but contribute to average transaction size and create additional branding opportunities for event attendees, tourists, and Cider Club members. Merchandise should carry the Hub’s branding and reflect the culinary identity — not generic promotional items.
Operating Model
The gift shop is compact, curated, and low-labor. Positioned near the main exit along the primary circulation path, it captures impulse purchases from guests who have already formed a strong flavor memory during their visit. The assortment launches deliberately limited — the most distinctive, highest-margin, and easiest-to-explain items first — and expands as vendor relationships deepen and sales data confirms winners. Branded kits and pantry items can be assembled in the Hub’s commissary or back-of-house prep space; locally sourced packaged goods are purchased wholesale from regional suppliers. Inventory is reviewed quarterly to maintain freshness, protect margins, and avoid SKU complexity.
The retail program does not cannibalize stall-level food sales because it serves different use occasions — gifting, home cooking, pantry stocking, and tourism purchases — rather than competing for the same immediate dining decision. When properly merchandised, it adds revenue without adding the labor and infrastructure burden of another full restaurant stall.
Revenue Projections
At conservative assumptions — 30% of daily visitors purchasing one gift shop item at an average of $18 — and an estimated 200 visits/day in Year 1, the gift shop generates approximately $18,000–$35,000 in gross retail revenue annually. At Year 2 volume (300 visits/day, higher tourist penetration from OMDPNM and M2M co-marketing), the program scales to $30,000–$55,000/year. At 50–65% gross margins on branded kits and pantry goods, net contribution is meaningfully positive with minimal incremental labor. These figures are included in the financial model as a discrete revenue line under “Gift Shop and Retail Merchandising.”

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.heading: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.text:
Strategic Purpose
The Hub’s Tabski POS handles the back-end of multi-vendor ordering — automated percentage-rent collection, per-stall KDS routing, and unified sales reporting. The mobile ordering platform is the consumer-facing layer on top of that infrastructure: a guest app that allows customers to browse all vendor menus, place pickup and to-go orders from multiple stalls in a single digital transaction, and manage loyalty rewards — all before or during their visit. The two systems work together. Tabski handles vendor-side operations; the app handles the guest relationship.
The platform is treated as core operating infrastructure, not a convenience feature. It materially expands the Hub’s revenue capture, improves throughput, and strengthens the long-term customer relationship in ways that a counter-only ordering model cannot replicate.
Operational Benefits
Throughput: Pre-queued digital orders reduce counter congestion during lunch rushes and weekend peaks. Vendors receive orders via KDS before guests arrive, allowing preparation to begin immediately. For a 13-stall hall with simultaneous peak demand, this meaningfully improves throughput and perceived wait time without adding staff.
Order Accuracy: Digital orders eliminate verbal miscommunication at the counter. Modifications, allergen flags, and special instructions are captured in writing and routed directly to the stall’s kitchen display screen, reducing waste and remakes.
Forecasting and Labor: Digital order history creates reliable demand data for vendors: which items sell by day, time, and weather; when to prep more; when to reduce. This data is valuable for coaching conversations during monthly P&L reviews and for optimizing labor scheduling across peak and off-peak periods.
Revenue Impact
Off-Premise Expansion: Pickup and to-go ordering captures revenue from customers who prefer not to dine in — NMSU students ordering between classes, downtown office workers on compressed lunch breaks, families with young children, and El Paso day-trippers who want to grab food before heading home on I-10. These customers represent genuine demand that a walk-up counter alone cannot efficiently serve.

chunks.documentTitle: Las Cruces Culinary Innovation Hub Comprehensive Business Plan
chunks.sectionTitle: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.heading: 6.4 Mobile Ordering and Digital Commerce Platform
chunks.text:
Higher Average Ticket: Digital ordering naturally supports upsells, combo suggestions, and add-ons (“Add a cider flight? Add a gift shop item to your pickup?”) that counter staff cannot consistently execute during busy periods. Industry data across multi-vendor food halls consistently shows 12–18% higher average ticket on digital vs. counter orders.
Direct Revenue from Platform: A modest convenience fee on digital orders (e.g., $0.50–$1.00 per transaction) generates direct Hub revenue. At 30–50 digital orders per day in Year 1 (15–25% of estimated daily transactions), this produces $5,000–$15,000 annually — a small but incremental contribution that scales with volume.
Cross-Category Integration
The platform’s value compounds across the Hub’s other revenue streams. It can sell gift shop products (Section 5.5) for add-on or standalone retail pickup. It can manage event pre-sales and Cider Club member early access. It can push targeted promotions tied to seasonal vendor menus, new incubator launches, and OMDPNM-tied tourism campaigns (e.g., “Order ahead for your post-hike lunch”). This cross-category capability makes the app a unified customer engagement platform, not a single-function ordering utility.
Loyalty and Retention
The app creates a durable post-visit relationship through loyalty rewards, digital offers, and push notifications tied to events, seasonal menus, and new vendor launches. Unlike a walk-up customer who leaves no data, an app user creates an identifiable profile that the Hub can engage repeatedly. For a destination food hall in a smaller metro like Las Cruces, converting a first-time visitor into a regular depends on staying top of mind between visits — and a loyalty-linked app is the most cost-effective tool available for that job.
Tabski Integration Note

chunks.sectionTitle: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.heading: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.text:
Q.1 Purpose of This Supplement
This supplement documents the regional tourism context that supports the Hub’s visitor demand assumptions. It draws from two primary sources: (1) the Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument Economic Impact Report (BBC Research & Consulting, August 2023), prepared for the Las Cruces Green Chamber of Commerce using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling; and (2) the BLM Las Cruces District Office Annual Manager’s Report for FY2024. Together, these documents establish that the Las Cruces gateway economy already receives substantial visitor traffic that generates meaningful food-and-beverage demand — and that the market’s existing programming infrastructure successfully converts visitor attention into downtown commercial activity.
Q.2 OMDPNM Economic Impact — Key Figures (2022)
The following figures are drawn from BBC Research & Consulting (2023), “A Decade of Opportunity: How the Designation of Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument is Boosting Southern New Mexico’s Economy,” using IMPLAN regional input-output modeling for Doña Ana and Luna Counties:
Total annual economic impact (2022): $35.0 million, including direct and secondary effects
Total non-local visitor spending (2022): $29.9 million within 50 miles of the Monument
Restaurant spending by non-local visitors (2022): $6.2 million (calculated from Figure 8 spending category breakdown: day visitors $257,589; overnight non-facility $441,606; overnight commercial $2,582,440; overnight non-participating $2,930,621)
Jobs supported in Doña Ana and Luna Counties (2022): 305
Tax revenues generated (2022): $1.9 million for local, county, and state governments
Total cumulative economic impact since designation (2014–2022): $234 million
Annual visitation trend: 183,900 (2012, pre-designation) → 612,781 (2022) → 613,645 (FY2024, BLM) — more than tripling and holding steady, exceeding original predictions by 51%
73% of non-local visitors cited OMDPNM as the primary reason for their visit to the Las Cruces area
Q.3 Hub Implications
The OMDPNM data establishes three facts directly relevant to the Hub’s demand case:

chunks.sectionTitle: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.heading: Supplement Q: Regional Tourism Context — Organ Mountains–Desert Peaks National Monument and Las Cruces Visitor Economy
chunks.text:
Visitor restaurant spending is already $6.2 million annually from monument visitors alone, before accounting for the 2.5 million total out-of-market visitors documented by Placer. This is not speculative demand — it is documented, recurring restaurant revenue from people already in the Las Cruces market who have no dedicated destination dining venue to visit.
Las Cruces responds to programmed experiences. The BLM FY2024 Manager’s Report documents 19 guided hikes, an archaeological fair, a 10th-anniversary celebration with 948 attendees, a girls’ outdoor camp, and social media reach of over half a million people. Visit Las Cruces has built “Monuments to Main Street” to channel this engagement into local business activity. The Hub’s weekly events, monthly cultural festivals, and quarterly signature events are the commercial counterpart of this proven community engagement model.
The economic multiplier is real. OMDPNM’s $29.9 million in direct non-local visitor spending generated $35.0 million in total economic impact — a 1.17x multiplier. The Hub operates at the direct-spending layer of this same economy. Every dollar captured at the Hub from monument visitors, I-10 travelers, or regional day-trippers represents new money to the Las Cruces economy, not a reallocation from an existing restaurant.
Q.4 Marketing Partnership Opportunity
The Hub should pursue a formal co-marketing relationship with Visit Las Cruces’ Monuments to Main Street (M2M) program, which already routes monument visitors into downtown businesses. Tactical actions: (1) apply for inclusion in the M2M business directory before Grand Opening; (2) propose a “Trails to Tables” promotion that pairs monument hiking events with Hub dining reservations; (3) schedule Hub cultural events during peak monument visitation periods (May anniversary, holiday weekend hikes); (4) co-brand the Hub cider bar’s NM craft cider program with the local outdoor identity — “Hike the monument, drink the cider.”

This food hall incubator operations playbook is an operations and planning document, not legal advice. New Mexico Environment Department, City of Las Cruces, fire/building officials, New Mexico Regulation and Licensing Department Alcoholic Beverage Control Division, New Mexico Taxation and Revenue, employment agencies, insurers, and applicable professional advisers control final requirements.

chunks.heading: 1.1 New Mexico Incubator Benchmark - SVEDC
chunks.text:
The South Valley Economic Development Center (SVEDC) in Albuquerque is a useful New Mexico benchmark for the Las Cruces Culinary Hub because it combines economic development, commercial kitchen access, food-business incubation, business advising, partner networks, and measurable community outcomes. SVEDC is an initiative of the Rio Grande Community Development Corporation, a 501(c)(3), and was created through a public-private partnership with Bernalillo County. Its public materials describe support for healthy economic development in the South Valley since 2005.
SVEDC's food business incubation structure is especially relevant because it separates early concept validation from later-stage incubation. Its incubation programs are described as a safe environment for new and emerging entrepreneurs, supported by experienced mentors, partner organizations, staff guidance, and facility amenities. Its two named program pathways are Semilla for early-stage entrepreneurs and Mariposa for food-industry businesses that are ready to scale with facility, equipment, and guidance support.

3.3A SVEDC-Informed Academy Option
SVEDC's Semilla Program provides a more intensive benchmark than a short pre-incubator course. Public materials describe Semilla as a 6-month, approximately 24-week pathway built around the sequence Validate, Verify, Launch. It combines one-on-one support, online reference guides, videos, readings, practical worksheets, cohort networking, mentorship opportunities, and clear benchmarks. SVEDC states that participants either validate and launch or gain enough clarity to make a low-cost decision not to proceed.
For the Las Cruces Culinary Hub, the Food Entrepreneur Academy can operate in two tiers: an 8-12 week launch-readiness version for vendors close to stall placement, and a deeper 24-week concept-validation version for early-stage entrepreneurs who need more time before taking on food hall operating obligations.

1. Overview and Purpose

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text:
A commercial kitchen is a licensed food-production environment designed to prepare, cook, cool, hold, package, serve, or distribute food under controlled sanitary conditions. In a shared-use kitchen, multiple operators may use the facility under assigned schedules and rules. In a restaurant-style kitchen, one operating team may support several menu lines, service periods, catering orders, retail products, and events.
The operating goals are food safety, consistency, efficiency, compliance, accountability, and scalability. Every workflow should identify the responsible person, required records, dependencies, and critical control points. The kitchen should be able to prove not only that food was produced, but that it was produced under a controlled system.
Operating Goal
Required System
Evidence
Food safety
Active managerial control, training, temperature control, separation, sanitation, corrective action.
Logs, inspection reports, training files, incident reports.
Consistency
Standard recipes, prep sheets, batch controls, portion tools, plate/package standards.
Recipe cards, batch sheets, manager line checks.
Efficiency
Logical layout, station readiness, accurate par levels, clear ticket/service flow, maintenance planning.
Prep lists, production schedules, shift notes, KPI review.
Compliance

Compliance binder and digital backup.
Shared-use accountability
User agreements, storage assignments, schedules, cleaning verification, damage/incident reporting.
Vendor files, access logs, cleaning logs, chargebacks if applicable.
2. Physical Layout and Workflow
The preferred flow is receiving -> storage -> prep -> cooking -> cooling/reheating/holding -> plating/service/packaging -> dishwashing/cleaning. Layout decisions should reduce cross-traffic, backtracking, and ambiguity. Raw food, ready-to-eat food, allergens, chemicals, dirty wares, waste, and clean equipment should have clearly separated paths whenever feasible.
