chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 2.1 Layout and Adjacency Principles
chunks.text:
Receiving should connect quickly to storage without routing deliveries through active plating or customer-facing service.
Raw animal protein prep should be physically or procedurally separated from ready-to-eat prep, bakery, packaging, and allergen-sensitive work.
Clean wares should exit dishwashing into protected storage, not into the dirty dish return path.
Chemicals and maintenance supplies must be stored away from food, food-contact surfaces, single-service items, and retail products.
Shared-use kitchens need visible storage assignments, user-specific labels, and scheduling rules to prevent operators from using one another's ingredients or tools.
Allergen-sensitive production should be scheduled, tooled, labeled, and cleaned with extra control; where possible, produce allergen-sensitive batches before allergen-heavy batches.
Staff circulation should not force cooks to cross dish return, trash, or mop-sink areas while carrying finished food.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.sectionTitle: 2.2 New Mexico Shared-Kitchen Benchmark - The Kitchen Table Santa Fe
chunks.heading: 2.2 New Mexico Shared-Kitchen Benchmark - The Kitchen Table Santa Fe
chunks.text:
The Kitchen Table Santa Fe provides a practical New Mexico benchmark for shared commercial kitchen planning. Its public materials describe an accessible, affordable commercial kitchen for food entrepreneurs with 2,500 square feet of cooking and prep space, 14 rentable workstations, 24-hour/7-day access, a hot kitchen, two prep kitchens, dry storage lockers, walk-in refrigeration, walk-in freezer storage, personal lockers, dishwashing, freeze dryers, and event/pop-up dining capacity. The facility opened in May 2023 and reports 34 current members.
For the Las Cruces Culinary Hub, the useful lesson is not to copy Santa Fe pricing or site design exactly. The transferable operating model is the combination of membership onboarding, required compliance documents, flexible storage add-ons, 24/7 scheduling controls, commercial-grade equipment, on-site management, security monitoring, deep cleaning, waste/grease handling, recycling/composting, and event-space integration.
KTSF Benchmark Detail
Operational Use for Las Cruces Culinary Hub
Membership model with monthly included hours and add-on hours
Use member tiers or vendor usage plans to control access, forecast labor/utilities, and prevent informal kitchen use.
Required member agreement and security deposit
Require a signed kitchen use agreement, rules acknowledgment, and deposit before access is granted.
Food Manager certificate requirement
Keep manager-level food safety certification records in each vendor/operator file.
CRS number requirement
Require New Mexico business tax registration evidence before commercial kitchen use.
Health department food permit requirement
Do not allow public food production until the operator's permit path is confirmed.
Commercial general liability insurance with additional insured requirement
Collect certificates of insurance and additional insured language before facility access.
Local business license requirement
Require Las Cruces or applicable municipal business registration before regular operations.
24-hour access, video-monitored security, and scheduling via The Food Corridor
Use controlled access, scheduling software, and camera/security policies for shared-use accountability.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.sectionTitle: 2.2 New Mexico Shared-Kitchen Benchmark - The Kitchen Table Santa Fe
chunks.heading: 2.2 New Mexico Shared-Kitchen Benchmark - The Kitchen Table Santa Fe
chunks.text:
A la carte dry, refrigerated, freezer, and reach-in storage
Price and assign storage separately from kitchen time; label all storage by operator.
Event space and pop-up dining room
Design the kitchen to support classes, pop-ups, tastings, vendor showcases, and sponsor/community events.
Commercial Kitchen Equipment Planning Notes From KTSF
KTSF's published equipment list is useful as a planning reference for a shared kitchen that supports diverse operators. Relevant categories include mixers, tilting kettle, tilting skillet/braising pan, ice machines, worktop refrigeration, walk-in refrigerator, walk-in freezer, low-temperature dishwasher with pre-rinse, three-compartment and two-compartment sinks, hand sinks, stainless work tables, double convection ovens, gas ranges, charbroiler, utility carts, mop sink area, and freeze dryers.
The Hub should treat this as a benchmark equipment palette, then right-size equipment by menu mix, vendor count, production volume, utility capacity, ventilation, cleaning load, and NMED/plan-review requirements. Specialty equipment such as freeze dryers should be justified by vendor demand, retail product strategy, training value, and maintenance cost.
3. Regulatory Compliance and Food Safety
New Mexico food operations should confirm permit class, plan-review expectations, inspection requirements, food handler/manager records, and operational rules with NMED or the applicable local authority before opening. This manual uses FDA Food Code and HACCP concepts as operating standards, but New Mexico rules and local permit conditions control.
Compliance Topic
New Mexico Planning Claim
Operational Requirement
Food establishment permit
Retail food establishments and related food operations generally require NMED/local permit review under New Mexico food rules.
Confirm permit class before buildout; maintain permit and inspection records.
Food code basis

chunks.sectionTitle: 7.6.2.8 NMAC incorporates the 2017 FDA Food Code with New Mexico modifications.
chunks.heading: 7.6.2.8 NMAC incorporates the 2017 FDA Food Code with New Mexico modifications.
chunks.text:
Train to local requirements, not generic national assumptions.
Certified Food Protection Manager
New Mexico rules address CFPM expectations for covered establishments, subject to exceptions/agency interpretation.
At least one supervisory food-safety manager should maintain current certification before opening.
Food handler records
Food handler cards or approved training records must be maintained where required and available for inspection.
Collect records before staff or vendor users work in the kitchen.
Mobile or temporary food
Mobile units and temporary food events have separate rule considerations.
Do not use food truck/pop-up operations without confirming permit path.
Manufactured/packaged food
Packaged or processed foods may trigger manufactured-food/labeling requirements.
Gift shop products need approval, labels, records, and vendor responsibility terms.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 3.1 Active Managerial Control
chunks.text:
Active managerial control means the facility anticipates food safety risks and controls them before inspection or complaint. The Person in Charge should be able to explain what hazards exist, how they are controlled, where the records are, and what corrective action occurs when a standard is missed.
Maintain current permit, inspection, training, and log records in a compliance file.
Review logs during each shift rather than filing them unread.
Train staff to stop production and notify a manager when temperatures, sanitation, illness, allergen, pest, or equipment standards fail.
Use corrective action records to show what happened, who was notified, what food was retained/discarded, and how recurrence will be prevented.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 3.2 HACCP-Style Control System
chunks.text:
Principle
Implementation in This Kitchen
Hazard analysis
Evaluate biological, chemical, physical, and allergen hazards for each menu item, process, and retail product.
Critical control points
Identify receiving, cold holding, cooking, cooling, reheating, hot holding, packaging, and sanitation points where loss of control matters.
Critical limits
Use local code, approved process, validated recipe, or manufacturer instructions for time/temperature and sanitation limits.
Monitoring
Assign who checks, when they check, what tool they use, and where the result is recorded.
Corrective action
Define discard, reheat, rapid cool, relabel, stop sale, retrain, repair, or notify authority steps.
Verification
Manager reviews records, observes behavior, calibrates thermometers, and validates corrective actions.
Recordkeeping
Keep logs long enough to satisfy agency, insurance, grant, and internal quality needs.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.sectionTitle: 3.3 Employee Health, Allergen, and Inspection Readiness
chunks.heading: 3.3 Employee Health, Allergen, and Inspection Readiness
chunks.text:
Employee health: staff must know when symptoms, diagnoses, or exposure risks must be reported to the Person in Charge under applicable food code rules.
Allergens: menu, prep, service, and packaging systems must identify major allergens and prevent accidental cross-contact where allergen claims are made.
Thermometers: each critical station should have an accurate, clean, calibrated thermometer or assigned temperature device.
Sanitizer: sanitizer concentration must be verified with the correct test strips or device at setup and during use.
Inspection readiness: permits, CFPM/food handler records, logs, pest records, cleaning schedules, and corrective actions should be available without delay.
4. Daily Operations Workflow

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 4.1 Opening Workflow
chunks.text:
Person in Charge performs facility walk-through: security, odors, pests, leaks, refrigeration alarms, standing water, utility status, and equipment condition.
Log refrigeration/freezer temperatures before food is moved or deliveries are accepted.
Set hand sinks, sanitizer stations, prep surfaces, dish machine/three-sink setup, and waste stations.
Start equipment only according to manufacturer and safety instructions; confirm hood/ventilation before heat-producing equipment is used.
Review schedule, operator bookings, prep lists, special events, allergens, maintenance notes, and expected deliveries.
Assign staff by station and identify the manager authorized to make food safety corrective decisions.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 4.2 Receiving Workflow
chunks.text:
Receiver matches delivery to order guide and approved supplier list.
Inspect vehicle and packaging condition where practical; prioritize refrigerated, frozen, and hot-held items.
Measure and record temperatures for TCS items using a clean thermometer or approved method.
Reject unsafe temperature, damaged packaging, spoilage, pest evidence, unapproved substitution, missing label, or questionable product.
Label accepted goods with date received, owner/operator, use-by date where applicable, and allergen note if needed.
Move cold/frozen products immediately to assigned storage; do not allow deliveries to sit in prep aisles.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 4.3 Storage Workflow
chunks.text:
Use FIFO and visible date labels; shorter shelf-life products move first even if received later.
Store raw animal products below ready-to-eat foods and separate by cooking risk hierarchy.
Keep allergen-heavy ingredients and chemicals from contaminating common prep or retail products.
Shared-use operators may use only assigned storage unless management approves temporary overflow.
Unlabeled, expired, leaking, or unassigned product is documented and discarded or quarantined under policy.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.sectionTitle: 4.4 Prep, Cooking, Cooling, Reheating, and Holding
chunks.heading: 4.4 Prep, Cooking, Cooling, Reheating, and Holding
chunks.text:
Step
Required Practice
Critical Control Point
Prep
Work from approved prep list and recipe; sanitize surfaces; label all batches.
Time out of temperature control, allergen cross-contact, tool sanitation.
Cooking
Cook to approved internal standard and recipe specification; verify with thermometer where required.
Critical cooking limit and corrective action if not met.
Cooling
Use shallow pans, small batches, ice baths, blast chillers if available, and active monitoring.
Cooling time/temperature and log completion.
Reheating
Reheat rapidly to approved standard before hot holding unless local rule/process says otherwise.
Reheat limit and time control.
Hot/cold holding
Use functioning equipment; monitor on schedule; correct immediately if out of range.
Holding temperature, time marking, discard decision.
Packaging/service
Protect food from contamination; verify label/allergen and order accuracy.
Final quality and allergen check.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.sectionTitle: 4.5 Dishwashing, Cleaning, Closing, and Manager Handoff
chunks.heading: 4.5 Dishwashing, Cleaning, Closing, and Manager Handoff
chunks.text:
Separate dirty return from clean storage and food production; scrape and pre-rinse only in assigned areas.
Wash, rinse, sanitize, and air dry; do not towel-dry food-contact items unless approved by procedure.
Clean food-contact surfaces first, then non-food-contact surfaces, then floors, drains, trash, and mop areas.
Store retained food safely with complete labels; discard food that lacks safe time/temperature or identity control.
Manager verifies logs, trash, grease, chemicals, refrigeration, security, and next-day prep notes.
Handoff report records shortages, maintenance needs, incidents, rejected deliveries, waste, and corrective actions.
5. Inventory and Purchasing
Inventory must protect cash and compliance. The kitchen should use approved vendors, order guides, par levels, receiving standards, and variance tracking. Shared-use facilities also need owner/operator labels so inventory responsibility is never ambiguous.
Tool
How It Works

Weekly; after menu change.

Monthly.

Daily/weekly review.

Every shared-use item has owner/operator, date, product name, and storage location.
Each shift.
6. Equipment and Maintenance
Maintenance is part of food safety. Refrigeration, hot holding, dishwashing, ventilation, fire suppression, grease management, and water systems directly affect safe operation.

chunks.documentTitle: Commercial Kitchen Operations Manual
chunks.heading: 6.1 Utility and Equipment Failure Response
chunks.text:
Power outage: keep cold storage closed, start time tracking, protect food, and follow local authority/insurance guidance before reopening.
Refrigeration failure: move food to verified alternate cold holding, log temperatures, quarantine questionable product, call service vendor.
Hood/fire suppression issue: stop heat-producing equipment under the affected hood until safe operation is confirmed.
Water interruption: stop operations that require handwashing, warewashing, produce washing, cooking water, or sanitation until approved alternate procedures are in place.
Grease interceptor issue: stop operations contributing to overflow or backup; protect food areas and call service provider.

9. Risk Management and Contingencies
Event
Immediate Action
Documentation / Follow-Up
Suspected foodborne illness
Notify manager, preserve records, identify food/time/staff, follow authority guidance.
Incident report, menu/batch/log review, agency communication.

Stop use/sale, isolate product/equipment, clean/sanitize, decide discard with manager.
Corrective action, disposal log, retraining.
Injury
Stop work if needed, provide first aid, secure hazard, notify manager.
Incident/injury report, workers' comp process if applicable.
Pest activity
Protect food, clean affected area, call pest provider, seal/repair source.

Chemical spill
Isolate, use SDS/PPE, prevent food contact, discard exposed food.
Incident report and storage review.

Activate emergency plan, evacuate if needed, shut down equipment if safe.
